text: A memorandum in the first person singular on travel expenses in copper for what seem to be two different trips. The text was already used in Geography, where lines 1-23 are quoted in footnotes 1243//1432 and 1479.

text: 22. The sign KIB with the value /dur4/ seems to be used here for /tuhx/. Its shape is similar to that in *146:23.25 (Dur4-hu-mì-id), which suggest they were written by the same scribe. Forlanini 2012, 297 doubts whether the reading Tuhx-pì-a in our text, important evidence for its location between Wahšušana (which he would like to locate near Ankara) and Durhumit, is justified. The writing is indeed unique (the occurrence in Kt a/k 253b:27, mentioned in Geography footnote 1241, is uncertain and the context does not favor a place-name), but the reading seems probable, considering the occasional ‘creative’ use of signs by OA writers and because no town called D/Turpiya is known. The fact that expenses in copper from Wahšušana to what I take as Tuh/piya were 1½ mina of copper and from Tuh/piya until Durhumit twice as much, 3 minas, corresponds with the distances between Durhumit, Tuhpiya and Wahšušana, as drawn on Barjamovic’s map.

text: Barjamovic in Geography uses our text as an important source for the reconstruction of the geography of the area east and west of the middle course of the Kızılırmak, with the cities Tuhpiya, Wahšušana and Šaladuwar. He assumes that Wahšušana is located east of the Kızılırmak and north of the Tuz Gölü, possibly at the crossing of the river at Büklükale, on whose lower terrace pottery sherds of the kārum level II type were found (personal communication M.T. Larsen). If so it is situated on the copper route that ran from Durhumit to Burušhattum, at the point where a crossroad east of the Kızılırmak and a road from Kanesh met (Geography 307 with note 1243, where he also adduces VS 26, 66:3-15; see the separate folding map “Anatolia ca. 1880 BC”, added to Geography). On p. 354f., with note 1479, he uses our text also as evidence that the copper road coming from Wahšušana passed through Šaladuwar (across the Sahiriya river) before reaching Burušhattum, located further to the south-west, possibly in the area east of Hittite Kuwaliya and north of the Sultan Daǧ, near Bolvadın (see his map 20). Forlanini 2012, rejects these last proposals (including the location of Durhumit) and we have to wait for a further evaluation of the facts, hopefully helped by new textual or archaeological data. During the recent excavations by Mrs M. Omura on the tepe of Büklükale, under some later deposits thus far only architecture from the Early Bronze Age has been exposed (personal communication). Excavation of the lower river terrace (mentioned above) might provide valuable textual evidence, to confirm or disprove Barjamovic’s and Forlanini’s proposed identification with Wahšušana or Durhumit.

text: 1. I take buṭnātum as "pistachio trees", a word not yet attested in Old Assyrian. While its occurrence in Anatolia is not surprising (see now buṭnātim Burušhaddêtim in T. 125:16f., from Mari, cf. J.-M Durand, in Studies Veenhof, 2001, 130), the use of an Assyrian name is, since Assyrians normally use native Anatolian town names The writer may have translated an Anatolian name or he himself may have called the village after a prominent local feature, its trees. This might explain why it is not a real place name, but a designation of the type "the town of..." (āl ...), used in combination with a personal or divine name, a gentilic, or a noun referring to a specific local feature. Cf. āl Kupilšan (our text lines 17f.), āl I-a-ša (Ka 1113:4, usually contracted to A-li-a-ša cf. CCT 2, 39:26 and now R. Kuzuoǧlu, ArAn 7 (2004) 75ff.), āl ZI-ZI-im, "the town of ....." (RGTC 4, 7, with discussion), āl dUTU, "the town of the sungod" (RGTC 4, 7), āl iṣṣurātim, "the town of the birds" (AKT 5, 56:3), āl tí-im-ni-e, "the town of ......." AKT 5, 20:18 and 21:16). The latter is perhaps a gentilic, comparable to ālum ša Hatti’ē (KTS 1, 8a:4f.), and especially to āl Kà-ni-ší-e/i, "the town of the Kaneshites", now attested in *149:14f. and *151:6.

text: 10. There are several references to bridges (titurrum), most probably only for smaller rivers, see Copper 13, and Geography 22ff. They are mentioned both as topographical landmarks (KTP 26:2ff., wages paid to a transporter "until the bridge"; Kt m/k 127:5f., an escort "which went until the bridge") and as a facility for the use of which (ana t., Kt n/k 1582:8), “at which” (ina t., Kt t/k 25:10) or “for the cost of which” (ana ša t., Kt m/k 127: 8) a fee had to be paid. Bridges of course also made ideal tolls, hence in AKT 3, 34:7, "they levied a toll of 20 shekels (of copper) per donkey at the bridge" (ina titurrim ... issuhū). See for a possible (wooden) bridge over the Kızılırmak in the vicinity of Šamuha, Geography 152f.

text: 6. I do not know what bar’āum means. The verb could have the silver as object and the kaššum as dativus commodi, but it seems more likely that it was used independently and figures as explanation for the consumption of 10 shekels of silver in Kanesh. A meaning “to be delayed / to have to wait” could link the verb semantically with the verb bitrû / šutabrû “to last long” , of which CAD B 280.2 quotes one OA occurrence (CCT 3, 44a:18), to which we can now add POAT 8:47 (iṣṣēr ša panîtim tuštabriam) and perhaps a Š-stem in Kt h/k 73 (aṣṣer ša GN ušabra’akim). text: 15-20. The trip started in Wahšušana and apparently ended in Assur (l. 19), which is only mentioned when the total costs for food are summarized. The only expense listed for the long last stage of the trip, after crossing the Euhprates near Hahhum, is a payment for the inn in Burullum (= Burallum in *149:10). This was an important road-station that occurs in several OA “itineraries”[1] and is also known from texts from Mari and Tell Leilan. It was located on the west Bank of the Tigris, east of Tell Leilan / Šubat-Enlil in the area where we also find Habura and Mardaman.[2]

text: The following two records, already published in Veenhof 2008b as nos. 2 and 5, concern shipments of merchandise belonging to Šu-Ištar and Iddin-Suen, who occur several times in records listing (shipments of) textiles (*316, *319, *317). In the account *320 Iddin-Suen is the owner of a shipment of nearly hundred textiles and the statement on how many of these were given as import-tax and pre-empted shows that they were imports that had arrived from Assur. The two records of travel expenses published here must refer to similar but bigger shipments, for the textiles mentioned in *320 imply a load with a value of only ca. 1 talent and 40 minas of tin. The lists of textiles, in which our two traders figure together with several others, indicate that these men had joined forces by entrusting their loads to a collective caravan (ellutum), whose leader upon arrival settled accounts with them for the costs of transport and clearance in the local palace on the basis of the ”declared value” of their share in the shipment.

text: The writer, leader of a caravan, paid in all 41 minas 15 shekels of tin (l. 4), obviously, as parallels show, for the ‘road-tax” (da’atum) and in this case also for buying fodder. The statement in lines 22f. is surprising, because the tariff of lines 22-23, when applied to a load with a value of 8 talents 16½ minas of tin, yields only ca. 31⅓ minas, which is neither the figure of lines 4 - 41¼ minas - nor that of lines 19 - 34½ minas, the “loose tin” that the transporter had received. The difference could be explained by deducting from the figure of l. 4 the unknown cost of fodder that was included or by adding the additional expenses itemized in lines 6-15, due to the loss of a donkey (apparently repaired by hiring one for the final stages of the trip) which, together with the straw bought in Kanesh (for the donkeys?), amounted to 8 shekels of tin and 11¾ shekels of silver (equivalent to ca. 1½ minas of tin). This still does not explain the totals mentioned, but it is clear that the transporter – as happened frequently – had not enough “loose tin” available to meet all the costs and had to be reimbursed on the basis of this account for what he himself had advanced. The amount paid for the road-tax and for fodder according to lines 1-4 amounts to c. 8,6% of the value of the load, which compares well with that of *151, where it is c. 8,1 %, also “including the fodder”. These percentages are too high for a journey from the crossing of the Euphrates to Kanesh and must cover the whole trip from Assur,[3] but they presumably were not specified for the first stage, because no specific, additional expenses were incurred.

text: Texts 146-151 were first published in Veenhof 2006 and Veenhof 2008b, to which *145, *152 and *153 are added here, not because they would be related to the other texts - *147 may not even be from Elamma’s archive and the excavations numbers of 148-151 suggest that they were stored together, presumably by the same person, - but to present all such “itineraries” together. The first three and the last two deal with journeys inside Anatolia and *148 and *149 also cover the journey through Northern Mesopotamia, *149 from Wahšušana via Kanesh to Assur, and *148 the other way around, from Assur to Luhusaddiya. *150 and *151 cover a trip that started after crossing the Euphrates (where he have to locate the “Town of the Kaneshites”, see Veenhof 2006:22f.) and *152 and *153 deal with expenses during a trip in Anatolia. We do not know who traveled and wrote these memorandums (in the first person singular), hardly the same person in all cases (but see the note on *145:22). Some may have been written by Elamma or by one of his sons or servants, but 148-151, considering their excavation numbers, seem to belong to a file in which Enna-Suen, Šu-Ištar and Iddin-Suen play a prominent role. *150 and *151 were probably written by the leader of a caravan who charged its participants specified, proportional shares in the expenses of the journey.
label: gold

text: In Veenhof 2006 and 2008b I discussed the possible locations of the better-known towns and tried to reconstruct the routes followed. The data on Anatolia were taken up by Forlanini 2010:137-140 and I will not resume this discussion and refer the reader now to Barjamovic’s Geography, to whom I had made the records available before their publication. I only mention here that Forlanini (p. 138, note 21) does not accept the equation of Tapaggaš with Tapigga = Maşat Höyük and so deprives us of a rare fixed point, but that Barjamovic maintains it (p. 258 note 987). Furthermore, that on 182 he makes the interesting suggestion that the “town of the Kaneshites” could have been “an idiosyncratic way of referring to the Assyrian settlement of traders at Hahhum, since it turns up in a position where one would have expected to find that city mentioned” - q.e.d.
label: gold

text: Using such texts for geographical reconstructions, as pointed out in Veenhof 2006, repeated by Forlanini and amply documented by Geography, is difficult. They render account of expenses, so that places were nothing was paid are absent and they also do not mention how many days a trip or its stages took. Uncertain is also whether the sequence of towns reflects a linear journey or includes smaller trips from a "central place" to smaller towns in their neighborhood for commercial purposes This seems likely for the texts dealing with journeys in Anatolia, e.g. the return trip from Burušhattum to Ušb/pug/kattum in *145:11f., and for several small towns or villages visited according to *146 and *147. But some could be towns or villages along the caravan route, only mentioned when specific expenses were made there. The journeys recorded in *148 and *149, which ended in and started out from Assur, probably reflect linear caravan journeys, mentioning mostly well-known road stations on the caravan route (see for Hamizānum the note on *149:5). Birtu’um in *149:11 is thus far unique and was only mentioned because additional transport costs were paid for the trip from Burallum to this town. The trip of *153 was a short one by five persons in the north of Hattum, perhaps from Wahšušana, via Tawiniya and Tišmurna to Durhumit.
label: gold

text: The terminology used for the expenses varies. Most frequent is “I gave”, usually with the purpose (ana) of the payment (porters, personnel, inns, officials; an unknown “him” in *152:18-22), but we also have “I incurred” (ikšudī and ikšudanni), usually not specified (but in *147:24 said of the wages of the porters; note for the impersonal ikšudam in *149, AOATT 413ff.), and occasionally “I weighed out” (*151 passim), also in the D-stem (*145:4, and *151:5, 20). The first two texts also use “I spent / ... was spent” (agmur, gamer) and the noun gamrum, usually specified as “(for the journey) until GN”. These are unspecified “travel expenses” (gamrum ša harrānim, see AOATT 248-53), which could include extra food, pasturing, additional transport costs (taššiātum), crossing a river (*146: 22), using a bridge (*147:10), etc. In addition there are payments of taxes, the šaddu’utum due to the colony in Burušhattum, paid in silver (*145:9-11), and the import-tax paid to local authorities, normally in towns with an Assyrian commercial presence: 6 shekels of tin on textiles in Hanaknak and 3 minas of refined copper for the kaššum in Durhumit (*146:10 and 24), 6 shekels of silver paid to ....., probably in Kuburnat (*147:34f.). *152:21-22 mentions “his road-tax” together with fodder for the donkey”. The “gift” of 12 shekels of tin to the “commander” (rabi sikkitim) in Karahna (*147:19f.) may also have been a kind of transit-tax. Such payments were probably based on agreements with the local rulers whose towns were passed, whereby instead of a tax in natura (e.g. a piece of textile) also tin or silver could be paid.[4] A regular feature are gifts to local chiefs and officials, such as the bead of tin for the alahhinnum (*146:20), but such persons are regularly designated by the generic term kaššum, “official, dignitary” (*146:19, 25), either because the writer did not know his title or considered it not important.[5]
label: gold

text: It is interesting to note where silver, tin or copper was paid, because in different areas, depending on the composition and provenance of the caravan, different types of "money" were used. In *145 most payments were in copper, apart from that to the colony and the inn in Burušhattum. The caravan of *147 (arriving from the south) pays tin (presumably the “loose tin” taken along from Assur for expenses en route), also the small gift (12 shekels) to the commander in Karahna, but silver is used for the import-tax of l. 25 (in Kuburnat?). In *149:19 and 23, and *150:5-13 payments in southern Anatolia were made not only in tin (with “tin for in the hand”), but also in silver, presumably because one wished to spend silver that was becoming “cheap” in Anatolia, while the exchange value of tin increased there, from ca. 1:15 in Assur to eventually ca. 1:6-8 in Anatolia. The beginning of *152 mentions the sale of a few textiles for silver, which was then used to buy copper, and all the following expenses are in silver. In *153, which records very small payments, some were in copper, but on various occasions one also paid very small amounts of silver (presumably also in line 1, as da’atum), while a servant received both some silver and some copper for his expenses (lines 11-13).
label: gold

text: At times the size of the expenses may give a hint of the distance covered, e.g. in *145, where most expenses for the trips from town to town amounted to 3 minas of copper, but the short journey from Wahšušana to Tuhpiya required only 1 ½ mina of copper and the long one from Durhumit to Kanesh 5 minas. During the trip from Kanesh to Wahšušana also 3 minas of copper were spent, but here “small wares” (lines 28f.) too were used for paying. Occasionally porters were used, in *145 during the first two stages and in *147 to reach Šamuha and for the trip from Karahna to Kuburnat. Perhaps more difficult terrain was passed, a donkey had died or additional merchandise was transported. That donkeys were used is shown by the cost of nabrītum (*145:19), “stabling”, a place where donkeys could stay and graze (see OAI, 267f.). Payments to inns for accommodating persons and donkeys (lodging, food, water) are well documented (see Geography 34-37). Their use in towns with Assyrian trading stations (Burušhattum, Hurama, Šalatuwar, Wahšušana) may indicate that their premises did not offer visiting caravans sufficient facilities for passing the night and guarding the load, because they were not walled compounds or the caravans were too big. An inn offered both, cf. AKT 6, 560:22-24, “we gave 3 shekels of silver to the inn in Qaṭṭarā, where one guarded the goods” (ana bēt ubri ša Q. ša unūtam iṣṣurūni).

text: Elamma’s wife Lamassutum – also written Lamassatum, without vowel harmony– is well attested in the archive, both during and after her husband’s lifetime and she also occurs in some texts found in other archives. Kt 94/k 543:4-5 mentions: “1 mina 10 shekels of silver / under my seals to Lamassutum / the wife of Elamma; 3 shekels of silver / a consignment for the same woman” (šēbultam aššiātima), entrusted somewhere in Anatolia to Ellil-bāni, presumably for delivery in Kanesh. There are several references to her as sender of small amounts of silver to Assur, especially to her daughter Ummī-Išhara (see Ch. II, B). She also figures as writer and as addressee of some letters exchanged with relatives and we meet her in contracts, because she conducted some business of her own, both before and after her husband’s death.
label: gold

text: A few records of Lamassutum were found among the texts of what must be Ir’am-Aššur’s archive (see Ch. XI, introduction). They are a debt-note for ⅔ mina of silver, which a certain Dadiya owes her (dated only by a double week eponym; Kt 94/k 120), a contract with Iddin-Aššur about the conditional sale of his daughter Ab-šalim (or a loan with his daughter as pledge, dated to eponymy year 100; Kt 94/k 127), and a damaged agreement between her and Ilī-bāni on a sum of silver (Kt 94/k 123). The archival context of these records and the documented family relations suggests her identity with Elamma’s wife. Lamassutum also figures anon-ymously as “the wife of Elamma”, e.g. in Kt 93/k 73:11 (see Appendix text 23f).[1] In other cases the identification is uncertain, because Lamassutum, “guardian angel”, was a popular name for girls. According to Michel (2008, 60f. with note 32) also a sister of Elamma’s father had this name and she or a namesake must have written the letters CCT 4, 40a, KUG 39 and Prag I 467 from Assur to Pūšu-kēn and Imdīlum. She also may have been the one who received the small shipments of silver recorded in CCT 6, 27b:9 and TC 3, 207:26. And if she was identical with Elamma’s aunt she was different from Lamassutum, daughter of E-ra-dí (Prag I 569:8). The identity of the Lamassutum attested in EL 180, AKT 1,1:3 (during eponymy year 88) and AKT 6, 12:4’, and of the one mentioned in AKT 4, 45:6 and 20 (probably the sister of Uṣur-ša-Ištar) has to be established by more prosopographical research.

text: Three records deal with the sale of the slave-girl Kukra. *154 is an agreement between her and Šamaš-abī, that he will pay her within ten weeks the rest of the price for Kukra; if not the slave-girl becomes her property. *155, designated as “tablet concerning Kukra of the son of Zuzānum” (=Šamaš-abī)”, records a testimony given under oath by four witnesses at the behest of the Durhumit colony, but since the envelope was not opened we do not know what they testified on. *156 is a deposition by the same four witnesses, also summoned by kārum Durhumit, in which they declare that the slave-girl “of Šamaš-abī, son of Zuzānum” had been bought by Šallim-Aššur, son of Iphurum. This tablet could be a copy of the tablet inside the unopened envelope *155, but its implications are not certain, because damage of the bottom of the tablet deprives us of five or six lines of text and the envelope has not been opened.

text: A reconstruction of the affair is difficult, also because the two depositions are undated. I assume that Šamaš-abi, son of Zuzānum (who occurs in Kt 93/k 9:13-14 - courtesy of C. Michel - as a transporter and as witness in AKT 6, 838:5, undated) had bought the slave-girl (the seller may be mentioned in *156:2-4, see below) with money advanced by Lamassutum, part of which - 20 minas of refined copper, equivalent to ca. 20 shekels of silver - he failed to pay back. Later he may have sold the slave-girl to Šallim-Aššur, apparently without having paid back Lamassutum. She then must have summoned him and her claim may have led to a lawsuit before the colony, in the course of which *155, a deposition by the four witnesses, played a role. In *156 they confirm that the slave-girl really had been sold (again) by Šamaš-abī, but we do not know how the case ended. It is difficult to consider the agreement *154 the result of the intervention by the colony, because it is not presented as its verdict or as a solution by mediators or persons “who solved the case” (pāšir awātim). Moreover, if the slave-girl had been sold to a new owner Lamassutum could not stipulate that the girl would become her property if her new owner defaulted, unless this sale was contested, because the seller could not sell his encumbered property. The kārum may have decided that the sale by Šamaš-abī was not valid, because he still owed part of the price of the girl to Lamassutum, but such a verdict is missing. It is more likely that *154 documents an early phase of the transaction, which established Šamaš-abī’s debt and stipulated what would happen if he failed to pay in time. One could then assume that the defaulting Šamaš-abī, instead of handing over the slave-girl to Lamassutum, had sold her, perhaps even in order to use the price paid for her to pay Lamassutum. That the debt-note *154 was found in Lamassutum’s archive does not contradict this, because the tablet may have been preserved after its sealed envelope had been broken.

text: The description of the girl sold as “the slave-girl Kuzizi” indicates that the Anatolians did not sell their daughter into slavery, but a slave-girl they already owned, presumably to meet a debt-claim. Nevertheless, the sellers retain the possibility of buying her back, which they can do by declaring “We take her along”, using the verb tarā’um that is typical for such situations (see Kienast 1984, 74ff., on the “Retraktklauseln”, in the combination šaqālum + tarā’um). They can get her back by paying twice the sale price, which makes it difficult (since they presumably are already in debts) to make use of their right (see Veenhof, Studies Matouš II, 295ff. and R. Westbrook, Property and the Family in Biblical Law, Sheffield 1991, Ch. 5, on the “price factor” in redemption). Lines 19-21 consider the possibility that the sellers (try to) take the girl along without paying and state that she then becomes the full property of the buyer, as a chattel slave. Cuneiform law does not have an abstract definition of “ownership”, but stating, as in our contract, the right to sell what has been bought (which implies that redemption is then excluded) is its nearest approach. Cf. in Old Babylonian CT 4, 7a, a dispute about the ownership of a house acquired by exchange, where one party declares (lines 25-32), “He gave me the full price of my house and a house in exchange for a house, so that I am satisfied. .... I can give it where I wish. What claim do you have one me?” In our contract the possibility of selling the girl may not only have been an expression of full ownership, but have been intended by Lamassutum, if the slave-girl was merely sold to cover a debt and she wished to see money.
label: gold

text: Protection against vindication by a third party is provided by stipulating that the buyer in that case will make the sellers with their property (their house) liable for it, for which the verb dagalum, “to look at, have a claim on, to acquire ownership of” is used (see Veenhof 2001, 129, 3). In this clause, as in the one about attempts by the sellers to recover their property, the buyer is speaking and the writer of the record quoted what Lamassutum said verbatim, as happens more often, especially when mentioning specific securities claimed by the buyer (or creditor); (cf. *154:12-13)

Since double week-eponyms disappear after eponymy year 98, this contract must date to the period when Lamassutum, while her husband was perhaps still alive, was already engaged in private business. What this business was remains unclear, because the amount of the debt is missing and debt-notes almost never mention the reason of the debt. Aššur-lamassī occurs many times in records of the archive (see also Appendix, text 10, from year REL 88) as witness, as transporter of silver and textiles, and involved in his own, modest transactions (*129:3, 12 kutānū; *68:18, 11 kutānū). Here he may have contracted a (small) loan or have taken some merchandise, probably textiles, in commission from Lamassutum.

text: Lamassutum must have been producing textiles in Kanesh, presumably woolen pirikannū-textiles, perhaps with the aid of her slave-girls (*164:23 mentions five of them), when her husband was still alive. Lassen 2010, 165, mentions a few other texts in which Lamassutum is involved with wool, but I am not certain that it is always the same woman, because the name was rather common in Old Assyrian. Lamassutum in our contract needs soft wool for making the weft. To obtain this type of wool she contracts (and presumably provides money to) Aššur-taklāku, who has to send it from Haqa, situated north of Zalpa, on the road from Assur to Tegarama (Geography 111). It may have been available there thanks to imports from the north, from Luhusaddiya or the region around modern Çorum, a centre of wool production and trade (see Lassen 2010, 168f.). Aššur-taklāku may have passed Haqa on his trip to Assur, and if he fails to carry out his commission and travels straight to Assur, he has to supply double the quantity contracted as a penalty. That the debt-note was preserved unopened in Elamma’s archive might indicate that the commission was not carried out.

text: This record about the last will of Lamassutum, dated to month II of REL 107, was edited and commented upon by me in Veenhof 2012a, 196-200 (text 4), to which I refer the reader. The comment given below summarizes the main issues relevant for the business and family history of Elamma. Our text is not the testament, but a memorandum that quotes, after Lamassutum’s death, what she said or spoke in the first person singular (“my seals”, lines 3 and 5, and also lines 17, 19, 35, 36), to all appearances in her last will that we do not have. The memorandum, also writes about her in the third person singular - “all this Lamassutum, wife of Elamma, left behind”, lines 26-28 - may have been drawn up for the use of those, probably her representatives mentioned in lines 28-30, who had to carry out her dispositions, presumably because all the assets mentioned and probably also the original would be sent to Assur (as lines 33-34 state), where the final division of the inheritance would take place. I note that a house in Kanesh does not figure among her assets, perhaps because Elamma’s house there had been inherited by Elamma’s eldest son, who may have been obliged to let his mother live there (as was the case in *297, discussed in Veenhof 1998, 141-144).

Naniya features as witness in *112:8; Bur-Suen appears as transporter of silver for Elamma in *47:4.26 and *19:11.36, and as his debtor for 55 shekels of silver in *70:13; (an) Ilī-tappā, son of Idnāya, is witness in *312:3. There are too many different Ennam-Suen’s to identify him, but he may well be the man of that name many of whose records, edited in this volume, were found in Elamma’s house (see Ch. XIII).

text: The assets Lamassutum left behind were substantial: silver objects, cash silver and debt claims on various persons amounting to in all 8⅔ minas of silver, plus ten textiles and ten slaves and slave-girls. The origin of these assets is not mentioned, some may have belonged to her dowry or have been given to her by her husband (e.g. the silver cups and toggle-pins), but since he died several years earlier she may also have obtained some as her share in his inheritance (wives did inherit from their husbands, see Veenhof 2012, 176-7). The temple funds (ikribū), put at Elamma’s disposal (lines 5-6), may have been passed on to her in this way and possibly also some of the other claims listed in lines 6-14. Other assets were debts owed to herself, resulting from her commercial activities, as documented in the debt-notes published above, and from the fact that she had made amounts of silver available to Assyrians, among them her relative Ir’am-Aššur, “for (to make) purchases” (lines 15-19), probably in Assur. But this expression is also used in l. 22, where sale in Anatolia of textiles “given” to Pilah-Ištar (presumably her son) is meant. The nine pirikannu-textiles he received in fact may have been woven by her or her slave-girls, for in *159 she commissioned a trader to buy wool for her. Lamassutum also owned quite a number of slaves, perhaps including some she had bought herself, such as the one recorded in *157.
label: gold

text: That her representatives had to entrust “all this” for shipment to Assur may imply that outstanding claims had to be collected and the slaves were sold (apart from one), to send their yield in silver there. But we cannot exclude that eventually some debt-notes were assigned to her sons, to be collected later in Anatolia. That the final accounting and division of the inheritance would take place in Assur – where also Lamassutum’s sons had to go for this purpose (lines 31-33) and where Ummī-Išhara lived as priestess - is known from other texts. The final injunction, “My daughter ... and my sons shall act in accordance with the testamentary dispositions applying to them”, obviously quoted from her testament, might reflect some fear about the execution of her last will, but it may also have been fairly standard clause. Other testaments show that “executors” (bēl šīmātim) would monitor the division.

text: As pointed out in the Introduction Elamma had a large number of children, in alphabetical order (we do not know their chronological order): Abu-šalim, Aššur-ṭāb (probably his eldest son), Ennam-Aššur, fIštar-lamassī, Pilah-Ištar, fŠalimma, Šu-Bēlum, fUmmī-Išhara and Uṣur-pī-Aššur. Not all of them are well attested and several figure in records that have found their place in other chapters, such as the one on Ištar-lamassī (X) and Šalimma (XII), and children also figure in the texts in the chapter on Lamassutum (VIII) and Ir’am-Aššur (XI). This chapter brings documents that have not found their place in these chapters.

text: A. Letters
label: gold

text: A letter by Ummī-Išhara, who lived in Assur as ugbabtu-priestess (see *164:35), occurs frequently in the archive, often as recipient of small amounts of money sent to her from Kanesh.[1] By means of this letter to her brother Pilah-Ištar she tries to solve a conflict between them, arisen when the latter left Assur to travel to Kanesh. Damage and the wording of the letter cause some problems of understanding. The cursive writing, occasional mistakes and peculiarities (lines 4, 13, 15) are perhaps indications that Ummī-Išhara herself wrote this very personal letter.

text: 1. A Bēlānum, here in Kanesh with Lamassutum, is known from ten texts in the archive, only twice with a patronym, son of Šu-Aššur (*204:12, *280:22). It is difficult, also because we cannot be sure that all references are to the same person, to form an idea of his status and activities. In *154:16 he is witness for Lamassutum as creditor; in *280:18-21 he takes tin on behalf of Elamma’s son Pilah-Ištar and in *348 somebody states that Belānum had sent him to Assur with silver for making purchases. He could be the writer (l. 1, Be-l[á-num]), together with Hinnāya, of the letter *89 addressed to Elamma.
label: gold

text: 2. A Šamaš-bāni occurs in some texts of the archive. *190 is a letter by Ennam-Aššur to Ir’am-Aššur (Elamma’s son-in-law) and him, and *240 is a letter that a Šamaš-bāni, together with two others, wrote to Šu-Ištar. In *236 Šu-Ištar asks him to collect a debt owed by Idnāya and to instruct Šamaš-bāni not make things easy for the debtor. When the memo *327 mentions that its anonymous writer and Šamaš-bāni both gave 2 minas of silver to ”the lady”, his association with Lamassutum suggests identification with the man of our letter. He could also be the man of whom Elamma’s letter to Lā-qēp, *20:27-29, writes: “Šamaš-bāni, son of Akitim, brought you 5 minas (of silver) under my seal”, but our letter must have been written after Elamma’s death.

text: This letter was sent from Kanesh, where Lamassutum lived, to the place where the main addressee, Šamaš-bāni, stayed. It must have been delivered by Pilah-Ištar (see l. 19), who also brought the missives of his brother Ennam-Aššur along from Kanesh, as his mother there announced, perhaps including the transport contract drawn up for this lot, which then would have mentioned the witnesses (here already named in lines 13-16) present when Ennam-Aššur entrusted this lot to Aššur-šamšī. Why the “stupid” Aššur-šamšī refused to release the textiles is unknown, but the letter makes it clear that the textiles, shipped under the seals of Ennam-Aššur (l. 6), had to be handed over to the addressees in order to be “counted out” to Pilah-Ištar, who probably would have to sell them. He was ordered “to act in accordance with our instruction” (l. 28), an instruction not contained or repeated in this letter, but presumably given him when he left Kanesh.

text: 25-26. Barjamovic, who collated the tablet, in Geography 171 proposes AN.NA li-°ší-ib¿-ma and translates: ”leave the tin to them and have it placed all over the packs for [...] (tucked) inside the wool and the hides”. But the traces - ŠÍ-IB looks more like RA – do not support this reading and wašābum only occurs with animate subjects. One expects something like “let it be unpacked”, “split up” or the like, because tin was shipped in large packets, called šuqlum, while a riksum was much smaller. The absence of a preposition before riksē makes it the object of šitakkanā, but l. 26b is unclear.
label: gold

text: Comment
label: gold

text: The letter is interesting in showing how traders might try to maximize their profit. A donkey loaded with tin and some textiles, having crossed the Euphrates, has entered Hahhum, from where it will travel into Anatolia (the use of “to bring down”, šērudum, is remarkable for such a journey)[2] to sell the goods. The writer suggests to sell the tin locally if they can get 1 shekel of silver for 8 shekels of tin, which is a modest yield, less than the ideal of 6:1, but acceptable in the south, for it saves the trouble of the journey northwards, which implies that the writer means a sale in or around Hahhum. If they cannot get that price the merchandise has to be “shipped on” (šētuqum) and there seem to be two possibilities, which in the interpretation of Geography 191, are: via Šalahšuwa presumably on to Kanesh (from where the letter may have been written), or via Timilkiya on to Durhumit, presumably via Kuburnat. In the latter case a more profitable solution is to let “people from Kuburnat” – probably located ca. 100 km. south(east) of Durhumit – if they are around, take the tin along, hidden in their loads of wool and hides (which they had acquired in the south). For that purpose small packets (riksū) of tin have to be made, which means that the donkey was unloaded and the large packets (šuqlum) were broken up into smaller ones. This interpretation is suggested by the letter BIN 4, 48 (see AOATT 312 no. 9), where riksu’s of 10 or 15 minas have to be made and hidden in loincloths to be smuggled into a town, exactly the same procedure as suggested in CCT 6, 22a:8-10. This interpretation suits the idea, also entertained by Barjamovic, that one will travel north via the “narrow track”, which starts north of Hurama, a way of evading taxes with amounts to smuggling.

text: Letter by Šu-Išhara to three men, two of whom most probably are sons of Elamma, while the third, Uṣur-ša-Aššur, is the main addressee. The writer had entrusted a shipment of wool belonging to “the merchant” to the latter, to convert it immediately into silver in order to prevent its seizure. He had been urged to send its yield in silver within a few days with (as must be implied) Abu-šalim, probably Elamma’s son, who occurs elsewhere as transporter (see*41:9, and see the note on *18:19-26). But seven months later the addressee still has not done so and he is now urged to do it immediately, by sending the silver with Abu-šalim and his brother.

text: 9-11. We can only guess why merchandise might be “seized” (either by a creditor or the Assyrian authorities.) It might have to do with the death of Elamma’s son Aššur-ṭāb (which is the background of the following three texts), who in that case would be meant by “the tamkārum, “the real owner” (l. 10). His death would have caused problems in completing transactions and realizing transfers. This might also explain why his brothers were involved to ship the money and perhaps the role of Uṣur-ša-Aššur, who had to testify in texts *171-172. But since this is not certain, I have not included this letter under B.

text: B. The death of Elamma’s son Aššur-ṭāb
label: gold

text: The following three texts deal with the death of Elamma’s son Aššur-ṭab (also clear from *174:27-28, where his son Aššur-imittī figures alongside Elamma’s widow and his other sons in a legal confrontation). The texts document how his nephew Aššur-ṭāb dealt with the assets he had left behind and how the dead man’s representatives, two brothers and his brother-in-law, monitor what happened. According to *171//172 the latter had summoned him and asked before witnesses what he had done and would do and in consequence of an appeal by them the Burušhattum colony had made these witnesses testify. This indicates that the affair had been brought before the colony, but nothing is known of its outcome.

text: Much remains unclear, notably what authorized Aššur-ṭāb to undertake his actions, while the dead man’s representatives (including two of his brothers) were still around. Perhaps there was a formal partnership between the two namesakes. The records *171//172 show that the case was handled by the Burušhattum colony, where the testimony was given there (in the presence of Aššur-ṭāb?), but this does not necessarily mean that the confrontation between the parties had taken place there. That might have been in Kanesh, where Lullu lived and where Aššur-ṭāb’s letter *170 was probably sent, to end up in the family archive in Elamma’s house. Aššur-ṭāb in *171:15-17 states that “he carried” the dead man’s silver and that it would “go overland”, probably meaning that he would bring it, possibly to Kanesh, perhaps even to Assur, if the liquidation of Aššur-ṭāb’s business was to take place there. It is possible that *355:9’-13’, “195 minas of copper for Lullu”, at the end of a list of items of which it is said “all this Aššur-šamšī paid (or: promised, ēpul) for the debt of Aššur-ṭāb”, also refers to arrangements after the death of Aššur-ṭāb. Anyhow, as more often, lack of knowledge of the background and of the solution of the affair, deprives us of a real understanding.

text: An unopened case containing the text of a verdict, dated to the year REL 114, rendered by two arbitrators to solve a conflict between Amur-Ištar and Ennam-Aššur. It deals with the possible existence of an unpaid debt in the form of a “working capital” (be’ūlātum), owed by Aššur-imittī, son of Hali-abum, the father of the former, to Elamma, the father of the latter. text: 7-11.The content of the oath, introduced by –ma after “he swore”, is a statement in the subjunctive, la ukallimu, without introducing conjunction. The key word “he will swear” is resumed in line 12, now as an indicative with conditional force, to state what are its consequences, expressed by a verbal form in the present future (iddan). A similar redaction of the content of a verdict about the swearing of an oath, with a resumed itamma, is found in POAT 1A:5-19 and Kt c/k 51 (AMMY 1990, 51):3-10. Note also Prag I 681:28-28, where this is expressed by itammama ištu ittamû, “he will swear and after he has sworn ...”.

text: The issue of the conflict resolved in this record was a be’ūlātu-loan given by Elamma to Aššur-imittī, recorded in text *67, dated by a double week eponymy and thus earlier than REL 97. By it Aššur-imittī owed a “working capital” of no less than 63 ½ shekels of silver, probably an old working-capital of 30 shekels (recorded in the memorandum *70:3-4) to which a new one for the same amount and some interest were added. The fact stated in the final lines of *67, that “the tablet in the City concerning his working capital (i.e. the original one excerpted in *70:3-4) is invalid”, probably is at the root of the problem. The two parties in *173 are the heirs of Elamma, represented by his son Ennām-Aššur, and Amur-Ištar, who was probably the son of Aššur-imittī, from whom Elamma’s heirs claim back the “working capital” given to his father. The heirs of Elamma apparently had tried earlier, after their father’s death, to claim payment, perhaps on the basis of the mention of the debt in memorandum. But when Amur-Ištar, in the presence of two witnesses, he asked them to be shown the valid be’ūlātu-contract as proof, Ennam-Aššur had been unable to do so. But he seems not to have given up his claim and this must have le,d, some years later (our verdict is dated to eponymy year REL 114) to the joint initiative of both men to engage arbitrators to solve their conflict. They decide that if Amur-Ištar confirms under oath the fact that his opponent was unable to show him the contract, the heirs of Elamma must drop their claim.

text: This contract can be linked with Prag I 609, which explains what had happened with Elalī’s trust: “As for the tablet about 8 minas of silver plus the interest on it, which amount Elalī, son of Ištar-pilah, had given as trust (iqīpu) to Ennam-Ašsur, the deaf (sakkukum), in Hahhum (5) and for which he had drawn up in Hahhum his certified record, which Išme-Aššur, son of Hinnāya has in possession – (10) I, Ēnah-ilī, Aššur-taklāku and Puzur-Ištar, son of Imdī-ilum, each took 2 minas of silver and supplied (15) a sealed quittance, which Iliya, son of Puzur-Aššur, has in his possession”. This shows that the affair was even more complicated. The original debt-note was in the possession of a son of Hinnāya - why is not clear, perhaps simply as safe deposit, because he lived in Hahhum? - and four different traders, among them our Ēnah-ilī, subsequently had each acquired 2 minas or one fourth of the original trust, a fact recorded in a tablet (singular!) they had sealed (lines 14-15, apparently one tablet for all four jointly), but their relation to the original trustee remains unclear. Who the speaker (“I”) of Prag I 609 was is not clear, because we do not know from which archive this memo originates. It would be nice if this was Elamma, because it explain why Ēnah-ili, a trusted agent of him, had collected the silver «in his name», after Elamma's death, to give it to his widow, but this would imply that the division of the trust into four, recorded in Prag I 609, had not yet been realized when Elamma died. An alternative is that Ēnah-ilī in Prag I 609, in Hahhum, already acted as agent of Elamma, so that his action described in our record amounts to acquiring Elamma's share, apparently in the meantime augmented by 15 shekels as interest. Many things remain unclear, because it is not stated what the purpose of the original trust given to Ennam-Aššur was, although it seems likely that the silver was the value or price of merchandise arriving from Assur in Hahhum, which had to be shipped on and sold. We also do not know why this trust was subsequently divided into four; could Puzur-Aššur could not handle it or was he in financial problems? The division reminds me somewhat of the transaction described in text 2 of the Appendix, where 4 talents of tin of Hinnāya are divided in his house into three, apparently to traders who intend to sell it with profit. It is anyhow very likely that Elalī in the meantime had died, because lines 21-22 consider the possibility that investors (was the money of the trust perhaps part of his joint-stock capital?) and the (other) sons of Ištar-pilah might raise claims. The purpose of our record is to ensure that the heirs of Elamma, who had received his share, protect Ēnah-ilī against their claims and against those of the original trustee, Puzur-Aššur. The existence of both our record and Prag I 609 show how complicated financial transactions carried out in subsequent stages cold be and how we may be puzzled or misled if we happen to have only one record from what must have been a larger file.

text: 7. In Veenhof 2012a,190-193, I argued (see the quote in the comment on *2:29-30) that kursīnum is not, as CAD G, 142f. suggested, the OA form of kušgusānum, “leather bag”, but can be identified, as I.J. Gelb first proposed, with Ugaritic krsn, a small jar. Its use in our text is comparable with that in ICK 2, 158:18; “testament Thierry”, RA 60 [1966], 132-4:18f.; Athenaeum 47 (1960):4-7// KTH 9:4ff., 16f. and *2:29, where kursīnum (singular and plural) occurs in enumerations of a person’s assets, named after the jar or pot, in which they had been placed. The plural shows that a house could have several of them, used for particular goods or associated with particular persons, whose names are occasionally mentioned (cf. lines 7-8 in our text). As such it came to refer to “small funds”, counting as assets, just like naruqqum, originally “(leather) bag” (alongside which it occurs in ICK 2, 157:18), became the technical term for the joint-stock capital, brought together by investors (too big for a small “purse”, kīsum), also as a legal and administrative entity.[3].

text: This record deals with the division of some of Elamma’s assets between three of his sons and his daughter, Ummī-Išhara, who lived as ugbabtu-priestess in Assur, during the year REL 115, long after he had died and also after the death of their mother. The other two sons – Aššur-ṭāb had died in the meantime - Abu-šalim and Uṣur-pī-Aššur were probably not involved, because this is an exchange of parts of their shares between four heirs only. But they are meant by “the (other) sons of Elamma” who might raise a claim (lines 38-39). Ummī-Išhara and Ennam-Aššur (who lived in Kanesh, but may have liked to have a pied-à-terre in Assur) wish to acquire a house-plot in Assur, measuring ca. 100 m2, presumably still undivided and owned by the four of them, and in exchange for it they waive the right to their share in debt-claims probably inherited from their father, totaling 12 minas of silver (lines 4-9). Their two brothers, Pilah-Ištar and Šu-Bēlum, are ready to “drop the (right to) their part” and give them the plot, but only after that property has been cleared, because they wish to be protected against future claims of the investors. The clearance (tēbibtum) according to l. 21 must be effectuated “for them”, for these two brothers, within three years. If they fail to do so, Ummī-Išhara and her brother will get 3 minas of silver instead and give up any claim on the plot.
label: gold

text: Lines 13-14 mention that the house plot in question “had been given to them (presumably the four children) by a committee of five” (hamištum). It probably was involved because the implementation of Elamma’s last will created problems, since the house-plot was encumbered or its ownership disputed. Elamma’s investors could have established their claim at the time of Elamma’s death, in order to secure the return of their investments, a concern also clear from the letter CCT 5, 3a (see Appendix, text 1), where two groups of people state that they are acting in the name of Elamma’s investors. Why and how such a ”clearance” (tēbibtum; first occurrence in OA) could prove impossible (line 22) remains unclear. That the last line (an appendix, added after the names of the witnesses) states that the transaction was “in accordance with what had been assigned to them in the testament” (of their father), suggests that what is at stake here is a reshuffle or exchange based on what had been assigned to each of the heirs in the testament, a feature also known from contemporary Babylonia. This could also have been the reason for the involvement of the “committee of five”, for we have more evidence for its role in arriving at a fair division of an inheritance. In EL 244 two sons of Pūšu-kēn will go to Assur in order to take cognizance of the decision taken for them by a committee of five there, “behind the temple of the god Aššur”, because “the decisions for/about us” are in the city” (lines 9-11). The two brothers must have disagreed on the division of their father’s inheritance and what the committee does is called šīmtam / šīmātim šiāmum, which is the terminology of making a testament, not that of a normal legal decision or verdict. The decisions (šīmātum) taken by the committee are comparable to what a man does who makes a testament and they may have been needed because there was no testament of Pūšu-kēn.[4] Something similar may have caused the intervention of the hamištum in our text.
label: gold

text: U. and E. are promised 3 minas of silver (to be taken from the 4 minas of Kurub-Ištar, mentioned in lines 5f.), if they fail to acquire the house plot, to “satisfy themselves with the price of the plot” (lines 22-26). This would be the value of half of the plot, on the assumption that Ummī-Išhara and her brother, as heirs, already were the owner of half it. Until the matter is settled P. and Š. retain their claim on these 3 minas, which means that its ownership by U. and I. for the time being was conditional. A problem is why lines 4-8 list claims to a total of 12 minas of silver (half of which would have been the share of Ummī-Išhara and Ennam-Aššur), while the compensation for the house-plot to be acquired by the two other brothers is only 3 minas, to be taken only from the 4 minas owed by Kurub-Ištar,
label: gold

text: This record also acquaints us with the rather surprising fact that many years after their father’s death four heirs still jointly own undivided assets, not only a house plot in Assur, but also various debt-claims, which have not yet been collected, presumably because they were not simple debts, but investments. It is possible that the death of their mother, several years after their father, is part of the explanation. But in a family of traders the division of an inheritance, consisting of various assets, investments, debt-claims and houses, could be complicated and take time. This is also clear from the following document that deals with a small amount of silver.

label: gold

text: The main person in our texts, Uṣur-pī-Aššur,[6] is a son of Elamma, but he appears only here and we know nothing about him. He also does not figure in *178, where four children of Elamma reach an agreement about dividing certain assets of what they had inherited. Also mentioned are Elamma’s daughter, Ummī-Išhara, in Assur, and his son Ennam-Aššur, living in Kanesh, who was the one in direct contact with his brother. It seems that Ennam-Aššur and Uṣur-pī-Aššur at this time were the only children of Elamma present in Kanesh, while the others were in Assur (cf. *177:11-13).
label: gold

text: Our texts concern three issues, the payment of silver to Uṣur-pī-Aššur by his brother, the fact that Uṣur-pī-Aššur had as wife a slave-girl, presumably from the household of his mother, and that Ennam-Aššur had made some payments for his brother in connection with a slave of the latter, who had fled and which Ennam-Aššur managed “to get out of” (šēṣu’um) the house of an Anatolian.
label: gold

text: The issue of the slave remains unclear. The verbs “to hold” (ka’’ulum) may imply that Uṣur-pī-Aššur detained the slave as pledge or security, either supplied a by defaulting debtor or perhaps a defaulting debtor himself, sold into debt-bondage. This could explain why he fled, but how and why he ended up in an Anatolian’s house is unclear, also because the verb šēṣu’um is used in different situations and may denote both that a pledge was taken along from a defaulting debtor by his creditor and that somebody obtained the release of such a pledge from the house of the creditor.[7] Had the Anatolian apprehended him and did he receive a reward or had he himself a claim on the man and did Ennam-Aššur pay him to get him free?
label: gold

text: The colonial verdict *177, possibly the result of an appeal by Uṣur-pī-Aššur, shows that there had been legal problems, for it states his right (on which it was based remains unknown, because lines 3 is broken) to live in and from the house(hold) of their father on the same footing as his elder brother, and to keep a slave-girl he had taken as wife, but forbids to alienate any property until Elamma’s other children, in Assur, have reported on the actual (legal) situation.
label: gold

text: Texts *176 and *178 begin with the issue that Ennam-Aššur in Kanish had given silver to his brother and I assume that the 15 shekels given according to *176 are identical to the 15 shekels borrowed from a money-lender at interest according to*178. He may have done so to prevent it from being formally recorded in a dated debt-note. Text *176 suggests that Uṣur-ša-Aššur had claimed the silver as part of the inheritance of their mother, but the gift of was conditional and *176 (drawn up in Kanesh by or for Ennam-Aššur, who could not ascertain there the details of the division) states that Uṣur-pī-Aššur will give it back if his sister in Assur can produce (?; the verb is missing) a valid record by which Uṣur-pī-Aššur had renounced any further claims on the inheritance. What he had already received is unknown. *164 registers the assets left behind by their mother Lamassutum, which will be shipped to Assur, and at the end quotes words from her last will: “My daughter ... and my sons will act in accordance with the testamentary dispositions applying to them”, but we do not know the latter. But the slave-girl Uṣur-pī-Aššur had taken as wife seems to have been one of the five owned and left behind by his mother in Kanesh, one of which she had already assigned in her last will to her grand-daughter Ilina (lines 23-25). I assume that Uṣur-pī-Aššur, perhaps with the silent consent of his mother, some time earlier had married (*177:8-9 uses the verb ahāzum) one slave-girl as concubine or wife and that the Kanesh colony decided that this “acquisition” was an accepted fact (kīma ahzuni ahiz). He could not be forced to give her up, so that she would become an asset of the inheritance still to be divided, but the verdict (also referred to in *178:14-16) stated that he could not convert her into money by selling her (*177:9-10).
label: gold

text: There is more evidence of the role of slave-girls as part of an inheritance. The agreement recorded in EL 287:18-32 states that, after the eldest(?) son has received his share in silver, the others will “divide the rest, barley, slave-girls, slaves and bronze objects (read sí-pá-ri!) in accordance with the testament of their father”. One son will take “here (in Kanesh) or in the City (Assur) a slave-girl as hierodule”(? ana ištariuttišu); three others “will each take one slave-girl from those with whom they had already intercourse (ša lamdū) and she will be deducted from their share”. The last will Kt o/k 196c (I. Albayrak, ArAn 4 [2000], 22f.), after assigning one slave-girl to the testator’s daughter (l. 15), in lines 23-27 first prescribes that the testator’s wife and sons “shall divide the silver, slaves and slave-girls that remain on equal terms” (“half half”, mutta muttat), but adds that “Aššur-idī’s concubine is relinquished to him” (šawissu ša A. waššurassum). This must mean that he can keep her and perhaps that this girl is not included in the assets to be divided, which would make this provision similar to the one in our text. *178:14 describes the slave-girl married by Uṣur-pī-Aššur as “belonging to the girl”, which probably means that she actually was part of the share assigned to Ummī-Išhara. If this is correct then the fact that Uṣur-pī-Aššur could keep her was a favor and the no-claim promise given to his sister (*176:6-15) could have been the result of accepting this favor.
label: gold

text: Text *178:17-19 describes how this affair ended, apparently stating that Uṣur-pī-Aššur somehow got rid of the girl (the verb is unfortunately unclear) and left, perhaps frustrated by the decision which prevented him for selling her. I hardly have to add that this reconstruction is hypothetical, because we are not informed about how this case ended and know little about the elusive Uṣur-pī-Aššur.

text: X. IŠTAR-LAMASSĪ AND HER DEATH (179-188)
label: gold

text: The group of records presented in this chapter deals with events surrounding the death of Ištar-lamassī. She was a daughter of Elamma, as is stated in Kt 94/k 181 (courtesy C. Michel), where she seals an undated contract in which her sister Šalimma (the wife of Ir’am-Aššur) buys a slave. She was originally married to the Assyrian Kūn-ilum, with whom she had two sons, Iliya and Ilabrat-bāni, and a daughter, Šīmat-Ištar, who lived in Assur as ugbabtu-priestess. After Kūn-ilum’s death she married the Anatolian Lullu, son of Hapi, and ten years later she died, almost immediately followed by the death of both her sons, which left her daughter in Assur as only heir. In the absence of sons, who would have been responsible for her funeral and the rites surrounding it, relatives and her second, Anatolian husband stepped in. He advanced the costs of her and her sons’ funeral, but had to be indemnified (also for money he had earlier advanced on behalf of Iliya), which was done by taking the money from what Ištar-lamassī’s sons would have inherited according to her last will. Relatives, Elamma’s widow Lamassutum and his eldest son Ennam-Aššur, together with the representatives of her daughter, Šumi-abiya (called her šazzuztum) and another Ennam-Aššur, and probably the men who had witnessed her last will (as its executors?) arranged this and ultimately sent what Šīmat-Ištar had inherited and what remained from the shares of her dead brothers to Assur.
label: gold

text: These operations generated a number of records, such as letters sent to Assur to relate what happened, records of the transfer of money and assets, and accounts of the expenses and payments made, which turned up in Elamma’s archive and provide us with a unique file. Unfortunately, there is no detailed report on the find-spots of the texts, whose excavation numbers suggest that they (or many of them) were found together and had been kept as a file. I studied this file in “The Death and Burial of Ishtar-lamassī in kārum Kanish” (Veenhof 2008a), where texts *180, *184, *185 and *188 were already published. The present edition contains a few minor improvements in the reading of the texts, due to collation and the general comments at the end aim at a better understanding of the structure and meaning of the file and the function of the persons involved. I refer to my previous study for various details, especially for what these texts learn us about the funerary rites, such as the “bewailing” of the dead and the removal of the chair of Ištar-lamassī. In the comments below I focus on the features that are relevant for the family history and the financial operations that conditioned how much of Ištar-lamassī’s testamentary disposition could be realized.

text: Neither the speaker (l. 12, “I entrusted”, etc.), nor the one addressed (l. 15, “you shall not claim”, l. 25, “I have a claim on you”) in this record are identified and the text is not dated. The speaker “entrusted” to the person addressed property – Ištar-lamassī’s share in an asset owned jointly with a certain Bizila[1] and various precious objects of silver and bronze - for paying what her son Ilabrat-bāni owed to Lullu. He then states that whatever silver remains after “you have satisfied the Anatolian” (i.e. Lullu, lines 21-23) counts as a debt owed by him to the speaker. The words “the house of my father and my mother” (lines 13-14) and the fact that the main concern is the debt of Ilabrat-bāni, suggests that the speaker was Iliya, the eldest son of Ištar-lamassī (which implies that “the house of my father” is what was left by Ištar-lamassī’s first, Assyrian husband, which her children would inherit). If so, the text must be dated before her sons had died. That the property was “entrusted” (paqādum, l. 12) means that the recipient had to use it for the purpose stated and lines 21-26 assume that not all silver was needed, so that the speaker maintains a claim on the recipient, described as “for i-le-e”. This probably means “(statuettes of) gods”, however surprising that may be, but see for these statuettes the comment on AKT 5, 35:5. The addressee is explicitly denied any claim on other assets of Ištar-lamassī or the family, described as “the price” of a house, textiles and precious objects, which means that these items were or would be sold, which suggests that Ištar-lamassī’s household was liquidated.

text: While what happened after the death of Ištar-lamassī and both her sons is in the main clear, problems of interpretation remain. The identity and role of most of the persons involved in the affair is understood, especially of those protecting the interests of Ištar-lamassī and her children, also the writers of most of our records. They are relatives, Lamassutum and her son Ennam-Aššur, representatives of Ištar-lamassī’s children, Ennum-Aššur, son of Aššur-dan and Šumi-abiya, son of A/Emua, and probably also those who witnessed Ištar-lamassī’s last will and may have been its executors (bēl šimātim), and perhaps also a few more people. They probably are the ones designated as “our brothers” (184*:12), who entered the house for the funerary rites and they must belong to the group to which *181:15 and *185:12 refer, mentioning actions ina puhrini / ippuhrišunu, “of us/them jointly”. Those trying to get at the money Ištar-lamassī left behind, apart from Lullu, are elusive, “the son of Hinnāya, creditor of your brothers”, who tried “to seize” it (*180:36-37), and anonymous persons who wished “to take it for the debt of her (Šimat-Ištar’s) brothers”. We also do not know who “the sons of Hanum” are, protected by *187:16-17 against any further claims of Lullu.
label: gold

text: Uncertainties are also due to the nature of the texts. Some are clear, such as the (unfortunately damaged) testament *179 and the two transport contracts *182-183, which have legal force. They were written in view of the shipment of the money that remained to Assur; the first records that it was handed over to the two representatives of the children, the second how these men sealed it and entrusted it to a transporter. Text *186, a witnessed protocol about the use of the assets of Ištar-lamassī, whose speaker and addressee remain unidentified, has legal force, as does *187, an unopened sealed envelope that contains a witnessed record establishing that Lullu has been indemnified for all expenses paid for his dead wife (“the lady”) and for Iliya (when he was in jail) and renounces (he has sealed the envelope) all further claims on the sons of Hanum. Text *180 is a letter sent to Assur, which ends fairly abruptly, and *181 apparently is the continuation of a letter, but not of *180, because it starts by quoting what the writers (“we”) had told persons who wished to take what Ištar-lamassī had bequeathed to her daughter. The latter is the main addressee of both, as is clear from *180:5ff. and *181:8. Found in Elamma’s archive they must be archive copies or perhaps drafts that remained in Kanesh. Text *184 is a memo written by the same “we” (l. 12); it mentions what was taken or paid (the main item are the costs of the funerary ceremonies; the verb is an impersonal passive, “it was paid”) from what Ištar-lamassī had left to her sons and ends with the statement that what remained of it “will go to their sister” in Assur, of which the two representatives of the sons will take care. Text *185 is an memo recording that eight persons, including the two representatives, made (and paid) the expenses for the funerary rites “from the silver that was in the house of Elamma’s wife” and that the representatives had sealed the containers (hušālū), apparently holding the relevant tablets (for shipment to Assur, together with the silver for Šīmat-Ištar, or for safekeeping in the archive?). One of these tablets might have been *186, a memo whose writers (“we”) specify how much silver was paid from what Ilabrat-bāni had inherited for the (presumably his) funerary ceremony (bewailing, meals and drinks on two days); after deduction only 4 7/12 shekels remained of his share in the cash.
label: gold

text: The sequence of the events and some texts raises problems. We do not know when Ištar-lamassī made her testament, but apparently there was time for her son Iliya “when he was still alive”, as mentioned in *180:5-7, to “take 7 shekels of silver from his share”, after his mother had “given” it to her children and when the money had already been deposited in Elamma’s house. This letter explains that, after opening her sealed “coffer” (tamalakkum) Ištar-lamassī “gave” her children their shares in her cash money on her deathbed, in the presence of the “we” and three affiliated traders (mer’ū ummiānī; perhaps the witnesses to the testament). From lines 10-11 (“we entered with your mother”) we get the impression that she was lying ill in her own house, where also her coffer was, and it seems likely that it was afterwards transferred to Elamma’s house (did Iliya take a part of his share before or after this?). The agreement between the division of the cash money as reported in *180 and mentioned in the testament *177 could mean that she implemented her existing last will on her deathbed, but it is also possible that she decided on the division of her cash money then and there, so that the written testament was the result of the formal gathering at her deathbed, when “she spoke her word” (*awassa taqbi). This expression is used twice for making one’s testamentary dispositions (in which the testator normally speaks in the first person singular) and in AKT 6a-44 is such an oral declaration in the presence of witnesses (see Veenhof 2012a, 170f.). The subsequent transfer of her money coffer to Elamma’s house (where also her last will was found) may have been a safety measure, perhaps because she was not certain about what her second Anatolian husband would do.
label: gold

text: The division of Ištar-lamassī’s cash money is clear from her last will (*179): of the 57 shekels of silver available (in her coffer, *180:12) Iliya received 37 shekels, Ilabrat-bāni 20 and her daughter 7½ shekels plus 2¼ shekels of gold (equal to ca. 20 shekels of silver) and also her mother’s seal. The same figures are found in *180:18-23, but here her daughter gets 8 shekels of silver. What was eventually sent to Assur to Šīmat-Ištar are 2¼ shekels of gold and 37 shekels of silver (*181:10-11, *182:1-2) and this last sum consists, as *183:1-2 shows, of the 8 shekels assigned to her by testament plus 29 shekels. This last amount is presumably what remained from her brothers’ shares after deduction of expenses for the “bewailing” and for paying a debt owed by Iliya to Lullu. Text *180:35 mentions that these together amounted to 27 shekels and *184:16-18 that they included the 7½ shekels paid for Iliya’s debt, so that the “bewailing” of the mother and her two sons cost 19½ shekels, indeed the figure given in *184:13. After deduction of these 19½ shekels from the total of 57 shekels available according to the last will, there remained 37½ shekels for Šīmat-Ištar, which is very close to what *181:10-11 and *182:1-2 state and identical if we assume with the last will that not 8 but 7½ shekels were originally assigned to her.
label: gold

text: It is not clear how the expenses for the bewailing of Ilabrat-bāni and the accompanying funerary meals, recorded in *188 and amounting to 15 5/12 shekels of silver, fit into this picture. Are they included in the 19½ shekels of *184:13 and do we have to assume similar expenses for Ištar-lamassī’s and Iliya’s funeral or was there one funerary ceremony and meal for all three? The question is also what we understand by bikītum, “bewailing”. Was it exactly what the word means, which may have implied the hiring and perhaps feeding of wailing women, or a more general term for the whole funerary ceremony? *181:7-9 speaks of expenses (only) “for the “bewailing of your mother and your brothers”, but *184:9-11 mentions “the bewailing of them and the removal of the chair of their mother”, a combination also used when *185:13-14 mentions the expenses made for it. Memo *188 not only makes a distinction between expenses for “bewailing” (l. 3) and those for food and drinks “on the day of the bewailing” (l. 7), but states that the latter are paid cash (lines 10, 23-24), while those for the bewailing are “booked” (lapātum), apparently to be accounted for later.
label: gold

text: What Ištar-lamassī and presumably her sons left behind was more than cash money. Lines *179:13ff. of the last will mention “tablets”, presumably recording debts for which houses were held as pledge, and various metal objects which a woman (presumably Šīmat-Ištar) and Ištar-lamassī’s two sons would get. In *186:1-3 we read about a share (an asset recorded) in a tablet and various valuable objects (a few of which are also mentioned in *179: 23-26), all of which were entrusted to somebody for paying the debt owed by Ilabrat-bāni to Lullu. We do not know the origin of these assets, they might reflect Ištar-lamassī’s own commercial activities, but also be what she had inherited (long ago) from her first Assyrian husband, who was engaged in trade, as we know from Elamma’s archive (cf. *81:30-31, *121:5-6), property which she must have kept for herself after her second marriage. *181:23-26 mention that also two sealed containers (ṣiliānū) with tablets were deposited in Elamma’s house. They may have contained the tablets mentioned in the last will (*179:17), the tablet mentioned in the memo *186:1-2, 23, and records that document the ownership of the house and textiles mentioned there in lines 16-17. The “silver from outstanding claims” (bābtum) left behind by Ištar-lamassī, mentioned in *181:2, must also have consisted of debt-notes and other records of claims (perhaps the tablets of *185:17), which the heirs could collect. Finally *186:16-20 mention “the price” of a house,[2] of textiles and of various precious objects, part of which would be used for paying the debt of Ilabrat-bāni.
label: gold

text: It is important to distinguish between what the sons and what Šīmat-Ištar had inherited and what was used to pay the expenses. *181:4 reproaches anonymous persons, presumably creditors (cf. *180:36-37), of trying to take what was bequeathed to Šīmat-Ištar “for the debt of her brother(s)” (a-HI-ša can also render ahhēša, plur.), but their attempt was frustrated. Memo *188 indicates that Ilabrat-bāni’s funeral was paid from his share (qātum) in the cash money as mentioned in the testament (*179:8-9) and his debt to Lullu would be paid by using assets of Ištar-lamassī (*186). The situation of Iliya, the eldest son, is more complex. He had been assigned more cash than his brother, 37 shekels of silver, but had already appropriated 7 shekels of it (*184:5-7). Moreover, he owed his father-in-law Lullu (*180:27-29) “the expenses for the jail” (gamrum ana kišaršim) the latter had paid for him after Iliya had spent all he had, a debt that amounted to 7 ½ shekels according to*184:17. How much he acquired as heir (apart from his own earnings, for he was involved in the trade, as the nishatu-debt owed to the līmum-office, mentioned in *181:18-21, shows) and what he owned at the time of his death is not clear. He had not only obtained some cash silver, but also the debt-notes mentioned in *179:17 and one qablītu-bowl (lines 23-25), and he may have been entitled to a share of Ištar-lamassī’s assets when they were sold (*186:16:29). His sudden death leaves these questions – at least for us – unanswered and we know nothing about the commercial activities of him and his brother. But their and their mother’s death were instrumental in generating an in many ways unique file, that sheds light on a little-known aspect of the life of the traders.

Lines 27-29 state that when the tablet (the one of lines 1-3) was entrusted to the addressee, “Bizila took responsibility for her share”, which must mean that she made sure that when the claim it embodied was converted into silver she would receive her share. text: Ir’am-Aššur was the son of Id(d)i-bāni[1] and married to Šalimma, a daughter of Elamma, as shown by Kt 93/k 513:17, “Šalimma, daughter of Elamma” (courtesy C. Michel). A long letter, *206, sent by her sister Ummī-Išhara from Assur to Šalimma in Kanesh, in which she tries to mediate between her and her husband Ir’am-Aššur, who lived in Assur and whom she refused to join, is edited in Ch. XII, devoted to Šalimma .
label: gold

text: Ir’am-Aššur’s name is usually spelled Ir-ma-Aššur, with contraction, but occasionally Ir-am-Aššur (*226:1 // B:18) and he even occurs as Na-ra-am-Aššur, son of Id(d)i-bāni (in *233:3). He owned the seal CS 1148, which carries an inscription mentioning its previous owner, a man from Ebla (see the drawing in Teissier 1994, 233 no. 527), used three times on texts from the archive. This chapter presents the texts of or concerning him that ended up in Elamma’s archive, no doubt in consequence of his marriage. But he is also known from his own archive, found in the first house excavated in 1994, texts numbered Kt 94/k 117-184, provisional transcriptions of which were kindly made available to me by Cécile Michel.[2]
label: gold

text: Ir’am-Aššur was a trader active in Anatolia and who traveled between Kanesh and Assur, where he also stayed for some time. He occurs dozens of times in texts from different archives,[3] with dates ranging from eponymy year REL 92 (*195) to year 111 (Kt 94/k 143). He apparently had some form of cooperation with Elamma’s sons, in particular after Elamma’s death. They considered him their senior (calling him “father and boss”) and in their trading operations also handled merchandise belonging to him. That he was somewhat older is confirmed by the appearance of his son, named after his grandfather, as witness for him in the undated *192:15-16. From his own archive we have a record relating to the division between him and his brother Aššur-rabi of the inheritance of their father, witnessed by four men (Kt 94/k 157, courtesy of C. Michel). It states “Ir’am-Aššur and Aššur-rabi, sons of Id(d)i-bāni, have sworn an oath by the City and they have been entitled[4], so that they will not raise claims against each other for anything, whatsoever, belonging to their paternal estate. (11) What their father’s sister and their own sister will leave behind (warkutum) will belong to the two of them” (ša kilišunuma). Here I focus on what texts from Elamma’s archive tell us; his business has to be reconstructed when his archive is published.
