text: These six documents document the rather difficult relations between Elamma’s son Ennam-Aššur (E.) and his senior brother-in-law Ir’am-Aššur (I.), who was married to E.’s sister Šalimma (cf. Ch. XII). E. is engaged in the trade in tin and textiles and also handles merchandise belonging to I. (190*:21, “my textiles”, which he entrusts to him, *191:31-32) and he seems to be in financial problems, because he has to pay one or more creditors in Assur. The background could be the death of his father (who is not mentioned; his mother Lamassutum features in *193:5) and the ensuing liquidation of his business, which must have entailed the payment of his debts by his sons. In this his sister in Assur, Ummī-Išhara, must have played a role and this could be the reason why she “needed” (hašāhum) silver of E. sent to Assur (*189:44-45, *190:13, *191:12-13). E. also encountered problems in Anatolia, because he had been stuck in Hattum for eight months, presumably due to political troubles. He utters various complaints against I., because the latter did not pay him his travel expenses and did not live up to his promises of providing him with tin from Assur. The documents illustrate the problems a junior trader might run into and his dependence on the cooperation with a senior partner. The differences between the texts show that the same events could be portrayed in different perspective, partly also in different order, which may reflect the mood of the rather desperate E. who, not without some rhetorical skill, mixes complaints with appeals for help and a plea for sticking to promises. The letters are also interesting in showing the commercial realities and problems that are at the basis of seemingly simple transport contracts and consignments. The following sketch of the events divides them into various episodes.
label: gold

text: a) Mentioned first in *190:4-14//*191:3-14 and later in *189:38-45: Some time ago (“pre-viously” in *190 and *191) E. had sent 2 minas 57 shekels of silver with (išti) Šu-Suen, son of Iliya, from Hattum to I. in Kanesh (*191:5), asking him to take it along to Assur. This is also recorded in the undated contract *193, whereby Šu-Suen hands this silver over to E.’s mother and I. in order to have the latter bring it to Assur in order “to pay it for the debt E. owes to tamkārum”, his creditor or boss. In the letters (*189:40-41 // *190:7-8) however, E. states that I. was to use it to buy tin for him, “some 10 minas” (*190:8), to be sent to him in Anatolia (*189:41, ušellâm, *190:8, ušebbalam). There it could be sold by E. with profit and the silver earned in this way (*189:42//*190:10, kaspum elliam) would be used to pay his creditor/boss (tamkārum), “on the basis of my tablet”; *189:42-3 writes “I will pay silver to my tamkārum and (to do so?) send it” (to Assur); *190:10-12 is shorter, “I will send the silver to my tamkārum”. Was this the original intention or a later adaptation of the goal (by inserting an intermediary step), stipulated in contract *193? In Assur, however (*189:44-45 // *190:13), as I. had told him, E.’s sister, no doubt the priestess Ummī-Išhara, required the silver and I. had given it to her, ana ša ṭuppika (*189:45//*190:14//*191:14). This suggests that there was a contractual basis for it, possibly a recorded liability or promise of E., perhaps the basis for the stipulation in text *193 that I. would use the silver to pay E.’s debts. I assume that Ummī-Išhara’s “need” for the silver was due to the fact that, after their father’s death, she was engaged in liquidating his firm, which implied paying the commercial debts that were the liability of the male heirs, her brothers. She accordingly must have obliged I. to give her the silver E. had earned and not use it for a new commercial enterprise. The same feature can be observed after Pūšu-kēn’s death, when his daughter in Assur, Ahaha, is desperately trying to pay the family’s debts, while her brothers in Anatolia only think of trading.
label: gold

text: b) Having disappointed E. by the outcome of a) I., “later” (urkītam *189:46//190:15), when he was about to leave (for Assur?), came up with a new plan to help E. and “give him courage” (*189:46-49//190:15-20). E. has to give him all the silver he has available and I. will buy for him 10 minas of tin, which will allow E. to earn money. E. manages to collect the modest sum of 1 mina 44 shekels of silver (*189:50-52//190:36-39//191:22-25), sufficient to buy tin in Assur (normally at a rate of ca. 15 shekels of tin for 1 shekel of silver), which he “gave to I. for making purchases” (*189:54) in Hurama, as witnessed by A. and I. (*190:39-40//191:26-27), “under my seals” (*190:39//191:25). This transaction is recorded in *192, witnessed by the same two men, but here (lines 7-8) the silver is said to be “under the seals of tamkārum”, which means of its anonymous owner, perhaps to prevent other creditors of E. to seize it. Since the transaction is for the benefit of E. he has to pay for the costs of the transport, both the “excise” and the “transport fee”, as *189:50-51//*190:37 and *192:2-6 duly mention. *189:54 then continues with E.’s complaint that in exchange for this silver I. has thus far not sent him any tin and in lines 56-57 asks to do so now; cf. *190:43-44, where E. also asks what he has done wrong (šillatam rašā’um) to earn this treatment.

text: c) In *190: 21-34 this sad story is preceded by a report about problems with the sale of a lot of textiles (*190:21, “my textiles”), which I. had entrusted (paqādum) to E. in Luhusaddiya (*191:31-32). A situation with unsafe roads (stative of sahā’um, D-stem) and unyielding local palaces (dannum, *189:16) had obliged E. to wait many months “in the interior” until the trade could be resumed, 8 months in *189:17, 7 months in *190:26 and 6 months in *191:34! The delay had also caused damage of the textiles by moths, apparently because they had not been regularly aired. When they had been finally “salvaged” (šalāhum) their sale proved difficult and their yield was poor, on average only 15 shekels of silver apiece, in all 2½ minas (the 3½ minas of *190:32 may be a mistake). This silver had been received (?) and sealed by I.’s representatives, but had not yet been shipped off (*189:29-32//*190:32:34, ša kīma kuāti, plural // šazzuzātikasic, cf. šazzuzātika in l. 30). Letter *190:32-37 reveals that this was because I.’s plan to let E.’s sister, in this case to all appearances I.’s wife Šalimma (who stayed in Kanesh), take it along on her intended journey to Assur, had failed, because she could not travel due to severe cold in Central Anatolia.
label: gold

text: This story is confirmed by letter *194, written by Dān-Aššur and Ennam-Suen, who must be I.’s “representatives” mentioned in *189:31. They offer a few more details on the composition of the lot of textiles, sealed by Kulumāya (also mentioned in *190:29), which had been delivered to them by E. While *189:22 simply states that E. had brought the textiles to I.’s representatives in Wahšušana, *194:9-15 write that, because they could not be sold “here” and because they had been affected by moths, they were subsequently brought by E. to Šaladuwar, further to the west, and were sold there. Then – so we must assume - E. returned to Wahšušana, presented the silver earned to I.’s representatives, which they had him bring to I. (in Kanesh?) under their seals. This story of the textiles features also in *189:14-32, before episodes a) and b), as continuation of E.’s complaint that he still had not received compensation for his travel expenses (see below d). This is understandable, since for I. the salvage of the textiles was a condition for paying them.
label: gold

text: d) The issue of the travel expenses (gamrum ša harrānim) to which E. is entitled forms the beginning of *189. It was raised in Hurama, where both men met and had a discussion (lines 2-11) and the expenses were those of transporting the textiles, incurred either to get them in Hurama or (more likely) to ship them on, possibly to “Hattum”. It is not certain that this is the lot of textiles entrusted to E. in Luhusaddiya according to *191:31-32, because this town is situated north of Hurama, were the discussion about the expenses took place (*189:3). That I. had to pay expenses and wrote for E. a “document concerning the textiles” (see the note on *189:3) indicates that the textiles belonged to I. and that E. handled them for him (alongside his own business, such as the trade in tin). I. had given him only a little silver, refused to pay E.’s expenses cash (*190:7-8, ana qātim tadānum) and would pay them only after (adi, l. 9) E. had salvaged the textiles (šalāhum, *189:9, cf. šēṣu’um, ‘to get out”, l. 20), by sending him silver from Hahhum, which he failed to do. E. then reminds him of the serious problems encountered, apparently unknown to I., and tells how thanks to the pains he took (anāhum) the textiles are safe, although at the cost of expenses equal to the price of three textiles. Text *190 gives a somewhat different picture by linking episode b) with the salvaging of the textiles and by making the latter an order of I. and thus a condition for his help (*190:21-22): “You said: Exert yourself for my textiles and salvage what you can, so that they do not get lost!”

text: The geographical data of the texts have been studied in Geography 137f., 159f., with the partly duplicating footnotes 437-8 and 546-7, where Barjamovic quotes and discusses texts *189 and *191, that I had made available to him. He describes Luhuzaddiya as “located on a separate route that branched out from the main Euphrates route in Hurama” and passed Kuššara, Šamuha and Kuburnat to arrive at Durhumit, thus connecting the south with Hattum, which he defines as the eastern part of Central Anatolia, “linked to the clusters east of Kanesh” (p. 164). He then offers the following reconstruction, into which I insert between brackets some data, referring to the texts of our file: “More than 6 months beforehand, while Ennam-Aššur was in Luhuzattiya, Irma-Aššur sent him a letter (from Hurama? *189:3 – K.R.V.), some silver and an order on what to do with a consignment of textiles arriving in Hurama from Assur. Thereupon (*189:14f. //*190:23f.) Irma-Aššur continued his journey to Hahhum, where he stayed for a while (*189:10-13) before finally leaving for Assur (implied by *189:41ff.). In the meantime Ennam-Aššur went to Hattum (also referred to as libbi mātim) (*189:18 – K.R.V.), but unrest broke out and the consignment had to be stored in villages there (*189:19). Once the situation had settled down, Ennam-Aššur sent the goods from Hattum to Wahšušana (*189:21-22, cf. *190:30). Furthermore, he sent Šu-Suen from Hattum to Irma-Aššur in Kaneš with a sum of money (*189:39, *190:5-6).”
label: gold

text: A slight modification of this picture is that at the start I. himself was apparently present in Hurama, where he instructed E. about how to ship the silver earned by the textiles to Assur (*189:32f.) and where E. (on the same occasion?) gave him the 1 mina 44 shekels of silver (*190:40, *191:27, cf. *192). This asks for a different meaning for the “missive” (našpertum) I. gave to E. there (see note on *189:3). The main question, also raised by the different order in which our sources relate the events, is whether all refer to one single journey, from Hurama to Luhusaddiya, to Hattum, to Wahššušana, to Šaladuwar and perhaps eventually back to Kanesh. I find it difficult to assume that E.’s activity in Hattum, mentioned at the beginning of *190 (line 4, “previously’) was in consequence of the meeting with I. in Hurama and the acceptance of a consignment of textiles in Luhusaddiya. *191:31ff. indicate that the textiles suffered under the long delay “in the interior” of Hattum and the position of *189:15ff. also suggests that the meeting in Hurama (*190:3) preceded these events. If so, the shipment by E. of almost 3 minas of silver of his to I. in Kanesh (*190:4ff., *189:38ff.) must have preceded these events and points to an earlier stay of E. in Hattum, which he may have interrupted in order to come to Luhusaddiya / Hurama to receive a new consignment. Why this consignment was picked up in Luhusaddiya (*191:31), after a meeting in the more southern Hurama, is unclear. Geography 135 mentions that “one could travel directly from Timilkiya to Luhusaddiya and so avoid taxation in Šalahšuwa and Hurama, but this required a royal guide or smuggling”, but these are not mentioned in our text.

text: It is not easy to understand this record. Ir’am-Aššur apparently had received silver of Šuli, via Ennam-Suen (l. 8), for a commercial purpose, which obviously should be paid back in some way to its owner. He may have been approached by the three men mentioned in lines 1-4, among whom a son of Šuli, or he has summoned them and in front of witnesses told them that his case already had been settled by three other men, including a brother of Šuli, so that Šuli’s son (and heir) is satisfied (l. 15) and Šuli himself cannot claim anything from him. The payment apparently had been indirect, perhaps in the framework of a larger settlement of accounts, which may have taken place if indeed Šuli was not longer alive (as suggested in the comment on line 5). The three men summoned acknowledge this by the rather puzzling statement “we have satisfied Šuli with the silver”. Our understanding is also hampered by their following remark, that they leave it to the/a tamkārum to sue Ir’am-Aššur for the silver he still owes on the basis of tablet. This may also point to a more general settlement of accounts that could result in new debt-notes, at times also ones that left the creditor anonymous (calling him tamkārum), e.g. because it was not yet clear who was entitled to the money (e.g. when a firm was liquidated). But there may be other explanations, since tamkārum could also mean the manager of a joint-stock capital or the boss of a firm.

text: According to Kt 93/k 513:17 (courtesy of C. Michel) Šalimma was a daughter of Elamma; in *206:23 she calls Elamma’s wife and his sons “her mother and brothers”. She was married to Ir’am-Aššur, son of Id(d)i-bāni (see for him Ch. XI), as we know from *206, which deals with the problems between them (see below and Veenhof 2007b).[1] Since Elamma’s son Ennam-Aššur in *190:34 addresses her husband as “my father, my lord”, he probably was somewhat older and this might apply to Šalimma too, since according to *208 she had two grown-up sons, Šu-Ištar and Aššur-imittī, active in Kanesh, to whom she writes a letter from Assur. She may have been Elamma’s oldest daughter, perhaps even a daughter from a first marriage, but there is no proof for that. She could have been the mother of Ir’am-Aššur’s daughter Suhkana, married off in Kanesh to a certain Aššur-mālik according to Kt 94/k 149 (edited by Michel-Garelli 1995, 298f.), and this Suhkana then could have been one of her “children” (šerrū) mentioned in Ummī-Išhara’s letter *206:31-33. But Suhkana may also have been a daughter from an earlier marriage of Ir’am-Aššur.
label: gold

text: The house in which Šalimma lived in Kanesh must have been the one of her husband Ir’am-Aššur, also after the latter had returned to Assur and she had refused to join him, as *206 tells us. When she eventually returned to Assur her two sons may have continued to live in it, as suggested by *208, unless they moved to the house she bought according to *210. We would expect records that belonged to her to have turned up in her own house, from which presumably the first group excavated in 1994 (Kt 94/k 114-187; see Ch. XI, introduction) in another part of the lower town originates. The information provided by C. Michel reveals that this group of texts includes a debt-note (Kt 94/k 137) in which Šalimma is the creditor of three Anatolians (Dalaš, Kikaršan and Taliya) for an amount of 15 shekels of silver, and a contract (Kt 94/k 181, an unopened envelope) about the purchase by Šalimma of a boy from an Anatolian man (Dušala) and his two sons. The presence in Elamma’s house of the letter *206, addressed to her and her mother Lamassutum, if not one of two copies, is not surprising and this obtains also for the letter once encased in the envelope *207. The presence in Elamma’s house of *209 and *210, in which Šalimma is creditor and buyer, and of the letter written to her sons, *208, may be due to what happened after her return to Assur, but we have no information on it. The family ties between Elamma and Ir’am-Aššur may also be responsible for the presence of a few records of members of one family in the archive of the other, such as some documents of Lamassutum in Ir’am-Aššur’s archive (a debt-note of her, Kt 94/k 120, and a contract with Iddin-Aššur about the conditional sale of a girl, dated to eponymy year 100).[2]

text: A long, emotional letter sent from Assur by Elamma’s daughter Ummī-Išhara to her mother Lamassutum and in particular to her sister Šalimma in Kanesh, on the problems the latter is causing by her refusal to join her husband Ir’am-Aššur in Assur, of which Ummī-Išhara, due to her efforts to mediate between the two, is becoming the victim. I have edited this remarkable letter, with a long commentary, in Veenhof 2007b, to which I refer the reader for detailed comments. The assumption that she did return in the end to Assur is perhaps confirmed by her mention in Kt c/k 30+:16-17 (courtesy Dercksen), a list of amounts of silver sent to Assur: “10 shekels (of silver) a gift/consignment (šēbultum) for Šalimma and Masātum”.

This is confirmed by the presence of two different seal impressions, observed by Mrs Omura, of which one belongs to Ir’am-Aššur. text: The Anatolian couple probably had become indebted by a loan or by the obligation to deliver goods already paid for and the debt rated in silver is to be paid back in grain. The fact that payment in silver (called “to give back”, ta’’urum) is only an alternative shows that the goal of Šalimma’s transaction was to obtain grain, presumably not for commercial purposes, but for her own stocks. Another contract that offers such a choice is Kt d/k 20B:13-16, concerning a silver debt of 45 shekels, “If they give (back) barley, it will be deducted from their account according to the current rate of exchange”. This implies that the 6 sacks of line 4 are the equivalent of the 15 shekels of silver, which yields an acceptable price of 2½ shekels of silver for one sack of grain.[3] I thus assume that lines 4-7 do not state the amount of interest to be paid, “6 sacks of grain (uṭṭutum), 1½ of which are wheat”, but that the main sentence consists of l. 4+8a: “6 sacks of grain ..... they will pay at harvest time”, into which the stipulation about interest is embedded, where the use of the verb šaqālum in l. 8 reflects that what the debtor had received was silver. The use of ina ŠÀ.BA, “thereof”, to denote the interest on a debt is strange and unique.[4] ŠÀ.BA is used to specify the composition of an amount of goods, e.g. that an amount of grain to be delivered must consist of two different kinds, barley and wheat - hulled barley and bread wheat, best attested among plant remains from Central Anatolia from this period [5] - and it seems possible that the writer of our contract was influenced by it. The amount of interest, 1½ sacks of wheat, considering that wheat is often 50% more expensive than barley,[6] would equal an interest of at least 2½ sacks of barley or ca. 40 to 50%, which is an acceptable rate. It is a pity that little remains of the text on the envelope, which might have given a clue. The obligation, mentioned after the payment clause, that they will give 10 breads as “additional gift”, is a well-known feature, studied by Matouš 1965, 180f., "Exkurs über Zugaben".

text: The due date for the expected payment in grain is harpū, the summer, the time of the harvest; that for payment in silver some months later, at the festival of Anna, in autumn, probably to leave the debtors some time to acquire silver by selling part of their harvest. This seems to be a more general pattern and for examples I refer to OBO 160/5, 242f., where the due date for grain is also designated as “at harvest time” (ina ebūrim) and “on the threshing-floor” (ina/ina erāb adrim), and that for silver also as “when the grapes are plucked” (ina qitip kerānim),[7] which means in early autumn.

text: “Seal of the Kanesh colony. The colony passed the following judgment: Amur-Ištar will swear by Aššur’s dagger (6) that he house has truly been bought with Šalimma’s silver, that he (tablet adds: his heart) honestly did not know that the silver belonged to Lamassutum. If he does not swear Lamassutum will swear by the tambourine(?) of Ištar (15) that the house was not bought with Iddin-Suen's silver, but was bought with her own silver. If she swears the house is her house. Should Amur-Ištar and Lamassutum (20) (both) not swear but reach a compromise, the colony will take 4 minas of silver from the price of the house.

text: This verdict may well concern the house bought by Šalimma from her sister and brother according to *208. The names of the persons mentioned in the verdict may support this view, for Amur-Ištar could be Elamma's brother of that name and Iddin-Suen the father of Elamma and Amur-Ištar. The ownership of the house depends on the question whether it was paid with the buyer's private money or with money «of the family» (inherited from Iddin-Suen). That Šalimma herself is not present and does not swear suggests that she had died (in Assur, where she had returned?) and that the ownership of the house had to be established before it could be inherited (by Amur-Ištar?). Amur-Ištar first gets the opportunity to swear to defend his case and it is remarkable that he not only has to confirm the purchase with Šalimma's money (as he no doubt had claimed), but also his honesty by denying any knowledge of what the other party has claimed. If he fails (refuses) to do so the other party is not automatically granted the ownership, because there are still two possibilities: purchase with the money inherited from the pater familias (which must have consequences for the inheritance) or with Lamassutum’s private money. Unfortunately we do not know what was the result of the oath procedure.

text: If both parties at the last moment - after the colony had convened and the verdict had been issued and before the oath ceremony- reach a compromise, the colony will be indemnified for the trouble they had caused it by a heavy fine to be paid by the parties. This heavy fine probably served as a deterrent, which is understandable in view of the great number of legal cases to be tried by the colonial authorities. Parties are warned to consider carefully whether they are going to make an appeal. In our case they might consider whether the price of an Assyrian house in the colony was high enough to run that risk.

text: [6] There are great differences in the prices of grain, see also Michel 1997a 101, with notes 49-51. They were conditioned by the time of the year, the situation (CCT 5, 37a:5, ina dannitim, “during distress, famine”), and the purpose (private comsumption or trade, purchase or sale). In TC 2, 53:1-16 wheat plus barley were purchased for on average 7 shekels of silver per sack and sold at double that price, followed by cases where persons “took” barley or wheat for much lower prices. In ATHE 12:22-25 the price of wheat was even 18 shekels per sack (4½ shekels per jar). In ICK 2, 2:2'-4' wheat was ca. two and a half times more expensive than barley (“30 sacks of barley instead of 12 sacks of wheat”), but in Kt 88/k 71:15-17 (see AoF 35 [2008] 97) the difference was only ca. 50% (barley at ca. 1 1/6 shekel per sack, wheat ca. 1 2/3 shekel) and in *343 barley cost 3 shekels per sack, wheat 5 shekels.

text: The house of Elamma contained about thirty texts related to a certain Ennam-Suen, letters written to and by him (alone or with others), legal documents, in which he is the key figure, as party in a conflict, as guarantor, and as creditor or debtor. In most cases the name of his father is not mentioned and the assumption that these texts concern the same man rests for several of them on their subject matter and the persons involved, and for all of them on the fact that they were found in the same house. As their excavation numbers, ranging from Kt 92/k 94 to 187, show (only *228 was found in 1991), they were discovered in 1992, according to Tahsin Özgüç’s letter to me “collapsed on the floor of the south side of the second room”. He adds that “they enabled us to describe the presence of a new Assyrian merchant”, which most probably (he does not mention a name) refers to Ennam-Suen. The 1992 group, however, also comprises a fair number of records of Elamma and Lamassutum (letters, memorandums, etc., mainly those with excavations numbers between Kt 92/k 142-162), which suggests that there were (at least) two different groups or files, probably arranged as such on shelves, which were mixed up due to their collapse on the floor. Data on the remains of containers or exact find spots to confirm this idea are not available.
label: gold

text: Ennam-Suen was a very popular name and we know some forty different men so named. Only two texts of our group give the name of his father, Amur-Šamaš in *232:4-8, where Ennam-Suen and his younger brother Āl-ṭāb appear as debtors of an unnamed creditor, and in *233:7-8, a quittance for a debt Ennam-Suen owed to Ilam-kurub.[1] Their subject matter does not link up with that of the other texts, but if Āl-ṭāb was indeed the brother of “our” Ennam-Suen, it becomes understandable why he acted as his guarantor in *226 during eponymy year 82,[2] which is only one year later than *232. The dated occurrences of Ennam-Suen in our file, always in debt-notes, eponymy years 82 (*229), 92 (*230), 96 (*231), and 99 (*228), have a time range which is entirely possible for one single trader. Moreover, the excavation numbers of the two texts mentioning his father, Kt 92/k 163(*233) and 164(*232) link them with other ‘Ennam-Suen texts’, which makes it likely that the same Ennam-Suen, son of Amur-Šamaš, is meant in all of them. While the quittance *233 would normally belong to the debtor’s archive, the debt-note *232 in its envelope would be expected in that of the creditor.
label: gold

text: An Ennam-Suen occurs four times in the lists of textiles published in Ch. XX, regularly together with Iddin-Suen, Šu-Ištar, Aššur-rē’ī and a few others, the first two of which also feature among his correspondents in the letters published in this chapter. This suggest that the Ennam-Suen in both groups is the same person. In the comments on the textile lists I argued that they probably deal with substantial lots of textiles belonging to traders who had cooperated in a joint caravan (ellutum), which arrived in Kanesh and were cleared in the palace. The Ennam-Suen of this chapter probably is also the one who in *219:9-10 (a letter of Aššur-imittī to Ennam-Aššur) is involved in the settlement of a problem concerning a lot of textiles. Other occurrences of an Ennam-Suen in texts of the 1992 group, without mention of his father’s name, such as *245:8 (witness to a seizure by Šu-Ištar of silver belonging to Bēlum-rabi), do not allow conclusions on his identity. In particular not because in our group we twice meet a different Ennam-Suen, who is the son of Aššur-ṭāb. In *279:17-18 he testifies before the Wahšušana colony about a settlement of accounts between two traders, and in *284:16-17 he witnesses Ṭāb-ṣilli-Aššur’s “seizure” of Šu-Suen.

text: It is impossible to identify one of them as a man whose close relationship with Elamma could account for the presence of his tablets in Elamma’s archive. Witnessing a debt-note may be due to a relation with its creditor, but not necessarily so, and cooperation in a joint caravan (ellutum), “an organizational form for joint conveyance of merchandise” by “groups formed on an ad hoc basis” (OAI 167f.), does not prove a lasting partnership. This applies also to *53, whose anonymous writer (who could be Elamma) states that he will collect an amount of silver as “one third share (šalšātum) in the caravan of Ennam-Suen”.
label: gold

text: Most other occurrences of an Ennam-Suen in texts from Elamma’s archive also prove little. In *209:4 he is witness for a debt with Šalimma as creditor, in *251 he acts together with Muti-Aššur as judge in a conflict between Aššur-mālik and Šū-Bēlum, and in *76:10-13 // *77: 5-10 (see the comments on these texts) we meet an Ennam-Suen indebted for two amounts of copper to the anonymous writer of these texts. Most promising is *164:28-30, which mentions that Ištar-pilah, Ennam-Suen and Maṣi-ilī as Lamassutum’s representatives will see to the conveyance of what she bequeathed to Assur. This responsible task suggests a relationship, in particular with Elamma’s widow, who still lived in Kanesh. A hypothetical explanation, if our Ennam-Suen was the son of Šu-Ištar, is that at some time, perhaps when he went back to Assur to become līmum in year REL 115, boxes with tablets of his were deposited in Elamma’s house (ana nabšêm ezābum), but this is difficult to prove. We can only study the texts as they have been preserved. They show him to have been an active trader, especially as owner of lots of textiles, and it is interesting that he occurs in these records together with Iddin-Suen and Šu-Ištar, who also figure in his other texts, notably in letters to and from him. The dates of these and other texts in which he occurs range (if indeed all concern the same man) from the year REL 82 to the years after Lamassutum’s death, which anyhow makes it impossible to identify the just mentioned Iddin-Suen with Elamma’s father of that name.

The verb nadā’um is regularly used for “depositing” textiles in the colonial office, as investment in a collective transaction and this could be done in installments, in which connection also the adjective panium, «first, earlier», and the adverb ina pana, «in the first place», occur. text: 22-23. This is an informative description of a judicial oath procedure, designated by the words ana mamītim palālum + personal object, which uses a verb restricted to OA (CAD P, palālu B; see now OALP 364-367) and only attested in such contexts. The occurrences show that palālum could affect a party, but also the witnesses he might summon. In our text palālum was the initiative of a man who tried to force his opponent to accept this procedure. In the somewhat similar verdict TTC 4 = EL 339:10-12 a formal interrogation leads to suing one’s opponent: “The attorney of P. and P.’s representatives will .... interrogate E. and he shall answer them (10) and where they are going to sue (him) they will palālum” (a-le / iše’ūni / ipallilū). RA 88 (1994) 122:30f., shows that this leads to an oath, “where we will palālum the attorney must make (him) swear an oath” (ašar ni-pá-li-lu rābiṣum / lutammi). The question remains whether this, expressed in our text by palālum ana mamītim, is (has to be) always the case. See also Veenhof, Lex., s.v.

text: Our letter mentions two possibilities for the palālum procedure:
label: gold

text: a) The plaintiff writes a letter in which he states his grievances to his representatives in the place where his opponent lives, they can make him swear, in which case the resulting sealed tablet (with his testimony or acknowledgment) must be returned to the opponent's repres-entatives, in the place where the plaintiff lives.
label: gold

text: b) If this does not succeed, the plaintiff must “force the opponent to move” (nasāhum, Š-stem), to come to where the plaintiff lives, where he will swear the oath (lūmā). The writer adds lines 31-32, “I will come if you take responsibility and then we can discuss the matter there” (where you live). He uses the stative of the verb maṣā’um, typical for expressing that a plaintiff, in an appeal to the authorities, is ready to accept the responsibility and bear the costs of the legal action undertaken, especially the forced transfer of a person who has to appear in court (cf. already OACC 257-259). The oath sworn (l. 30) is not the end of the proceedings, for it can be followed by a discussion (atwûm) on the basis of the contents of the oath and the facts so established, to solve the problem.
label: gold

text: The wording of the oath was carefully formulated in advance, to cover the relevant issues and prevent a verbal escape, as shown by records that start with the statement: “Listen oh god, lord of the oath” (e.g. EL 284 = CCT 5, 14b). In Elamma’s archive *287, a sealed, unopened envelope with the inscription “This is the tablet of the oath of K. son of A.”, must have been such a case.[4] I assume that in our letter the suggestion to write down “the grievances” in a letter had a double purpose: to state that and why the accused has to swear and to record the issues at stake, so that the representatives could carefully formulate what he had to swear.

text: Comment
label: gold

text: Was the writer, called Šarrum-kīn, whose name is preceded by MAŠ, perhaps the (later) king Šarrum-kīn, who as prince as some time would have been present and active in Anatolia, in Wašhaniya? The issue of the letter is a conflict of the writer with one of the three addressees (“you”, l. 6), who accuses him of having removed textiles from the house of the writer (l. 12). The writer rejects this accusation and states that the (local Anatolian) palace is responsible for it, during his absence. He mentions that it had used the service of four Assyrians, “affiliated traders” (lines 9-14), who had searched his house and removed the textiles. This is a remarkable procedure, which implies that the palace had a valid claim and had decided (or was authorized?) to realize it by using Assyrians, perhaps because they could read the sealings on the (bags with) textiles, to identify those of the man they were after. The writer is ready to provide his opponent with a written statement (“tablet”) to that effect (l. 20), presumably (a copy of?) the testimony recorded under oath by these four witnesses, mentioned in lines 19f. If that is not enough he is ready to submit himself to a formal oath procedure, which should clear the facts and allow to solve the matter in a discussion (atwûm, l. 32).

text: Three letters from Šu-Ištar: “Get rid of the maid!” (215-217)
label: gold

text: The following three letters – the third one could be a second page or a letter without proper address – all deal with the same issue, a maid (amtum) who is wicked (raggat) and contracts debts, of whom the writer, who stays elsewhere, wants to get rid (halluqum). He describes what she has done and asks Ennam-Suen, alone in *217 and together with Kukua and Uṣur-ša-Aššur in *216, and presumably also in *218 (address missing), men who live in Kanesh (“there”) where the maid also lives, to sell her. But not to people of Kanesh and Assyrian traders, but to foreigners, men from Talhat, a town across the Euphrates in Northern Meso-potamia (see Veenhof 2008b, 18ff.).[5] In this way she will not turn up again in Kanesh (*216:29) and her buyers must be instructed not to bring her back (*218:19).
label: gold

text: We do not know who the maid was. Considering her role (see *217:13-15) and the fact that in *217:18 she is designated as awīltum, probably the Anatolian wife (for whom the designation amtum was used) of the writer, who is called “her lord/owner” (*216:15), a term that does not necessarily mean he owned her as a slave, because bēlum is also used for the husband who is his wife’s “lord”. Šu-Ištar may have acquired her from her parents by paying an amount of silver (some marriage records - AKT 1, 77:18, TPAK 1, 161A:1, and Kt n/k 1414:6 - do mention the payment of a bride’s “price”, šīmū). While selling a slave-girl was her owner’s right, selling one’s Anatolian bride would have been unacceptable, unless the girl’s misbehavior might have been a sufficient reason for doing so. Marriage contracts mention such a “misdeed” (šillutum, Kt 91/k 132:13 and Kt d/k 29A:10, not necessarily restricted to sexual misbehavior) and the latter stipulates that in that case she is sent away with only a single toggle pin (ina ištêt tudittim, l. 11) to fasten her garment. The best parallel to the treatment of the maid in our text is provided by Kt 94/k 141, in which an Anatolian girl married as amtu-wife will be “stripped of her garment and cloak and sent away naked(?) if she is false or commits any act of impudence”.[6] Because these contracts mention sending her away, but not the right to sell her into slavery, the relation between maid and “lord” may have been different in our contract and I also note that the sale to foreigners looks like a questionable deal (one might translate halliqāši also by “make her disappear”), which has to carried out by cheating her.
label: gold

text: Šu-Ištar is probably identical to the man of that name who occurs in several lists of textiles, where also Ennam-Suen figures, and he could be the one who has a legal fight with Ennam-Suen in *224. Our three letters exhibit a few peculiarities, such as the plene writing of the pronominal suffix (*216:15.20.23; *217:12; *218:6), the use of TA for dá, and ahhū’a attunu written with crasis as a-hu-a-tù-nu *(216:11 and *218:1), while *216 and *217 spell qibima in the address with the sign bi2, which is uncommon. These features may be due to Šu-Ištar, if he himself wrote these letters that deal with a rather personal affair.

text: 10. The purpose of the action designated as karābum (see the note one l. 11) is indicated as ana li-ta-tim, which is difficult. There is a noun litum (lit(t)um or lītum) in OA, four occurrences of which CAD L 151 registers under lē/ītu, “cheek, side”, assuming (under 2,c, on the basis of occurrences in OB letters of the qualification ša litika) a meaning “persons and assets for which one is responsible / under one’s authority”, stating for OA: “with the connotation of assets”. Registering our word under lētum must have been suggested by the (unique) plene-writing in TC 2, 53:7’, “We paid 13½ shekels (of silver?) ana le-e-tí-im”, in a series of small payments for various expenses, some related to transport. But in most OA occurrences of litum, where small amounts of silver or copper are given to a person “at the time of” (inūmi or ina) his litum», and “when he made his litum” (Kt. 86/k 201:1-3, 10-12, 25-27), a meaning “assets” makes no sense. Dercksen 2011:63-65 opts for some kind of ritual, which involved a meal. He bases his interpretation on texts like Kt c/k 1147 and Kt 91/k 201. In lines 1-11 and 22-27 of the latter small amounts of silver (between 1 and 2 shekels) are given to various men, when they “went up” (elā’um) to a temple (twice that of Išhara) or “when he made his litum” (inūmi litišu ēpušu), mentioned alongside such a payment for a trip to the City (of Assur). Other texts mention the occasion as ina litišu (5 times i-li-tí-šu). But what kind of ritual or ceremonial act litum was remains unclear. And since the phrase li-tí-šu ēpuš could very well contain a plural litū (also in i-li-tí-šu), the connection with li-ta-tim in our text is also ambiguous. The meaning of the action thus remains unclear, see also Veenhof Lex., s.v.
label: gold

text: 11-16. The meaning of ana litātim akrubka is not clear. The action apparently cost silver, since it deprived Ennam-Suen of what would accrue to him. To make up for it(?) his opponent promises to guarantee him his expenses, perhaps those due for the act of karābum. This verb is well attested in OA with a personal dative, “to pray, invoke a blessing for somebody”, usually “before” (mahar) a deity, cf. CAD K 196, 3, a. There are also a few examples of a meaning “to vow / offer” something to a deity, an “offering” (ikribum), or a precious object (RIMA 1, 43, no. 2:8; POAT 10:23). The writer of Kt 91/k 156 mentions that three times he offered / vowed small amounts (once 90 shekels of copper and twice 1 shekel of silver, probably its equivalent) for a named man (ana PN akrub). And the one of Kt 91/k 201 did the same (amounts of 1½ shekel of silver and 1 mina of copper) on three occasions, twice for a man “when he went (up) to the City” (13-18, 31-33).[7] Dercksen 2011, 64, who quotes these texts, renders the verb as “to give for a sacrifice”, but since the verb in our texts is not used with a personal dative, but with a personal accusative object (lines 11-16) this interpretation is impossible here.

text: The situation is complicated, because somebody else than the debtor paid to somebody else than the creditor and there is no mention of a quittance. Therefore the person collecting the debt instead of the creditor is obliged to clear the debtor from future claims by the creditor. Such a claim would be possible if the recipient of the payment had not passed it on to the creditor or had not informed him about it. The relation between Pilah-Ištar (attested in ICK 2,132:41; TC 2, 56:3’; TC 3, 251A:2; Kt 87, 384:24; and *232:1, where he is witness to a debt owed by Ennam-Suen and Āl-ṭāb) and the creditor is unknown. Pilah-Ištar could be his representative or associate, or Kurub-Ištar could have ceded the debt-note to him, perhaps even in order to meet a claim. Note the absence of the clause that, if the debt-note turns up it is invalid, usually inserted in quittances if the debt-note could not be immediately returned to the debtor. That this contract was still in its envelope indicates that it had not been necessary to (open and) use it, because no problems had arisen.

text: As we learn from *232:7-8 (dated to the year REL 81), Āl-ṭāb probably was a brother of Ennam-Suen, both sons of Amur-Šamaš, which explains why he (together with Aššur-šamšī) took the risk of acting as guarantor for him. According to *226:8 (from the year REL 82) Ennam-Suen had also guaranteed and paid for him 12 shekels of silver, and *225 records how, together with Šu-Ištar, he had guaranteed for Āl-ṭāb in a transaction concerning men from Kilir. He may also have been the man who according to *326 had paid 43 shekels of silver on behalf of Āl-ṭāb. That a guarantor tried to protect himself against the risk of subsidiary liability, which could force him to pay for the debtor, is known from several texts (see Veenhof 2001:122), but establishing a hypothecary security on property of the debtor is rather unique. The high value of a house in Assur made it an attractive security for a substantial silver debt.

text: The texts published here belonged to or concern men called Šu-Ištar and the question is whether they refer to the same person and if so who he was. Both questions are difficult to answer, because only one text in this chapter mentions the name of his father, Luzinu. If this is a variant of or mistake for Luzina, we could identify him as this well-known trader, who occurs a dozen times as father of Šu-Ištar. In *243 Šu-Ištar, son of Luzinu, features as the owner of two textiles sold by Liptānum to Iddin-Aššur and he probably kept this document about items he owned. The excavation number of this text (Kt 91/k 511) does not link it with the group Kt 91/k 534-551, to which most ‘Šu-Ištar texts’ presented in this chapter belong and in which Šu-Ištar plays a role as writer or recipient of letters, creditor or party in a conflict.
label: gold

text: Šu-Ištar was a popular name and in the Kültepe texts there figure at least forty different Šu-Ištars. The names of their fathers are usually given in legal documents, especially when they are witnesses, but we also have witnesses without patronym (e.g. Šu-Ištar in *199:19, during eponymy year 94). In Elamma’s archive we meet - apart from the week eponym Šu-Ištar, son of Aššur-bāni, and Šu-Ištar, the father of the year-eponym Ennam-Suen (REL 115) - six men whose father is called Šu-Ištar and at least five Šu-Ištars with different fathers; the latter are:

text: The first, the son of Dadānum, is the best attested one, also outside our archive. He features in ATHE 1:1, during the year REL 93, and as witness in three undated records of Elamma’s archive, *15:3, *110:24 (an agreement involving Elamma), and *202:14. In*3:16 and 22 Elamma is told that this Šu-Ištar, together with Ennam-Aššur, exports (šēṣu’um) or bringen (wabālum) merchandise to him, obviously from Assur, where he is also in *15:3 (as witness) and in AKT 1, 7:25. His role as transporter is confirmed by TC 3, 26:34, where he will convey messages from Assur to Kanesh, by BIN 4, 13:5-6, where his seals are on a load of merchandise, and by AKT 6, 865:10-11 (courtesy of Larsen), where he conducts textiles to Anatolia. According to VS 26, 47:7-8 he ships silver from Kanesh to Assur, in TC 1, 70:24 he is present there as witness when silver is entrusted for transport, and in CCT 5, 29a:16-17 he is in Hahhum. He was not only a transporter, but also himself a trader and Prag I 750:5-6 mentions a debt-note of his for 12 minas of silver.
label: gold

text: We already met a Šu-Ištar in *223, as guarantor of Āl-ṭāb, and in the letters *215-*217 (Ch. XIII) as correspondent of Ennam-Suen. The spelling of these letters, as pointed out in the introduction to them, shows a few scribal peculiarities, which do not return in other ‘Šu-Ištar texts’. Šu-Ištar also occurs five times as owner of lots of textiles in the lists presented in Ch. XX (alongside Ennam-Suen, Aššur-rē’ī, and others) and one of them, *121, deals with textiles owned by him and Ennam-Suen. Important is the presence in the archive of *151, which lists the expenses of a shipment of merchandise of Šu-Ištar, specified on the basis of its “declared value” (awītum; almost 5 talents of tin, equal to probably three or four donkey-loads of tin and textiles), which indicates that it was part of a larger, collective caravan (ellutum). It cannot be accidental that *150 is a very similar record about a shipment of Iddin-Suen, who appears alongside Šu-Ištar in several of the textile lists. Something similar may well be the background of *126, according to which “we – I, Kura and Šu-Ištar – came together and gave account (awātam tadānum) to Pilah-Ištar, son of Uzua, because of the losses”, presumably suffered by such a caravan. It is not unlikely, though difficult to prove, that the texts of the present chapter concern this Šu-Ištar
label: gold

text: Texts of Šu-Ištar in this chapter shed light on his commercial activities and contacts. Some record debt claims of his, which he would have carefully kept: *241 is a copy of a debt-note for silver due from Ikūnum, with an added memo on various other debt claims (in all for ca. 110 shekels of silver); *242 a contract for a silver debt (amount missing) due by Ilī-ālum, with an agreement on its payment. Text *243 is a deposition dealing with textiles that belonged to him, and *244 one by witnesses concerning a private summons, whereby Šu-Ištar tried to collect a debt of 4 shekels of gold owed by Puzur-Aššur, son of Itur-ilī. *235 and *236 are letters of Šu-Ištar to his representatives Puzur-Aššur and Ikuppi-Aššur about an overdue debt of 3 minas of silver owed by a certain Idnāya; *237 he wrote to Kudādum and two Anatolians. These letters must be archive copies or they were later returned to him by the addressees. Of the letters addressed to him *238 (by three men) deals with a large number of textiles packed in bags, which he “left in the house of Galua”; *239 deals with a possible debt to Iliš-tikal and *240 with the sale of wool and a silver loan. In the transactions mentioned in *238 and *240 Pūšu-kēn is somehow involved and *240:14 mentions an agreement between Šu-Ištar and Ir’am-Aššur.
label: gold

text: Because it seems rather likely that tablets with consecutive excavation numbers belonged to one group or file, a few more tablets with numbers between Kt 91/k 534-551 may have belonged to Šu-Ištar, although this is difficult to prove from their content. In the letter *273 (Kt 91/545) the name of the addressee is missing, *338 (Kt 91/548) is an anonymous memo in the first person singular, while *299 (Kt 91/k 535) records a debt owed to “the creditor”. This group also comprises some completely isolated tablets, such as *271 (Kt 91/k 539), a letter from Abduata to Unapše, *263 (Kt 91/k 543) an isolated letter from Šat-Tašmētim, *267 (Kt 91/k 547) a letter(?) by Šamaš-bāni, and *268 (Kt 91/k 550) a letter by Puzur-Ana and Aššur-rabi to Šu-Bēlum. Since it is better to keep separate what cannot be proved to belong together, I did not include these last texts in this chapter. The just-mentioned four letters figure among the “Letters from and to various persons” of Ch. XVI; the other texts find their place in Chs. XIX and XXI.

text: In 1992 Professor Tahsin Özgüc asked me to take care of the edition of the cuneiform tablets excavated by him in kārum Kanesh during the year 1991 and the beginning of 1992, when the excavation of the second house investigated in 1991 was completed. I gratefully accepted his invitation and when studying the more than 600 tablets during the following years it turned out that they belonged to three different archives. The first consisted of Kt 91/k 100-284, which according to the excavator was found in 1990 «north of the Elamma house in LII-LIII/126-127 plan square». I hope, my age and health permitting, to publish this archive in the future. The third archive comprised Kt 92/k 188-263, found in 1992 in the house in grid quare LV-LVI/126-127, and it was published by me in 2010 as Kültepe Tabletleri V (TTKY VI/33c), «The Archive of Kuliya, son of Ali-abum». The second and largest archive, comprising Kt 91/k 285-568 and Kt 92/k 94-187, is the archive of Elamma, son of Iddin-Suen, and his family; it is published in this volume. Workon this large archive took many many years, with many visits to the Museum in Ankara and was frequently interrupted due to various administrative and academic duties, including the publication of some other books.[1] Moreover, I gave priority to the publication of the above-mentioned «Archive of Kuliya», which also yielded the first «Kültepe Eponym List» (KEL A), which I edited separately in 2003.

text: It is a plesant duty to thank all those who have made this publication possible. In the first place the excavator and his staff, who retrieved these cuneiform documents from a heavily damaged house. Fikri Kulakoǧlu, the current director of the Kültepe excavations, apart from showing me the ruins of Elamma's house in the lower town of Kanesh, provided me with some additional information on the circumstances of the discovery. I am grateful to the directors of the Anadolu Medeniyetleri Müzesi for giving me the opportunity to work in their museum and to the ladies of the Tablet Seksyonu, who made the tablets available to me during my many visits over the years, in particular to Sherife Yilmaz, who also helped me with information on some tablets and carried out some collartions. I am grateful to Cahit Günbatti, Irfan Albayrak and Hakan Erol, of the University of Ankara, who answered questions and helped me with various collations. text: The help of and cooperation with all those named have substantially improved the quality of my book. Of course, not all problems of reading and interpretation could be solved and I take responsibility for remaining errors and imperfections of the manuscript that was handed in camera-ready. But I do hope that the result will convince others that cooperation and sharing of data between all those working on «Kültepe tablets» is very profitable for all parties. May the new initiative of the «Kültepe International Meeting» (started in Sept. 2013) stimulate personal contacts and provide a forum for exchange of data, views and scholarly discussion.

text: The publication of new cuneiform texts always requires philological notes and comments on their reading, translation and interpretation, because a simple translation is often not sufficient for their understanding, certainly not for those not initiated in the world of Old Assyrian trade, but he edition of a large archive allows only a limited space for them. The notes added to the texts give, when necessary, short information on the reading and meaning of the words, comment on points of grammar, refer to parallel texts, provide some prosopographic and chronological data, and may refer to the literature. The comments on the texts in the present editions deal in a concise way with the meaning and implication of the texts, but in some cases, where I considered a text especially interesting or important, more elaborate comments were necessary. Realizing the limitations of an archival edition, I have over the years edited a number of important texts from the archive that required a more detailed commentary in articles, often in a Festschrift for a colleague. I list them here by their number in this volume (full titles can be found in the Bibliography) for easy reference.

text: New texts also acquaint us with new, rare or difficult words and with additional, more specific or clearer attestions of them, not yet or not well treated in our dictionaries, which were completed before most of the texts excavated since 1948 became available. To account for my translations they had to be discussed in notes of lexical content, some of which became long and occupied too much room in this volume. Some could be presented in the above-mentioned publications of a number of important texts, to which the notes in this volume then refer. In other cases I decided to take them out of this volume and to present them in a forthcoming, alphabetically arranged article, «Contributions to Old Assyrian Lexicography», to be published in the journal Orientalia (Roma), to which I refer in the notes to some texts in this volume by means of «Veenhof, Lex., s.v. ».[2]

text: The photos acompanying this volume of course can only show a selection of the tablets. Principles of selection were in general the importance of a text or text type, the presence of seal impressions and the state of preservation, to show the basis for the reading of a damaged tablet. The selection also includes some exceptionally well or badly written texts, some large or very small tablets, and it tries to document to some extent the varieties in the style of writing (by professional scribes or amateurs), and the peculiarities of «hands» of the better attested letter writers. The photos also provide material for a good Old Assyrian signlist, which is still missing.

text: The archive published in this volume was found was in the house excavated in grid square LVI/127-128, in level II of kārum Kanesh. T. Özgüç 1994, 369,[1] described it as follows: “The archive[2] covers an area of 130 m2 and has its entrance on a north-south street. Burnt in a fierce conflagration, this building has also suffered damage from the laying of deep stone foundations for a superposed Ib house, and by insertion of a large stone cist-grave” (see T. Özgüç 1994, 372, plate I). Özgüç-Tunca 2001, 220, describe the house, which according to the ground plan shown below measures ca. 110 m2, as “one of the largest and richest edifice(s) of the level II in Karum”. T. Özgüç, after dealing with a set of cult objects found in room 2, writes: “The archive of the merchant was found along the base of the east wall of room 3 and in rooms 4-5, in groups once packed in boxes, bags, sacks and straw mats. On top of each group lay one or two bullae. Unopened envelopes were placed at the bottom, tablets on top. In contrast to other archives, here we did not find tablets stored in jars”.

text: Professor Özgüç told me that the excavation of Elamma’s house was only completed in 1992[5] and described the results obtained then as follows: “The discovery of the tablets collapsed on the floor of the south side of the second room (not mentioned in the article of 1994 – K.R.V.) has enabled us to describe the presence of a new Assyrian merchant with rich documents (Kt 92/k 94-187).” He also mentioned the discovery of the “isolated texts” Kt 92/k 3-5, which do not belong to Elamma’s archive, but are included in this volume (as *147, *358 and *274) to make them available. The presence of an archive of “a new Assyrian merchant” probably applies to texts of Ennam-Suen, at least two dozen documents (letters and legal records, see below Ch. XIII), but room 2 also contained many records belonging to Elamma. The two groups of archival texts must have been stored separately, as the excavation numbers still suggests, for most of those between Kt 92/k 142 and 162 are records of Elamma, while most with numbers between Kt 92/163 and 181 belong to Ennam-Suen. In salvaging them they apparently were mixed up to some extent.[6] Why and how records of Ennam-Suen ended up in a room of Elamma’s house is unclear. Somewhat deviating information, which distinguishes two groups, is found in Özgüç-Tunca 2001, 220, where these texts figure as “Archive III”, excavated in 1990-1991. They write: “It was deposited in the small room of the house” [room 4 or 5? – K.R.V.] and “one group of documents seems to have been packed in a bag or wrapped in some woven material”, while another group “was found in a burned wooden frame work which indicates that the tablets originally were on shelves”.
label: gold

text: These pieces of information, in the absence of a detailed excavation report that links find spots and excavations numbers, are insufficient for classifying the archival texts according to their original grouping in the archive. We are not even told which tablets were found in rooms 3, 4 and 5 and which bullae “lay on top of each group”. Therefore the texts are edited here in a classification and order that tries to combine thematic (types of texts and transactions), prosopographical (focusing on writers and addressees of letters, parties in judicial records, creditors and debtors), formal (types of records) and chronological (based on eponymic years) criteria. These criteria of course may overlap and even conflict, in which case practical solutions have been chosen. It has resulted in presenting the texts in 22 groups (chapters), to which I have added an Appendix that presents the information on Elamma found in texts from other archives.
label: gold

text: 1.2. The composition of the archive
label: gold

text: This volume publishes the 372 documents, including 7 bullae, that belong to the archive, and in addition the following texts that according to the information on their find spots (mwentioned in § 1.1) and their contents almost certainly do not belong to it. Fragments of sealed envelopes, Kt 91/k 564-568 =(*361-*365, in Ch. XXII), texts concerning Šu-Bēlum, Kt 91/k 556-561 (=*246-*251, Ch. XV), and Kt 92/k 3-5 (= *147, *358 and *274), simply to make them available. I have not been able to study Kt 91/k 537 (a destroyed tablet) and Kt 92/k 170 (exposed in the museum). Kt 91/k 555, the eponym list KEL B, published in KEL 10-11 with fig. 4a, is not repeated. A tablet with two short incantations, Kt 91/k 502, will be published separately, and the two letters Kt 91/k 562 and 563, addressed to Nuhšatum and belonging to the archive of her husband Ennam-Aššur (edited as AKT 3), will be published in a Festschrift for Prof. Cahit Günbattı. The volume contains the archive as excavated, but we know that soon after Elamma’s death documents already were removed, notably by a certain Aku’a, son of Baziya, who took along two boxes with tablets (see Appendix, texts 1 and 7).
label: gold

text: The texts can, as usual, be divided into three categories: a) letters, b) legal documents and c) a variety of memorandums, lists, notes, and drafts. Their numbers are in what follows preceded by “ca.”, because it is not always possible to categorize broken pieces. Numbers between brackets refer to those in AKT VIII.
label: gold

text: a) There are ca. 109 letters: 37 (27%) are addressed to Elamma (of which 31 to him alone) and 11 are written by him, two of them with a co-writer. Several of the latter must be archive copies kept in Kanesh, but some were apparently sent to Kanesh by Elamma when we was traveling in Anatolia or visited Assur. Many letters were essential for the caravan system, other letters communicate various pieces of information and not a few of the latter were written when problems had arisen. The “caravan letters” consist of what Larsen has called “notifying messages” and “caravan accounts”, which inform the addressees, in Assur or Kanesh, that shipments of merchandise and money have been sent off or have safely arrived. In those from Kanesh Elamma may indicate what purchases should be made and those from Assur report on how the silver and gold that had arrived were used to buy merchandise, pay debts and which costs were made to equip a caravan. Family members of Elamma – his wife, a few sons, two daughters and a son-in-law- are represented by 20 letters, several of which seem to date from the time after his death. One (170) deals with the death of Elamma’s son Aššur-ṭāb, another (180) informs Šīmat-Aššur in Assur about the death in Kanesh of her mother and her two brothers and a third one (206) is a very personal and emotional one by Elamma’s daughter Ummī-Išhara, priestess in Assur, to her sister Šalimma, who refuses to join her husband Ir’am-Aššur, who has returned to Assur.[7] There is also one by the just-mentioned Ummī-Išhara to her brother Pilah-Ištar, in which she tries to repair their relationship – he had left Assur in anger, after a row, and she “had not exchanged a word with him” – by apologizing and promising him two fine garments. A few letters (189-191), sent by Elamma’s son Ennam-Aššur from somewhere in Anatolia to the just mentioned Ir’am-Aššur in Kanesh, inform us about their at times problematic cooperation in the sale of textiles. In addition there are 11 letters written by and to Ennam-Suen, and 40 letters of many different writers and addressees, whose presence in the archive we cannot always explain. Some of them are interesting or informative, such as a letter by kārum Kanesh to “the travelers” (285), carried and used as credential by its messenger; a letter by Unapše, remarkable for its mention of a scribe “who understands the Shubarean (Hurrian) language”;[8] and an emotional letter by Šat-Tašmētim, who tells about her misery and urges her addressees to come Assur in order to prevent harm to their “paternal house”. A few tablets are “second pages” of letters (without address, nos. 274-277), two letters are in unopened envelopes.
label: gold

text: b) There are ca. 150 legal documents, 85 of which are witnessed contracts, among them 61 debt-notes, quittances and records of payments. The archive also comprises 4 sale contracts (of houses and slaves), 10 transport contracts (often related to the “caravan letters”), and 8 other contracts (about a joint-stock fund, guaranty, testaments). Of the remaining legal documents 32 are judicial records of various kinds, such as depositions, testimonies, records of summonses, mediation, arbitration and also a few verdicts and one oath. Finally there are 36 other witnessed records (about transport, agreements, settlements, promises, seizure, etc.). Of these “certified records” (ṭuppum harmum), preserved for their legal value, 45 are in sealed envelopes that remain unopened. This deprives us of important information, such as the contents of a testament (120), a declaration under oath (287), a verdict (196), and the data on a joint caravan of three traders, among whom Elamma (49).
label: gold

text: c) Ca. 105 texts belong to the third category, documents without witnesses and never encased in envelopes. They range from big memorandums of up to 50 lines (69 and 70) to short notes on very small tablets with only a few lines of script (205, three lines). We have 14 large memorandums listing debt claims and 77 short memos and notes on investments, payments, textiles, losses, consignments, claims, silver, gold, the accounting of caravans (ellutum), transport, and travel expenses. Some of the latter (145-153) contain important information on the movement of caravans inside Anatolia, mentioning a few new place-names, among them what is called “the town of the Kaneshites”.[9] In addition there are a dozen lists of textiles, silver, bread, and jars with beer (kirrum), a few bullae,[10] and an eponym list, KEL B, mentioned above.
label: gold

text: The archive comprises 57 tablets with envelopes, 9 of which were found opened, and 9 fragments of envelopes. On the envelopes ca. 190 different persons have impressed their seals (“KIŠIB A son of B”). Of the cylinder seal impressions, numbered CS 1136-1260, ca. 100 are new and there are 10 new stamp seals. They have been drawn by Mrs. M. Omura, who will publish them and together we managed to identify the owners of at least 75 seals.
label: gold

text: The first six chapters of this volume present texts that certainly or very probably belonged to or concerned Elamma and shed light on his business activities and family relations. After a first chapter with some important “basic records”, the texts are grouped on the basis of their subject matter and/or their nature or typology, as the titles of these chapters show. It means e.g. that the (long) chapter with “caravan documents” contains in the first place many “caravan letters”, but also relevant transport contracts, memorandums and account texts, in addition to records about collective caravans (ellutum). The chapter on debt-notes (III) also contains big memorandums in which debt-notes are excerpted and an occasional quittance. A variety of letters that do not focus on caravans are presented in chapter IV and legal records of various nature are presented in Ch. V. After chapter VI on “memos, lists and notes”, chapter VII edits records specifying travel expenses, even though not all of them can be shown to concern Elamma’s business.
label: gold

text: Elamma’s house also contained a number of texts that belonged to or concerned family members, notably Elamma’s wife and later widow Lamassutum (Ch. VIII), his children (Ch. IX) and especially two daughters, Ištar-lamassī (Ch. X) and Šalimma (Ch. XII), and also documents of the latter’s husband Ir’am-Aššur (Ch. XI). Many, but certainly not all, must date from the time after Elamma’s death and among them there are some files on particular events and problems, such as the one on Ištar-lamassī’s death, presented in Ch. X. They must have been left in or brought to Elamma’s house after his death, when his widow and some sons continued to live there for a couple of years. For a discussion of such questions and the implications and dating of these records I refer to the introductions to the chapters mentioned.
label: gold

text: A number of texts do not seem to have belonged to the archive of Elamma and his family, not only the two dozen texts of Ennam-Suen (Ch. XIII) mentioned above, but also ten texts of or concerning a certain Šu-Ištar (Ch. XIV). In both of them the absence of patronymics, especially in letters, makes it difficult to identify the persons in question (who have very common names), as the introductions to these chapters show. Almost all Šu-Ištar’s texts bear excavation numbers between Kt 91/k 534 and 551, which also suggests that they were a separate group, deposited in the archive for reasons unknown to us, but the archeological record does not reveal where and how they were found. There are more texts whose relationship to Elamma’s business and family is not obvious, among them a few contracts in which only Anatolians figure. Such texts find their place in the thematic text groups of chapters XVII-XXI. Further study, new sources and more prosopographic data in due time may reveal for more of them why they ended up in Elamma’s. I have spent much time in trying to find answers to these questions, but the absence of a general OA prosopography and the existence of many unedited texts makes this difficult and time consuming. Further study would have unduly delayed the publication of Elamma’s archive.
label: gold

text: The last chapter, Ch. XXII, presents the fragments of sealed envelopes, including those (as mentioned above) that did not belong to the archive, and the bullae found in Elamma’s house.
label: gold

text: Continued study of the texts, after the format of the volume, the numbering of the texts and the indices had been completed, inevitably led to the discovery of a few more links between individual texts and possible identifications of persons. This should in a few cases have resulted in moving texts to a different chapter and renumbering them, which proved to be too complicated, although I did move a few texts, inserting them with an a-number. The links found are otherwise mentioned in the summaries of and notes to the individual texts.

text: 2. Elamma and his family
label: gold

text: Elamma, son of Iddin-Suen, was active as a trader for many years. His earliest dated transactions took place in the year REL 67, mentioned in the original contract *54 (where he was creditor as is shown by its excerpt in the memorandum *70:18-19) and in *74:15-19 //*75:10-12. The original contract *98 and the excerpts in memorandums *69:12-13 and *70:19-24 are dated to REL 75, while a settlement of accounts with Galdaya, recorded in the original contract *64, took place in REL 76. When he started his commercial activities is not known, presumably before REL 67, during the life-time of his father, possibly from the house in grid LVII-LVIII/127-128, which was later inherited(?) by his elder brother Ali-ahum. That Elamma’s original service contract with Galdaya was found there (see the note to *70:5-9 and text no. 8 in the Appendix) could be an indication of it. When he became independent is un-known, probably after his father’s death, when he inherited and the financial relation with his brother (cf. *1) was sorted out. Contracting a “harnesser” in REL 75 is a mark of success and this applies in particular to the acquisition in REL 78 of his own joint-stock capital (naruqqum), a copy of which is preserved as text *2. Several years earlier he may have built or acquired his own house and married, for debt-note *60 shows that already in REL 90, when Elamma was still alive, his (eldest?) son Aššur-ṭāb acted independently as creditor. It is excerpted in memo *69, which starts with five debt claims of Elamma, to continue in lines 42-51 with two of that son, dated to REL 95 and 90 (in that order). The latest contract where Elamma figures as creditor is from REL 89, excerpted in *69:1-11, but this was not the end of his active life. He served several times as hamuštu-eponym since REL 83 (see AKT 1, 58A:7), the last time (as far as we know) during month VIII of year REL 92, recorded in VS 26, 94:6-12. When he died is unknown and the fact that according to *159, from month XI of REL 95, his wife featured alone as creditor (*159) does by necessity mean that he was no longer alive. He must have been dead when his son Aššur-ṭāb died, since he does not figure in the relevant documents (*170-172). That he does not appear in our sources after REL 92 implies that he died much earlier than REL 104/5, as I assumed earlier (see OAA 1, 187 comment on text 135 = Appendix text 1), but when exactly remains unknown.
label: gold

text: Since the earliest dated contract from REL 67 hardly was the very beginning of his career and he died after REL 92, we may assume an active life as trader in Kanesh for a period of ca. thirty years. Texts 1 and 7 of the Appendix provide evidence of attempts by various people to get accesses to his strong room and archive after his death, but these sources are undated. He most probably died in Kanesh to be buried, as was usual, under his house, but due to the lack of an excavation report nothing is known about a possible tomb and the person buried in it that might support this idea and give an indication of his approximate age.

text: We can reconstruct the family tree of Elamma by using data from his own archive and those from that of his brother Ali-ahum, as reconstructed and discussed in Michel 2008, 59-63. The oldest part of the tree is due to her, since in Elamma’s archive Iddin-Suen only occurs a few times as his father, but never as an active trader; it also does not contain documents of his, The three Iddin-Suen’s who occur in the archive have different fathers and Elamma’s father is also not identical to the Iddin-Suen who figures among the owners of imported textiles (see Ch. XXI) and partakes in caravans (his awītum in *150:3), who must be younger and he is also not the man who wrote thee letters to Ennam-Suen (*211-*213). Since Ali-ahum was Iddin-Suen’s eldest son (see the comment on *1), he probably moved into his father’s house in Kanesh, which contained records from his father (see Michel 2008, 62).

Whose daughter she was is never mentioned and we also do not know whether she moved to Kanesh together with her husband or after he had married her. She (probably) is the Lamassutum who figures in some texts of the archive of Ir’am-Aššur (who had married her daughter Šalimma; see Ch. The earliest text in which she occurs is *159, from eponymy year REL 95, where she figures as creditor, and we meet her in *158, dated by a double week-eponym and therefore not later than REL 97. Both texts are from later in her life, probably even after the death of her husband, because she had by then grown-up children. She is further attested in REL 103 (in *154, as creditor) and in *161 and *174, both from REL 106, and for the last time in *162, again as creditor, during month II of REL 107. How long she survived her husband is unknown. That in *175, during month X of eponymy year REL 107, four of her children in Assur divide assets of the family probably means she had recently died. Her death is implied by the records that deal with what she bequeathed to her children (her warkutum), such as *174:1-3 and *164 (which even quotes from her last will), but these records are not dated.

text: The tree shows that the couple had 6 sons and at least 2 daughters. It also shows my doubt whether Ištar-lamassī, identified as daughter of Elamma (see for details Ch. X), was also Lamassutum’s daughter, because the latter does not address her as such and the woman seems to have been older. She died when Lamassutum was still alive, with grown-up children from a first marriage to the Assyrian Kūn-ilum (see for him below) after a second marriage of ten years to the Anatolian Lullu. The couple’s eldest daughter probably was Ummī-Išhara, who lived as priestess (ugbabtum) in Assur and is well known as recipient of small amounts of silver sent to her from Kanesh (see Ch. II, E, 3, and especially *8:13f. and *10:46), as writer of *165 and *206 and as addressee of *180. In *175 she is involved in dividing inherited assets with three brothers.[13] A third daughter was Šalimma (Ch. XII), married to Ir’am-Aššur (see *207, and for him Ch. XI) and their marital problems are the subject of letter *206 (see Ch. XII). Her age is not known, but she may have been an early child of Elamma if Suhkana, daughter of Ir’am-Aššur, married off in Kanesh to a certain Aššur-mālik, was also her daughter. According to her letter *208 Šalimma probably also had two sons, Šu-Ištar and Aššur-imittī, but both are difficult to trace due their very common names.

text: The “sons of Elamma” are mentioned as a group in *173:16 and *175. The eldest may have been Aššur-ṭāb, who already in REL 90 figures as creditor, in a memo that first lists debt claims of his father (*69:49-51). Identifying him is not easy, because the name is very common and he had a nephew of the same name. Elamma’s letter *80 could have been written to him. He died early as reported in letter *170, addressed to Lullu (Ištar-lamassī’s second husband) and his brothers Ennam-Aššur and Abu-šalim, who represent the interests of their dead brother in sorting out his inheritance according to *172, presumably for the benefit of Aššur-ṭāb’s son Aššur-imittī, mentioned in *174:27-28. Ennam-Aššur is best known and presumably the oldest son after Aššur-ṭāb, because his name comes first in enumerations (before Pilah-Ištar and Šu-Bēlum in *174:26 and *175:1-3, where Ummī-Išhara is mentioned first; before Abu-šalim in *170:2 and *171:2). Due to his extremely common name and the presence of several namesakes in texts of the archive,[14] it is not always easy to identify him. According to *89 his father, when he was to leave for Assur, had given him detailed instructions about amounts of silver that would arrive. He is later involved, alongside his mother, in the arrangements after Ištar-Lamassī’s death (*180-182) and we have some letters addressed to his brother-in-law Ir’am-Aššur (Ch. XI, A), whom he addresses as “my father, my boss” (*189:58). As representative of his family, in the year REL 114 he sought arbitration in a conflict with a man who had received a “working capital of his father” (*173). He also figures, alone or together with one or more of his brothers, in the address of the letters *167-8 and *170-1, and together with Ummī-Išhara he reaches an agreement with two other brothers on the division of some assets from their inheritance in *175. Texts *176-7 deal with arrangements between him and his brother Uṣur-pī-Aššur, apparently in connection with their father’s (bēt abišunu, *177:5-6) and mother’s (*176:11-14, warka<t> Lamassatim) inheritance. In these texts we also meet Elamma’s son Pilah-Ištar, who features in the address of some letters and in several records (*174:26, but not in those dealing with Ištar-lamassī’s death). In *165 he was in Assur, which he left with a caravan, in *166:26-28 he has to handle a load of wool that arrives in Kanesh under the seals of his brother, and *167 mentions that he will bring two donkey-loads of merchandise from Hahhum. Letter *89 tells that when Elamma left for Assur he sent amounts of silver (arriving in Kanesh) to his brother Ennam-Assur. Šu-Bēlum probably is “our Šu-Bēlum” of *77:3 (to whom 7 boxes with tablets were left!); he also features in *175, but remains rather elusive (see the remarks in Ch. XV). Uṣur-pī-Aššur only figures only in *176-*178 in connection with his inheritance, mentioned above. Finally there is Abu-šalim, identified as son of Elamma in Kt 93/k 467:1 (courtesy C. Michel). He figures in the letters *169-*172 and is probably meant in *18:20-26, which suggests that he was a young boy living in Assur; Ēnah-ilī’s remark “Abu-šalim will travel with me” (*28:20-21) could refer to the same situation. In *169:21-24 he transports merchandise in Anatolia together with his brother Pilah-Ištar, but I hesitate to identify him with the man who brought silver to Assur in *41:10, probably the same man whose 4 textiles were on its way to Kanesh (bought by him as transporter?) in *38:28.[15]

text: Ir’am-Aššur, married with Elamma’s daughter Šalimma (see for details Ch. XI) becomes rather prominent after Elamma’s death. He occurs together with Lamassutum, traveled between Anatolia and Assur and, as mentioned above, cooperated with Ennam-Ašsur. He had a house in Kanesh, where in the beginning of 1994 a small archive of his (ca. 60 texts) was found, but also had a pied-à-terre in Wahšušana (*203:5), where he had representatives (*189:21). He later lived in Assur, where his wife Šalimma was reluctant to join him (*206). His transactions as documented in texts found in Elamma’s archive are of modest size.
