text: Kūn-ilum (in what follows K.), son of Iliya (see TC 1,107 = EL 272; Kt 87/k 274:1; 318:4-5; Kt 91/k 141:36), after whom he called his eldest son, was another son-in-law of Elamma, the first husband of his daughter Ištar-lamassī (*183:2-3, *183:7-8, *187:7; see for details Ch. X); he must have died well before REL 90. Since the name is not very common, I assume that the references in Elamma’s archive are to him. He was a trader and there is evidence of mutual services and some cooperation with Elamma, but the nature of their business contacts and his own his activities are not very clear. According to *19:10 he had a transporter (rādi luqūtim) working for him (cf. TC 2, 16:14),[16] and in *94:5-10 we read about merchandise of his brought by Ēnah-ilī, which entered the palace. *80:10-13 shows that K. himself is shipping a number of textiles and *335:11-13 mentions that “7 minas of tin belonging to K. were brought away by Aššur-ṭāb”. Merchandise of K. traveled in Anatolia with a caravan, for in *81:30-31 Elamma mentions that 6 minas of the tin he had paid to the colonial authorities as šaddu’utu-tax were for K.’s account (kišdāt K.). *121, recording Elamma’s contribution to and deposit in the colonial office, also mentions “11 shekels of silver for 1 kutānu-textile of K” (a deposit probably made for him by Elamma). K.’s involvement in such transactions is confirmed by *351:6-9, which mentions “in all 3 ½ minas have been booked in K.’s name in the colonial office” (adding that 2 of the textiles deposited there belong to K.), and *352 mentions “3 minas 37 shekels of silver, K.’s share. He probably also features in Kt 91/k 153, where he settles accounts with Puzur-Ištar and the latter asks him about “the copper, the price for his textiles”, apparently because K. had taken care of their sale.[17]

text: The information on Elamma’s sons is rather limited and haphazard and mostly undated; the latest dated texts are *173, from REL 114 and *281:18f., from month VIII of REL 115. It is not clear to which extent and how they continued the commercial activities after their father’s business had been liquidated. There is some evidence of cooperation, also between Ennam-Aššur and his brother-in-law Ir’am-Aššur, but we have no letters documenting the traditional caravan traffic between Assur and Kanesh. Ennam-Aššur traveled at lot in Anatolia and letters sent to Ir’am-Aššur (*189-194, see Ch. XI, A) show that he was involved in the trade, but the transactions are modest. text: 3. The business of Elamma
label: gold

text: Elamma’s business consisted of two kinds of activities. The first and main one was the ongoing import from Assur and sale in Anatolia of woolen textiles and tin; the second was the trade in copper inside Anatolia. The skills these activities required were probably first acquired when assisting his father Iddin-Suen, accompanying caravans and helping in the sale of the goods in Anatolia. When he established himself as an independent trader he had a sound financial basis in the share in the considerable inheritance left behind by his father (text *1). Already before the year REL 76 he enlisted the services of a “harnesser”, essential for caravan transports (*64).[19] His initial successes must have inspired confidence and have qualified him to acquire in the year REL 78 a joint-stock capital (text *2) of nearly 28 pounds of gold, the equivalent of ca. 100 kilos of silver. He himself and his two brothers made ca. 9 pounds of it available, four named persons (Hinnāya, Iliya, Šu-Labān and a daughter of Ennam-Aššur) almost the same amount and merchants who wished to remain anonymous (designated as tamkārum) slightly more than 10 pounds. The contract records, probably as security for the investors, Elamma’s own “capital”, consisting of 1500 measures (standard jars of 30 liters?) of barley, 2 slaves, a “share”, and “pots”, i.e. smaller, specified funds. The “share” must have been still undivided assets of the inheritance, owned jointly with his brothers, items designated in some texts as being “of the paternal house” (É A.BA), such as the silver mentioned in *3:24-25 and *17:20-21. The joint-stock fund also comprised a small share (1 1/5 pound of gold) qualified as the joint property of him and his brother, presumably also a still undivided item of their father’s inheritance.
label: gold

text: Elamma’s caravan trade is reflected in the so-called “caravan documents” (Ch. II). It could only by carried out with the help of various persons, those who equipped the caravans in Assur, those who led them between Assur and Anatolia, and men who took care of the sales and purchases in Anatolia, in a wide area that a trader in Kanesh could not cover alone and for which he needed men who traveled with the merchandise “in the countryside” (called eqlum) or were settled in one the many other colonies and who may have acted as a kind of agents.
label: gold

text: 3.1. Investors and representatives
label: gold

text: The men to whom the shipments of silver sent to Assur are addressed and who equip the caravans we meet as the writers and recipients of “caravan letters”. Those addressed to Elamma come from Aššur-rēṣī (3, 27, 37, 38, 39), Dadiya (3, 27, 34-40, 90), Ennam-Aššur (3, 27, 35-40, 90), and Iliya (3, 39). Note the statement in 87:6-9, “Šumi-abiya is on his way to you with letters of Dadiya and Ennam-Aššur”. The same men also receive letters from Elamma: Iliya (6:3) Aššur-rēṣī (6, 16, 18, 79), Dadiya and Ennam-Aššur together (16-18, 79, 81), and occasionally Agū’a (81), Ali-ahum (Elamma’s brother), Atāya (79 and 81), Iddin-abum (81), and “my investors” (16). As the destination of the silver sent to Assur, also mentioned in transport contracts, we meet “my investors” (7:4; 8:3; 9:4), Ali-ahum (8:29, 35), Aššur-rēṣī (8:8, 29), Dadiya (8:8, 20:24, 29, 35) and Ennam-Aššur (8:8, 20:25).
label: gold

text: Elamma’s investors (ummiānū) are mentioned as recipients in *8:4 and *9:4, in the address of letter *16, and in *7:4-6 they occur alongside “my representatives and Hinnāya”. They probably are the merchants who had shares in Elamma’s joint-stock capital (*2), but it surpises to find Hinnāya, investor in *2, singled out in the address of *7. This happens also with Ali-ahum in *8, where the first shipments of silver is “for my investors” and the second and third are “for Ali-ahum and Dadiya”. Since “investors” always appear as an anonymous group it is difficult to identify them, but I assume that there were more persons than those listed as such in *2. Perhaps from a second joint-stock contract or long-term loans (ebuṭṭum) or investments in specific undertakings. After Elamma’s death his “investors and representatives” figure as addressees of text 1 of the Appendix, where they are informed about an unsuccessful attempt by another group of men, also acting “under the responsibility of the investors” (lines 27-28), to gain access to Elamma’s strong room in order to take along “all silver and copper there is”.
label: gold

text: Representatives of Elamma in Assur most probably were Aššur-rēṣī, Dadiya and Ennam-Aššur, mentioned above. They must be meant by “my representatives” (šazzuztia) in *79:25 (see the note on this line). Only the transport contract *7:5, exceptionally, mentions that silver was sent to Assur “to my investors, my representatives (ša kīma jāti) and Hinnāya”. They were no family members, but merchants in Assur, whose identity remains unclear. They receive the silver Elamma sent to Assur and equip the caravans for him and also borrow silver for him for that purpose (*16:9-13, *27:4-6, *38:9-12). They figure as recipients of small amounts of silver (usually less than 1 mina) sent to Assur (*10:30-33; *12:17-20; *20:15-19), apparently payments for the few textiles they had given along to Kanesh to be sold there for them (in *10:29-33 qualified as “the price paid for his textiles”; cf. *38:29-30; *40:26-27).[20]
label: gold

text: Iliya, the first investor in *2, who heads the group in *3 and *39 (cf. *6:3) too gives textiles along and gets paid for them (*9:13; *12:8f., called his tadmiqtum; *15:11, *20:15). He obviously is a senior and when he appears Ali-ahum is absent. He probably was less a representative of Elamma than a business partner and *102:5, “Iliya, one of youplur”, considers him to belong to Elamma’s firm; he was the father of Lā-qēp (*102:4-5, cf. *64A:1), with whom Elamma also had business contacts (see below § 3.3). Several texts reflect Iliya’s own commercial activities. *12 states that a shipment of silver (to which Elamma had added four packets) was sent to Iliya and Lā-qēp’s representatives in Assur and *43:6 mentions merchandise of him with a value of 4 talents 18 minas of tin. *129 lists 96 textiles of his and *128:2 records a balance payment by him for textiles, because he had taken part in a joint caravan or in connection with a deposit made for him in the colonial office. Letter *81 deals with the taxation by the colony of merchandise considered to belong to Iliya and mentions “silver belonging to that of his joint-stock capital”.
label: gold

text: A certain Atāya was another contact or friend in Assur, who figures alongside Elamma’s representatives in his letters *79 and *81, and as first addressee, alongside family members of Elamma, in *180, a letter sent to Assur by Lamassutum and others in connection with the death of Ištar-lamassī. The end of *79 is addressed to him alone where Elamma, who calls him “my brother” (l. 24) mentions a free loan (tadmiqtum) entrusted to his father – probably Buṣiya, mentioned as such in *168:2 - and asks him to assist his representatives in Assur. As a reward (“I will do you a favor”) he suggests him to send a few textiles to Anatolia, which (this is implied) Elamma will sell for him; the 35 shekels of silver Atāya obtains in *35:13-14 from what Elamma sent to Assur may be the outcome of this offer. *42:6 also mentions a kutānu-textile of him shipped to Anatolia, and *35:34-35 mentions a larger sum of silver he had “taken” and had probably entrusted to Ealmma’s representatives.

text: 3.2. “Transporters”
label: gold

text: Traders needed “transporters” to lead their donkeys or caravans, whose activities are described in the caravan documents by means of the verb wabālum, “to bring, deliver” (with and without ventive), radā’um, “to lead (donkeys), and “to carry” (našā’um), normally in the stative, “he is bringing, he has with him”. An important category were those called “harnesser” (kaṣṣārum, often with added “of PN”), who had been engaged by a service contract that supplied them an interest-free working capital (be’ūlātum).[21] Others, called sāridum, “packer”, were hired for a special stage or as supplementary personnel. Others again presumably were young traders or free-lance transporters. The names of those attested in Elamma’s caravan texts are listed in the tables in Ch. II, E, where one finds two dozen different men. Most prominent are Aššur-nādā, Dān-Aššur, Šallim-Aššur, and Šu-Kūbum, but only Šallim-Aššur is attested as a “harnesser”, because he has received a “working capital” and a clothing allowance (*36:16-20). This is not said of Šu-Kūbum, who according to this very letter brings the silver to Assur, but he probably is the “harnesser” whose 3 textiles are mentioned in l. 24; his “working capital” may not have been mentioned, because he had been contracted earlier. Text *19 lists a series of payments to men called rādi luqūtim of various traders, that is men “who drive (donkeys loaded with) merchandise”, and they are distinguished from two called “harnesser” (lines 17, 24). The presence of “harnessers” is also clear when the load comprises some “textiles of the harnesser”, because they regularly used their capital for buying and taking along to Anatolia textiles, which they could sell with profit in Anatolia. Elamma’s archive contains a few service contracts with such men (*65-67) and there are many references in the caravan accounts to silver supplied as “working capital” to them. Several probably were active in the same period and some may have started as “harnesser” to become junior traders in due time. This applies to some sons of well-known traders, probably designated as “junior/affiliated traders” (mer’ū ummiānim), whose services according to many letters were preferred for the shipment of silver. Examples are Dān-Aššur, son of Šalim-ahum, and Aššur-nādā, son of Aššur-idī, mentioned as transporters in *38:4-7. The absence of dates (transport and service contracts are rarely dated; few debt-notes survive because they usually were discarded when the contract ended and the silver was paid back)[22] does not allow a chronological approach. See for data on transporters also Ch, II, e, 4.
label: gold

text: An important man in the caravan traffic was also Ē/Īnah-ili. He brought silver to Assur (*13:21), 11 donkeys with tin and textiles to Elamma and Kurub-Ištar (*28) in Kanesh, and in *31//32 he entrusted three donkey loads of merchandise of the same men to Iddin-Aššur. He also transports merchandise of Kūn-ilum (*94:5) and in *82 Elamma and Kurub-Ištar instruct him and a certain Dada to buy tin and textiles with the silver shipped to “their father”. This last reference shows that he was more than a trusted transporter, which is confirmed by *174, where he took 8 minas of silver, acting for (kīma) Elamma.
label: gold

text: 3.3 Business associates
label: gold

text: Elamma had many business contacts and a large number of people occur in his records. Several of them occur only rarely or are just names to us, and here I focus on the more important and frequently mentioned ones. They are not called his “partners” and are no family members and their status is therefore not very clear, apart from those who had invested in his joint-stock fund (see *2), such as Hinnāya, Iliya (discussed above) and Šu-Labān; Lā-qēp, son of Ilya, was already mentioned in § 3.1. Larsen in OAA 1, xxxvif., dealing with such merchants in the archive of Aššur-nādā, calls them “(close) business associates” or writes “that some bond existed between them”.
label: gold

text: Kurub-Ištar
label: gold

text: An important business associate was Kurub-Ištar,[23] co-addressee of Elamma (who is always mentioned first) in several letters, including *94, a letter by Kūn-ilum. Iddin-Aššur asks them in *31-32 to decide what to do with several donkey loads, “yourplur merchandise”, entrusted to him by Ēnah-ilī, and in *8:27-28 Elamma speaks of “silver belonging to me and Kurub-Ištar”. This is also the case with silver and merchandise mentioned in *34, while in *82 Dada and Ēnah-ilī write them about silver “brought to youplur”. But cooperation did not mean their merchandise was always merged, for in *28 Ēnah-ili first writes them on loaded donkeys “I am leading to youplur”, and next, addressing Elamma alone, on a large shipment that “I am leading to yousing”. *129 lists textiles of both men separately (alongside those of Iliya) and *128:5 mentions a balance payment by him. Puzzling is *40, a notifying message from Assur about purchases made for Elamma, which mentions in lines 22-25 “20 shekels of silver, working capital of K., 2 shekels his clothing allowance, 3 textiles belonging to him”, perhaps comparable with *130:9-13, “117 dark textiles entered the palace, of which 2 are the share of K.” If this is the same man, he must first have been employed as “harnesser’”, to become later a kind of junior colleague, perhaps reflected in the mention in *127:13 of merchandise “shipped under his responsibility” (ša šēp K.)? This seems possible if we can identify him with “K., son of Ali-ahum” (who occurs also in Appendix text 28), hence a nephew of Elamma, who is mentioned in *175:5. There a debt of his of 4 minas of silver (no doubt owed to Elamma) is an item in an exchange of inheritance shares between children of Elamma. But C. Michel’s reconstruction of Ali-ahum’s family tree the family does not include a Kurub-Ištar.
label: gold

text: Lā-qēp(um)
label: gold

text: Another associate was Lā-qēp(um), son of Iliya, already mentioned above, but their relationship and its financial basis is not very clear. Outside the archive he is a.o. known from BIN 4, 168:4-5, where he figures as owner of 5 talents of tin and participant in a very large caravan (ellutum) of Pūšu-kēn. In *35:8-9 Lā-qēp acquires (ilqe) part of the dividend (šipkātum) that accrued to Elamma from his brother's joint-stock fund and *114 records that Elamma sent Lā-qēp silver to the value of the latter's outstanding claim (on him?). In *81 Elamma reports that he can indeminify himself for taxes levied by the colony from Iliya's silver, from his joint-stock fund through(?) Lā-qēp; *100:7-9 mentions donkeys belonging to him and Elamma and in *20 Elamma tells him that he sent him (from somewhere in Anatolia) a large amount of silver, which Lā-qēp has to forward to Assur. In *15 six donkeys loaded with tin and textiles are entrusted to him, presumably by Elamma, and *24 states that a similar load was delivered (in Kanesh?) by Lā-qēp's [caravan]. In *42 Lā-qēp and Šu-Aššur inform Elamma about a substantial lot of textiles and tin, apparently delivered to them (in Kanesh?), which three transporters will bring him. Lā-qēp features several times as owner of textiles in texts of Ch. XX, in particular in *322, and in *22 Elamma is informed about amounts of silver of Lā-qēp, paid out and owed to him, and he is asked to «let his silver go to Lā-qēp». In *67:14, *68:15, *126, and *199 Lā-qēp acts as witness for Elamma in various situations (debt claims, a settlement of accounts, an agreement). Since there were many men called Lā-qēpum it difficult to know which of the many occurrences in Elamma's archive refer to our man.[24]
label: gold

text: Hinnāya
label: gold

text: Elamma also cooperated with Hinnāya, «an important trader of high status, active in Assur and Anatolia» (OAA 1, xxxvi). The two had invested in each other's joint-stock fund (*2:11-14 and *4:4-20) and took care of each other's interests, such as the shipment of silver and merchandise, both in Assur and Anatolia, also in storing money and documents in each other's strong room and they occasionally settled accounts. Text 12:13ff. of the Appendix mentions textiles «taken in the name of Elamma and Hinnāya», and l. 39 «silver of Elamma and Hinnāya», and 15, 17 and 19 are letters written by Hinnāya that mention transactions and liabilities of Elamma. Hinnāya could have been a partner (tappā'um) of Elamma, but his status is never defnied. From text 1 of the Appendix we learn that a particular debt-note of him had been deposited in Elamma's strong room and in *21 he asks Elamma to store in his strong room a container with a large amounts of silver and gold. Several texts document their cooperation in shipping silver and buying or selling merchandise, either in Assur, in Kanesh or elsewhere in Anaolia. In *89 Belānum and Hinnāya tell Elamma that, after he had left for Assur, they saw to it that three large amounts of silver of his were sent after him, and from Assur Elamma informs Hinnāya in *30 that a shipment of tin and textiles is on his way to him. In *26 Hinnaya reports the arrival of a shipment of textiles Elamma had sent him and also tells him (lines 34-36) that he will sell textiles of his «that are in Zimišhuna». In *7 we read about silver sent to Assur, to Elamma's investors, representatives and Hinnāya, and in *36 Elamma is told that merchandise the latter have bought is on its way to him. A memo of Elamma, *44:34-40 mentions that 4 donkey loads of tin and textiles, part of a larger shipment, are brought to Hinnāya, who seems to be active outside of Kanesh; according to *91:7-8 he had a house in Durhumit. Some form of cooperation is also implied by *5:10-14, where Elamma, Hinnāya and Aššur-kāšid are said to have a share (admū) in Šu-Anum's caravan and texts 2-6 of the Appendix reveal how three traders, including Elamma, each took one third of 4 talents of tin of Hinnāya that had arrived with Aššur-taklāku's caravan, to sell it for him. The operation was apparently delayed or mishandled, so that after Elamma's death Hinnāya by juridical means and with the help of colleagues (he wote two letters on this issue to Pūšu-kēn) tried to get back what he was entitled to. Such joint activities and mutual help - in *19 Elamma lists many small payments he had made for Hinnāya by sending silver to the latter's transporters - required settling of accounts. *121 mentions balance payments» (niplātum) by Hinnāya (to Elamma?) and *122, with the subscript «About Hinnāya's account», mentions a balance payment, presumably to be made by Elamma (see the comment on these texts) and the settling accounts by the latter in Hinnāya's name (aššumi H.), presumably in the colonial office. Unclear is *175:4-5, where among the assets to be divided by children of Elamma we find «6 2/3 minas of silver, the house of Hinnāya», presumably a debt still owed (after Hinnāya's death) by his household.
label: gold

text: The status and identity of many other men who cooperate with or have business contacts with Elamma and render services for him is often unclear.[25] Contacts with Aššur-idī and his son Aššur-nādā (whose archive was published in OAA 1) are documented in various texts, see Appendix, comment to text 2-5, 12-15 and 20-21(two letters written by and addressed to them jointly); in *38:32-34 he transports merchandise from Assur to Elamma. For some writers of the letters presented in Ch. IV we may suggest an identification,[26] but many, represented by one letter only and without patronym, remain just names. A certain Aššur-mālik in *22-24 informs Elamma, who is apparently outside Kanesh, that he has shipped the silver and tablets Elamma had sent him to Assur and had arranged various payments of silver. He also reports about what happened with a shipment of textiles that arrived from Assur, part which (25 dark textiles) was brought to Elamma (lines 17-18). The same Aššur-mālik presumably features in text 23c, a joint letter of Elamma and him, and 23d, both dealing with the sale of textiles, and possibly in 25c. According to *125 Elamma “checked and handed over (isniq) to us” an amount of more than 14 minas of silver, the price of two donkeys loaded with tin and textiles textiles. This seems to mean that he acquired it by giving those who had (bought it for and) delivered it to him what it had cost in Assur, but who the “us” are is not stated. Texts *102-105 document a conflict with a certain Pilah-Aššur about a transaction in tin, for which Elamma offered to give him silver and which he would buy in Assur and bring to Kanesh, no doubt to make a profit from selling it in Anatolia.
label: gold

text: 3.4. Elamma, a licensed trader and participant in “caravans” (ellutum)
label: gold

text: The figures collected in the lists in Ch. II, E record the shipment of in all ca. 300 kilos of silver and small amounts (twice 2 minas, once 33 shekels) of gold[27] to Assur and the purchase or import of ca. 1400 kilos of tin and ca. 1350 textiles into Anatolia. This is hardly the grand total of Elamma’s transactions, considering the number of records preserved and the number of “transporters” attested in memorandums and debt-notes, who doe not figure in caravan accounts and letters. It is also likely that the usually undated documents – apart from memorandums that record debt claims - cover especially the later years of Elamma’s activity. Moreover, as texts 1, 2 and 7 of the Appendix show, records were removed from his archive after his death. If we extrapolate the amounts of silver, 50 and 75 pounds, mentioned in transport contracts *8 and *10 (in both cases by three different transporters) and read about loans taken out in Assur to make purchases (30 pounds of silver in *16, see the note one lines 9-13), we may assume bigger amounts/numbers. The merchandise imported from Assur, as the table of Ch. II, E § 3 shows, consisted of between 2 and 7 and most frequently of 4 donkey loads. This meant, starting from 2 donkeys loaded with tin and 2 with textiles, an investment for merchandise, donkeys, harness, personnel, travel expenses and export tax of ca. 30 minas of silver, while its net yield, after deduction of tolls, taxes and expenses, also depending the quality of the textiles, may have been ca. 45 pounds of silver. How many such transactions were carried out by or for Elamma and how much profit he made during his active life is impossible to say.
label: gold

text: Elamma apparently was a well-organized, careful and successful trader, with a steady import and turnover of a good size, although apparently less rich and powerful than men like Pūšu-kēn, Imdī-ilum or Šallim-Aššur. It is very likely that he belonged to the category of “dātum-payers”, a kind of licensed traders, who paid substantial, apparently annual contributions (called dātum) to the colony as an institution, who were also called “men of the (settlement of) accounts” and for that reason were exempt from paying the šaddu’utu-fee to the Kanesh colony (see for them and the dātum, OAI Ch. 6 and 7 and my observations in AKT 5, 85-87). Elamma is never called a “dātum-payer”, but there are good arguments for considering him one. The amount of silver mentioned for him in *121:1-6 (24 1/3 minas of silver plus some additions)[28] and the mention of deposits made at the colonial office (e.g. in *140) and of “balance payments” made at the settlement of accounts to reach the amount of the dātum,[29] fit his status as “dātum-payer”. Moreover Elamma’s words to the colonial organization in letter *81:19-21, “The merchandise belongs to me, why have you levied the šaddu’utu-tax?” almost prove it (see the comment on it).
label: gold

text: As a member of the colonial establishment Elamma also cooperated with other traders by taking part in large, collective “caravans” (ellutum), organized and led by one merchant, who took care of its organization and administration (which apparently included clearing the imported merchandise in an Anatolian palace, paying taxes, meeting expenses, etc.).[30] An impressive testimony of this is the record *5, which registers that Elamma[31] had a “deposit” (nadi) or share (adim) in seven different caravans, in the first three caravans together with Šalim-ahum, Ali-ahum + Hinnāya, and Aššur-kāšid, next in four caravans (including one of Pūšu-kēn alone).[32] Other such caravans in which Elamma had a share or invested are those of Ali-ahum (*35:4), of Aššuris-tikal (*19:20-21), of Ennam-Suen (*53:3), of Ilī-ālum (*113:5-6, mentions its expenses and losses), of Innāya and Šu-Nunu (*47:9-10, losses), of Pilah-Ištar (*51:12-14), and perhaps of Lā-qēp (*24:5).[33] The amounts of silver *5 mentions (ranging from 15 ¼ shekels - Elamma alone - to 4 2/3 minas – Elamma and Ali-hum) are not the value of his merchandise that traveled with the caravan, but what he was entitled to as a result of settling accounts. It included what was due by the palace, where the merchandise had been cleared (lines 5-6 and 30-31, ina ekallim nadi / adim; in lines 26-26 specified as “55 shekels of silver for 2¾ kutānu-textiles”, probably bought by the palace, at 20 shekels apiece).[34] Additional evidence of cooperation in such caravans is found in Ch. II, D, where *49 (unfortunately in an un-opened envelope) lists the “declared value” (awītum) of the merchandise of Elamma, Susāya and Ennam-Sin”, which suggests that goods of these three cooperating men was part of a caravan, whereby its declared value may have served as basis for charging them their share in the costs etc. Compensation for losses by a caravan was also paid (*127, see also *128, with comments). The final yield a merchant would derive from such a caravan is specified in texts such as *51-53, which either simply mention amounts in silver or, in *51, the merchandise for which it was paid. Other records may also concern cooperation in a “caravan”, e.g. the list of in all 306 textiles in *129, simply mentioning the number of pieces owned by (“of”) Iliya, Aššur-lamassī, Kurub-Ištar, and Elamma. It may have registered how many pieces each participant owned after the load had been cleared. Some of the lists of textiles owned by named persons (among which Elamma does not figure) and presented in Ch. XX may have a similar background, because they also mention how many were handed over as import-tax, were sold by pre-emption, were used for wrapping or were lost – typically features reflecting the procedure of clearing incoming merchandise in the local palace. The fact that the number of textiles of the individual owners is listed on one tablet suggests that the clearance concerned a joint caravan, whereby the resulting shares of each participant were registered.
label: gold

text: How exactly these “caravans” operated still raises questions and we would like to know how a merchant’s participation in it was (contractually?) arranged. How does participation in such “caravans” relate to what letters (called “caravan accounts, type 2”) tell a trader about his loaded donkeys, which a named transporter is “leading/bringing to you”. It is highly likely that small groups of donkeys would not travel alone, but that at the gate of Assur large caravans were formed, when donkeys of different traders, each accompanied by one or more “harnessers” or transporters, would join to make one big caravan. Was this a “caravan” (ellutum) of the type described above, organized, led and administered by one or two named traders, or was it a less organized, practical form of cooperation, different from such an ellutum? The former seems rather likely, but the “caravan accounts type 2” also report on the clearance of the merchandise in the local palace, payment of taxes, pre-emption of textiles by the palace, and balance payments in connection with the levy of taxes. This is different from what records about the accounting of an ellutum report, which mention that traders have deposits in and claims on the palace for what it had bought. The above-mentioned system of the “declared value” (awītum) as the basis for calculating and charging each participant a proportionate share in the costs, is not used or referred to in the “caravan accounts type 2”. This makes identification of the two types of caravans therefore difficult and raises the question how big Elamma’s participation in such “caravans” was, difficult to establish since most of the evidence we have refers to balance payments and claims of rather modest size. Here *50 is important, which deals with the “declared value” of a shipment of merchandise of Elamma alone, amounting to 4 talents of tin. On the basis of the standard values in tin for textiles and donkeys (see OAI 152) this could have been one donkey load of tin and two of textiles, which is in the range of what the caravan accounts tell us. Such a small group of loaded donkeys, accompanied by one harnesser (Kunnāya), must have been part of a larger caravan, perhaps an ellutum.
label: gold

text: 3.5 Commercial activities in Anatolia.
label: gold

text: While we have good evidence for Elamma’s imports of tin and textiles from Assur, we know very little of their sale in Anatolia. We read about small numbers of textiles given to or taken by various persons (among them family members and personnel), about tin and textiles taken by the local palace as import tax (nishatum) and about its purchase of the textiles (“the tithe”). Textiles are also textiles “deposited” in the colonial office and there are payments of limited numbers of textiles in connection with settling of accounts (in *121-122 and *128). But what happened with the bulk of the tin and textiles cleared is never mentioned. We have no “caravan accounts of group 2” (so called in OACP 122ff.), letters written in Kanesh that mention that substantial lots of merchandise, often with the donkeys that carried them, were given in commission (qiāpum) to agents and on what conditions (price, credit term, date).[35] We read in *26:34-36 that Hinnāya will sell textiles of Elamma that are in Zimišhuna, and in *80 Elamma writes to Aššur-ṭāb (his son?), who is somewhere in Anatolia, that Kūn-ilum is bringing him 6 1/3 heavy textiles and that Elamma will send him thin and Šulupkian textiles. As for the tin we have a few letters and contracts that shed some light on its sale. In *102 Elamma offers Pilah-Aššur tin (presumably 2 talents), for which he will give him, within 20 weeks, silver at a rate of 8:1, and in *107, Šu-Ištar is summoned by him to pay at first 12 ½ minas of silver for the tin – its amounts must have been in the range of a few talents - he had acquired from Elamma and the rest later. The contract *106 states that from “his tin that comes up” (from Assur) Elamma will send 2 talents to Šu-Ištar in Burušhattum, who will pay him silver as soon as he gets it. Several men who figure in debt-notes and memorandums may have been granted credit for merchandise bought from Elamma, but most amounts owed are modest (see the table at the end of Ch. III; for 1 mina of silver they could have acquired 6-8 minas of tin and 3 or 4 textiles) and there are not many of more than 2 minas of silver. The highest are 3 minas, due by Aššur-lamassī, son of Lā-qēp in *69:4-5[36], more than 4 minas by Idnāya in *55 = *6-10, and 8½ minas by Šuli in *70:19-24.[37] If these debts reflect credit sales most of them concern only small quantities of merchandise.[38] We may assume that Elamma himself traveled with merchandise inside Anatolia, as his son Ennam-Aššur later did according to *189-194 (albeit with textiles of Ir’am-Aššur), ina libbi mātim or in Hattum (*189:18, 39) and visiting Wahšušana (*189:22), Hurama (*191:26), Luhusaddiya (*191:40), and Šaladuwar (*194:15). I consider it probable that some of the records 145-147, presented in Ch. VII, «Traveling and travel expenses», are the result of such caravan journeys in Anatolia, although this is difficult to prove, because they do not mention a single name of a transporter or trader and therefor may as well concern Elamma as one of his sons. Elamma may also have «given» merchandise to agents or associates for sale in Anatolia, as shown by letter *25, which informs Elamma about the fate of tin and textiles of his he had “given” to Aššur-mūtappil, who brought the tin to Burušhattum, while the textiles were “brought back” to Wahšušana. We also have some letters addressed to and written by Elamma when he was outside Kanesh (*20-25, *42) and it seems very likely that he stayed or traveled there in order to sell the merchandise he had imported, but where or to whom and at which prices is not mentioned. There must have been cash sales to native Anatolians, which do not yield written evidence, while Elamma's debt-notes and memorandums on oustanding claims mention almost exclusively Assyrian debtors, which shows that he did not sell at credit to Anatolians. The only exception is a modest debt of 48 minas of copper owed by Habtuniš (*70:14).[39]
label: gold

text: We have to be careful in reconstructing Elamma's commercial activities and his turnover from the written evidence in the form of debt-notes and memorandums. Credit sales and commission of merchandise to agents usually were for short terms, ranging from a few weeks to one year. It is plausible that most such debts, also under the pressure of the substantial default interest, were duly paid, which meant that the debt-notes were returned to the debtors or at least their envelopes, which gave them their legal force, were broken. Of the debt-notes preserved in the archive (*54-*63, *65-*66) five are tablets (among which *55, the only one for a somewhat larger debt), which have no legal force and may have been preserved by the creditor for his administration after the envelope had been broken.[40] Seven (including *65-66, contracts for borrowing a «working capital») are still in their envelopes and accordingly may be assumed to have been old debts, never paid,[41] but they record small debts (ranging from 10 to 61½ shekels of silver, and 50 minas of copper). This suggests that all the other debts resulting from credit sale and commission were duly paid and therefore have left no trace in the archival documentation as we have it. Most of the debts listed in the memoranda were apparently overdue, but were enventually also paid, because the valid debt-notes of only a few of them were found in the archive. This leads to the conclusion that debt-notes and memorandums only offer an incomplete picture of the commercial activities of a trader. It can be supplemented by caravan letters and other accounts, but the resulting picture remains patchy and imcomplete.
label: gold

text: Copper owed to Elamma is mentioned in one debt-note (*61) and several memorandums, in particular in *76, which records at least 15 claims for in all ca. 20 talents of copper, most of good quality. Many claims concern amounts of less than 1 talent (30 kilos), some 2 to 3 talents (*70:1f.; *76:8, 10, 15); 4½ talents were due by Iddin-Aššur in *69:18ff., ca. 5 talents by Iddin-Amurrum in *70:26f. and *73, 2½+3 talents by Ganunu in *76:1-2, 9 talents by Šu-Išhara and Puzur-Abeh in *307, and 11 talents by Dazu’a-dIM in *70:34.[42]. If these debts reflect credit sales of tin and textiles that agents took on consignment, the amounts, with some exceptions, were not big, considering that one textile (depending its quality and its sale to a palace or an individual) could yield 15-40 minas and 1 mina of tin ca. 10 to 15 minas of copper. [43] They also reflect a pattern of many sales to many different people. An interesting transaction is described in the contract *289 (which does not seem to concern Elamma), where one Aššur-ṭāb has promised Ahu-waqar 1 talent of tin from Assur. He will get it when Aššur-ṭāb’s servant brings tin from Assur and he pays for it 5 talents of «refined, broken copper», which implies a high rate of exchange of 5:1 in Kanesh. A credit sale is also recorded in *307 (see footnote 38).
label: gold

text: The fact that almost all debtors were Assyrians suggests that Elamma (or his employees), when he traveled sold them tin and textiles at credit for copper, presumably in area of Durhumit, the centre of the copper trade, where they could acquire it. That Elamma himself visited Durhumit is confirmed by *61, which records a claim of copper and silver on Puzur-Suen. If he defaults he has to pay interest «according to the regulation of the Durhumit colony», to which the last lines add: «If he does not pay I will take it for his account in Durhumit».[44] A few texts, nevertheless, show that at times considerable amounts of copper were involved. In *25 Aššur-mūtappil tells Elamma that 35½ talents of copper were shipped to him (presumably Elamma) under his and Aššur-ṭāb's responsibility (iššēp A u iššēpia). From text 1 of the Appendix we learn that after Elamma's death his strong room contained both silver and copper (how much is not stated). In *171 Elamma's nephew Aššur-ṭāb (the same man as in *25?) acknowledges the sale of 21 talents of refined copper belonging to Elamma’s recently died son Aššur-ṭāb (which had been deposited in his house) for almost 18 minas of silver, which he is bringing to Assur. Copper was used for various transactions in Anatolia, such as purchasing slaves (*154:1-2, *258:37-38) and for paying travel expenses (*145), but it was in the end converted into silver and gold that was shipped back to Assur, and this must also have been the goal of Elamma's trade in copper.
label: gold

text: Elamma’s commercial activities were not restricted to dealing in tin, textiles and copper. There are no references to the expensive meteoric iron (ašium, amūtum), nor to trade in grain, but wool, traded in Anatolia, and lapis lazuli, imported from Assur, occur. In *47:7-8 Aššur-imittī, probably writing from Kanesh to Elamma elsewhere in Anatolia, having reported the arrival of silver under Elamma's seal, writes: «We paid 3 minas of silver for wool of the colonial office». This is probably not a simple purchase, but a payment to subscribe to a collective undertaking organized by the colony to acquire wool.[45] In *169 a certain Uṣur-ša-Aššur is reminded of the fact that the writer had entrusted him, seven months ago, 4 talents of wool loaded on 2 donkeys, «belonging to the tamkārum», to be converted into silver, which two sons of Elamma should bring him. Sale of wool for copper is also mentioned in *240:4-7 (not related to Elamma), and *72:41-42 mention 4 talents of wool were «left behind in the house». Wool was not only sold, but also used and *159 records that an Assyrian owed Lamassutum «30 minas of soft wool for making the weft», which she must have used for weaving textiles, such as the pirikannu-textiles that she had entrusted to her son Pilah-Ištar to sell them (*164:20-22). Lapis lazuli is mentioned in letter *47:20-26, where Elamma is told: «Of your lapis lazuli, which they brought here, they (apparently the colonial authorities) took as tithe[46] 53 shekels (which implies a total amount of ca. 9 minas); they bought 32 shekels at a rate of 2:1», adding that the well-known transporter Bur-Suen is bringing him the silver.[47]
label: gold

text: 4. The format of the edition
label: gold

text: The format and style of this volume are basically the same to those of AKT 4. The personal and geographical names in the translation and the index of names are rendered in the standardized way on which we have agreed in the Old Assyrian Text Project – e. g. I-na-/En-na-/En-nam/E-num/En-num-Sú-en/in are all rendered as Ennam-Suen; I-dí-Sú-en/in as Iddin-Suen, A-lá-hu-um as Ali-ahum, and I-ku-pí-Ištar as Ikūn-pī-Ištar – to ensure that the same person does not feature under different spellings in the translations and index. The index in several cases indicates abnormal or rare spellings and those interested in them can find them in the transliterations. The year eponyms are identified by nmbers preceded by REL, based upon the list presented in Ups and Downs. The names of the months in translation are rendered by Roman numerals (Bēlet-ekallim = I, etc.), hamuštum by “week”, IGI introducing witnesses by “witnessed by” or “in the presence of”. KÙ.BABBAR, “silver”, is always abbreviated as KÙ.B. and the “translation” of the figures used for its weight are occasionally adapted, so that e.g. 1 ma-na LÁ 2 GÍN is rendered by «58 shekels», and 1½ GÍN 22½ ŠE by «1⅝ shekel», etc. Kārum is translated by “colony” and bēt kārim by “colonial office”; wabartum is “trading station”. A mer’a ummiānim is an “affiliated trader”, tamkārum is often left untranslated (in letters addressed to or written by and debts owed to tamkārum), but in other cases by “agent” and “creditor”. Naruqqum is rendered by “joint-stock fund/capital”, tadmiqtum by “free/friendly loan”, and be’ūlātum by “working capital”.
label: gold

text: In transliterations of envelopes the presence of seal impressions between the lines of text or one the edges is indicated and the different seals used are numbered by capital letters, starting with A at the top of the obverse («seal A», etc.). After the transliteration the seals, as far as possible, are identified by giving their number, preceded by CS (cylinder seal) or St (Stamp seal), in the system developed by Nimet Özgüç and carried on by Masako Omura. Notes on the seals identify their owners and their use on other envelopes, but there are no descriptions or drawings, since they will provided in a volume with new seal impressions, including those on the envelopes found in Elamma's archive, which Mrs Omura is publishing. For the benefit of the philologists and the students of the seals, I have tabulated the seals, their owners and the sealers mentioned on the envelopes in two tables in Ch. XXIV.

text: 9-10. The words “we had promised / been ordered to divide” (both translations are possible), without a reference to their father’s testament, suggests that it did not exist and that mediators or arbiters had worked out a fair division.

text: 12-16, 23. The verb kabāsum, basically "to step on", in OA is used in a variety of meanings in specific contexts (see CAD K, 9, meaning 4, a-c). Kabāsum in line 23, with a personal accusative object, makes Elamma the victim of this action, whereby his brother (line 11, “without me”) violated his interests.

While the normal share in the inheritance of the “paternal house” - “domestic” assets, such as the building, its furniture, slaves, bronze objects, stocks, and cash silver – is called zittum in l. 20, elītum probably refers to additional commercial “assets”, such as investments and claims on agents and debtors, merchandise in transit, etc., frequently represented by relevant records. The exact size of the latter was usually unknown at the time the testament was written and had to be established by collecting evidence and settling accounts.

text: Elamma was angry because his elder brother, notwithstanding the order or promise to divide their father’s inheritance, had denied him access to and use of his share. He asked him before witnesses why he did so and so acquired a witnesses protocol that not only contained the answer, but also listed the assets of the paternal house and confirmed the obligation to carry out a division. At the end it recorded his frustration, asserting that he had been denied the use a capital of no less than one talent of gold. He underscores it by means of an oath (lines 23-25) that uses a formula known from dozens of judicial records, spoken in the presence of the mediators, presumably in view of possible legal action, if his brother does not satisfy him. We do not know how this conflict ended, but his brother probably soon gave him what he was entitled to, since neither in Elamma’s archive, nor in that of his brother (Kt 93/k, to be edited by C. Michel) is there any evidence for a subsequent legal fight. After the death of their father, following the pattern outlined in Larsen 2007, both brothers had their own “firm” and joint-stock capital and lived in kārum Kanesh in separate houses, opposite each other in the same street. But they did cooperate and had shares in each other’s joint-stock capital; *3:8f. mentions a share of 1 mina of gold invested by Elamma in his brother’s joint-stock capital and *2:2 a share of 2 minas of gold of Ali-ahum in that of Elamma’s. Interesting is the mention in *3:24ff. of “silver of the paternal house (É A.BA) which is (part of) the joint-stock capital of Ali-ahum”, of which Elamma and Ali-ahum each own a part (qātum). It suggests that some of the investments left behind by their father were still jointly owned, which is confirmed by *2:7f., which mentions a share in Elamma’s joint-stock capital jointly owned by him and his brother. Perhaps the shares they had in each other’s joint-stock funds were not investments actually made, but shares registered in their names in consequence of a division of their father’s capital.
label: gold

text: How could Elamma have survived as trader “until this day” (lines 20f.) without having obtained his share in the inheritance? Unfortunately we do not know when his father died, but it was probably rather early, because he does not play an active role in the texts of Elamma’s archive. We know that Elamma was already active in eponymy year 67, when according to *74:15-19 he gave credit to Aššur-dūrī (proved to be a claim of Elamma by *69:28-35). And in eponymy year 78, according to *2, he acquired his own joint-stock fund (naruqqum), brought together by a number of investors, which implies that by then he was already an experienced and trusted trader. But of course, what Elamma inherited from his father helped him to establish this position. The shares in gold Elamma himself invested in the naruqqu-fund, 1 mina 12 shekels, owned jointly by him and his brother and 3 minas 45 shekels of him alone, may very well derive from the enormous amount of silver left behind by his father, for such shares in gold were always acquired by contributing silver that was converted in gold at a rate of 1:4. And the assets designated in the joint-stock contract as “my cash (capital)” (šalṭī), consisting of “1500 measures of barley, 2 slaves, the share and the pots”, may be related to the large amounts of barley, slaves and “my share”, mentioned in our protocol, while the assets called “pots” could perhaps be or range under the elītum of our text.
label: gold

text: Since shares in joint-stock ventures could be inherited, some of the odd figures (1 mina 12 shekels, 1 1/3 mina, 1 2/3 mina) must refer to parts of larger shares that were divided between heirs. The one of 1 mina 12 shekels, owned jointly by Elamma and his brother, probably represented 1/5 of a share of 6 minas of gold (owned by their father?), the more so since also Amur-Ištar, another son of Iddin-Suen, had a such a share and another share, designated as “his cash” (šalissu), has the same seize. The odd figure of the total, 27 minas 51 shekels of gold, is also remarkable and must have made accounting and dividing the profit rather difficult. One wonders why Elamma’s own share was not made slightly bigger to arrive at a round figure.
label: gold

text: The assets of lines 29-30 remind us of text 1, the protocol about what Elamma and his brother inherited from their father. See for an analysis of the meaning kursīnum Veenhof 2012a, 190-193, where I concluded: “kursīnum, especially in the plural, must have originally denoted jars in which specific items (goods, “money”, and perhaps also the records relating to them), belonging or referring to particular persons, originating from specific transactions, or reserved for special purposes, were kept. Somehow marked for their contents or ownership they may have served as a practical system of storage and classification, but soon the term, just like naruqqum, must have acquired a metaphoric, more technical meaning to refer to “smaller funds” of various nature, which were basically accounting units and could count as assets of a family or firm and from which (also cash?) payments could be made”. See the note on *175:7.
label: gold

text: The contents and structure of the two available joint-stock fund contracts were analyzed by Larsen 1977 and 1999. A comparison of Elamma's contract (E) with that of Amur-Ištar = KayMus 313 (A; see now also Hecker 1999, text 1, with some improved readings)[1] is instructive. E's term, 10 years, is similar to the 12 years of A (an unpublished third contract in Ankara, in the Kt n/k archive, has a term of 9 years) and E's capital, nearly 28 minas of gold, is comparable to the 30 minas of gold of A. The terminology is largely the same, but while E states that the capital "enters Elamma's joint-stock fund” (19f.), in A it is simply called "A's joint-stock fund”. Moreover, E adds a stipulation about a settlement of accounts between investors and tractator (nikkassī tadānum, only occurrence of this expression). While E and A both state how much an investor gets in the case of premature withdrawal of his capital, A adds "he will not receive any of the profit". E at the end simply mentions the year the contract was drawn up, A. adds that he will trade (makārum) for twelve years. Before the date E mentions the composition and size of Elamma’s “cash capital” (šalṭum), which may have served as a kind of security and given his investors trust in his financial sitution.

text: We meet a variety of investors but, different from A, several of them are anonymous, recorded as tamkārum, “the creditor”, “the owner”. This may have been done, as several sources show, to facilitate the cession or sale of such shares, to keep their ownership secret, and occasionally also because it was disputed or unclear, especially in connection with the division of an inheritance. Interesting is AKT 1, 68 (Kt a/k 466), because it deals with the joint-stock fund of Amur-Ištar, son of Iddin-Suen, a brother of Elamma and also one of his investors (see above lines 9-11): “1 ½ mina of gold Aššur-idī gave to Amur-Ištar for the naruqqum. He will go and in the City he will inscribe in his joint-stock fund contract 1½ mina of gold in the name of tamkārum. The gold belongs to Aššur-idī; the list/share of the joint-stock fund has been made/realized”.[2] Similarly, Kt a/k 494 (Dercksen 1996, note 298), “the 2 minas of gold that have been marked in Puzur-Aššur’s naruqqum as (belonging to) tamkārum, that gold belongs to Adad-ṣulūlī, Adad-ṣulūlī is the tamkārum”.[3] Both texts show that in such cases it was essential to have a valid record identifying the owner. Why so many shares in Elamma’s contract are in the name of tamkārum is unknown.
label: gold

text: Two of the investors, Ali-ahum and Amur-Ištar, were brothers of Elamma, proof of cooperation between members of one family. The way in which the investment of Hinnāya (l. 12f.), a close business associate who occurs frequently in the archive, is listed is abnormal. Does “1 ½ mina of his joint-stock fund, H.”, mean that H. invested money from his own fund in that of Elamma, or rather “1½ mina of his (Elammas) joint-stock fund: Hinnāya”? Iliya, without patronym, is a merchant in Assur, one of the associates or representatives of Elamma there, known from several letters (*3:1, *6:4, and *39:1) as recipient of silver in *12:5; *20:15) and engaged in the trade of textiles (*9:15, *129:2, *54:11, etc.). Šu-Labān, considering the early date of this contract, could be the father of the well-known trader Imdīlum, but there is also a Šu-Labān, son of Ibni-ilī, witness in *307:2 (dated by a single, presumably rather early week-eponym, who occurs only here). It is interesting to see a woman as shareholder, a daughter of Ennum-Aššur, also a business associate of Elamma. Had her father given her a share or had she inherited it, as a daughter of Pūšu-kēn had?

text: The words “silver ša silver of A., which is in your joint-stock fund” (lines 4-5) are difficult for syntactic reasons and because investments in a joint stock fund were always rated in gold, whereby 4 minas of silver yielded a share of 1 mina of gold (cf. for such a share line 8). That here silver is mentioned can mean silver as equivalent of the gold that A. had invested in Elamma’s joint-stock fund, which would mean a withdrawal of capital from the fund to make purchases. But it may also mean (part of) the yield of the original investment, paid out in silver for making purchases (one never bought merchandise for gold). The odd figure of 48 shekels (l. 4) the first interpretation and suggests that A.’s share resulted from a division of their father’s share in five parts. One may compare the division of an investment share of 2 minas of gold of Pūšu-kēn between his children, which also resulted in shares of 48 shekels, cf. Larsen 1977: 131 with note 41. But while the latter shares are in gold and therefore were actually split up, in our case A.’s share is in silver, which suggests that the investment had been withdrawn and paid out in silver, to be used for making purchases. This must also be the meaning of the two sentences of 8-11, where “1 mina of gold you have invested with A.” somehow yielded “1 2/3 mina of silver we took for making purchases”. Because 1 2/3 mina of silver is too little for 1 mina of gold, we have to assume that either only part of the 1 mina of gold was converted into silver or that the silver is the yield, the share in the profits made with this investment, so that “1 mina of gold” means “for/of the 1 mina of gold”. The words “silver of the paternal house (which is part) of the joint-stock fund of A.” (lines 24f.) reflect the same reality. They probably mean investments left behind by Iddin-Suen that presumably had not yet been divided and had flowed into Ali-ahum’s joint-stock fund. The use of the expression “of the paternal house” (É A.BA) is typical for the situation not long after the death of a testator, when various assets were still undivided and joint property of the heirs, see Veenhof, forthcoming, § 4, with note 49. Here they are said to be silver and since a withdrawal of the capital (which entailed the conversion of a share in gold into silver) by both brothers is unlikely, the words probably refer to what these investments had yielded, of which both brothers would receive a part (qātum), which they could use to makes purchases. When according to *35:6-8, 5 1/3 minas of silver “your šipkātum” with Ali-ahum was taken and used, the situation probably was the same, not a withdrawal of an investment, but collecting profit or dividend, to be used for the trade.

text: 7. To state that a person is entitled to part of the yield of a caravan, because he has contributed to or invested in it, the writer uses the statives of the verbs nadā’um and adāmum. Nadā’um in the stative refers to a deposit one has made, money to which one is entitled, but that has not yet been made available. It applies in particular to what local palaces have bought from a caravan and still have to pay out to its members, as in lines 6f. of our text, which can also be expressed by stating that a trader ina ekallim adim, as in lines 30f. of our text. The statement ina ellitim ... nad’ū, in lines 9f., is ambiguous; it could be abbreviated from ina ellitim ina ekallim nad’ū, or refer to silver the (leader of the) caravan has not yet paid out and still keeps in deposit. See also Kt n/k 528:15-17, quoted in OAI 174 note 471, where as the result of the palace pre-empting textiles “you have a deposit of 20 textiles in the palace (ina ekallim nad’ātunu); they will give us the balance of 15 textiles in the colonial office”.

text: 6. The words “to make purchases with the merchandise” are surprising, since normally “merchandise” (luqūtum) is bought in Assur and sent to Anatolia. Luqūtum, literally “that what is acquired”, here must mean the yield, in silver, of goods that have been sold, which can be used for new purchases. In a few cases silver is actually called or ranges under luqūtum and one reads that silver and gold are bought (cf. *138:8-9, šumma kaspam watram / ašta’am, “if I have acquired additional silver”). It shows that our distinction between “merchandise” and “money” is too strict and that “to buy” means acquire by commercial exchange. Our letter may refer to transactions started by Elamma’s father (“the merchandise of our paternal house”) that were still running when he died and whose yield (in silver) became available to, accrued to (kišdātum) his sons.

text: As pointed out long ago by Larsen in OACP, OA trade could only function with the help of what he called “caravan documents”. He distinguished three types: a) “transport-contracts”, b) “notifying messages”, and c) “caravan accounts”. Type a) records that amounts of silver were entrusted to a transporter to bring them to Assur. Contracts concluded with transporters leading donkeys loaded with merchandise to Kanesh are very rare and Elamma’s archive contained only one of them, text *15, in an un-opened envelope. Type b) are letters written to notify the traders on both ends of what is sent off. Those written from Kanesh essentially report that amounts of silver and gold are “being carried” (the stative of našā’um) to Assur and they may state which purchases, if possible, should be made in Assur. Those written in Assur tell that the merchandise bought in Assur is “being led” (present tense of radā’um, which implies transport on donkeys) to Kanesh. Type c) “caravan accounts” also comprises letters written in Assur or in Kanesh. The former report that the silver and gold sent from Kanesh have been delivered (the past tense of wabālum in the ventive) in Assur and that goods have been bought and a caravan equipped, which is now “being lead” to Kanesh. They provide important information on quantities, prices, the equipment of the caravan, personnel engaged, export tax, expenses incurred, etc. Those written in Kanesh report on the safe arrival of the caravan there, how much taxes were paid in the local palace to clear the goods and which sales had already been effectuated. Some were sold for cash (ana itaṭlim tadānum), many via credit sales, when merchandise was given in commission to (qiāpum) or “laid upon” (nadā’um ina ṣēr) traveling agents, and that some were still in store. Records that list the expenses incurred during the trip from Assur to Anatolia, which probably served to settle accounts with the harnessers who had received “loose tin” for meeting them, also be long to the caravan documents. But it is difficult to connect them with a caravan journey documented in the above mentioned texts, because they do not mention names. They have been treated separately in Ch. VII, where the geographical data they provide are summarily analyzed.
label: gold

text: Elamma’s archive contains a number of these informative texts, which show that he was a trader of the “classical” type, like Pūšu-kēn and Imdīlum, for whom imports of textiles and tin from Assur were the basis of his business. These texts show the size of his trade, but only in general terms, since all these documents are undated and we do not know how many years they cover. The texts are also important in revealing who were Elamma’s main business associates: his “representatives” in Assur, who received the money arriving and carried out purchases for him, the men who transported the goods, who were the traders with whom E. cooperated in shipping silver and gold to Assur, and who were his friends and relatives in Assur.
label: gold

text: There are interrelations between these various categories of records, because a shipment of silver sent to Assur and registered in a transport contract, may also be the subject of a “notifying letter”, reporting on its arrival and use. There are a few examples of this in the letters presented below, but in what follows these texts are presented in groups according to the classification proposed by Larsen; correlations are pointed out in the notes and comments accompanying the texts. We also have a number of letters written by and especially to Elamma (*19 and *20 written by Elamma, *21-*26 addressed to him by various persons), which provide information on the arrival and use of shipments of silver and merchandise, whose content makes them somewhat similar to notifying messages, but they apparently deal with transactions inside Anatolia. I have added them as a separate category, B.1. “Letters sent inside Anatolia”, at the end of the section devoted to “notifying messages”. To category B.2. “Letters sent from Assur” I have added the short letters *31-*32, addressed to Elamma by a certain Iddin-Aššur, to whom merchandise was entrusted. They provide information common to “notifying letters” sent from Assur, but were probably sent when the transporter was already en route. A second addition is the memo *33, also dealing with a shipment of merchandise belonging to his brother, probably drawn up by Elamma in Kanesh rather than in Assur.

text: The term “transport contract” is problematic, since the texts are not contracts made with the transporter to whom the silver and gold were entrusted, who would normally have sealed the contract, which should have stated his obligation to deliver the goods in Assur (šēbulum). One may compare Old Babylonian contracts about such “consignments”, šē/ūbultum, to which even the Code of Hammurabi and a later royal decree[1] pays attention. Most texts state that a named transporter “has brought the silver (etc.) away”, for which the past tense ūbil is used, which does not include the notion of “to deliver” at its destination, for which the ventive ublam, “he brought here”, is used in letters from Assur that report on the safe arrival of the silver. One may compare *39:37, a “caravan account” sent from Assur, which does not write that the transporter “is leading it to you’ (iradde’akkum), but uses the past tense, irde’akkum, apparently because he has already departed. Some contracts specify the goal of the shipment, “to the City” or “to my investors/representatives”, some also its purpose, e.g. to buy tin and/or textiles (*9:5-9; 14: 8; cf. “to (buy and) stock barley”, 13:5-7). A few also mention that for that purpose the silver etc. was entrusted (paqādum) to the transporter, which is the only verb used in *11. The end of the texts mention the witnesses in whose presence this had happened, but we have not a single “transport contract” from Kanesh preserved in a sealed envelope, only several memorandums with the texts of two or more such ‘contracts” (e.g. *10). Most texts also mention that the excise (nishatum), to be levied in Assur, had been added to the silver shipped and that the transporter had been paid his fee (šaddu’assu šabbû).[2]

text: This large memorandum (8.2 x 5.5 cm) lists, with verbal forms in the first person singular, that in all almost 80 minas of silver were entrusted to various transporters for shipment to Assur. It must be a compilation of a number of separate transport contracts, for lines 8-12 are identical to the contract *11. Although transport contracts are not dated, it seems likely that these shipments took place during a restricted period, perhaps of one year. The shipments of twice 30 and once 15 minas were entrusted to Ennam-Aššur, Adad-pilah and Aššur-rē’ī respectively, and the latter also took along a series of smaller packets for various persons (l. 50). That among the women mentioned as recipients of silver in the final part (lines 38ff.), Elamma’s daughter Ummī-Išhara figures and that some of these amounts sent were supplied by Lamassutum (lines 39, 46) indicates that the person speaking is Elamma. Some payments of silver are also meant for his associates and representatives in Assur, Dadiya, Ennam-Aššur, Aššur-rēṣī, who receive the yield of textiles they had sent to Elamma and which had sold for them (lines 29-33). These cases are exceptional in mentioning the origin of the silver (cf. *9:11-15).

text: 1. ‘My principals” (ummiānia) are the persons who had invested in his joint-stock society (*2), who by this letter are informed about Elamma’s financial transctions. The address singles out his brother Ali-ahum, who belonged to them, but who may also have acted as Elamma’s representative, together with the three other men, known from many letters. text: 9-13. The letter in which the instruction to take out this loan was first given is not preserved, but letter *27: 4-6 mentions that the silver was borrowed from a “merchant” and its l. 13 implies that it was used for making purchases. The loan is also mentioned in Elamma's letter *17:23-25, where he mentions “my previous instruction” to contract it. The “merchant” could in fact be Elamma’s brother Ali-ahum, if the 30 minas of silver paid back to him with interest according to letter *38:9-12 are this same loan. This shows that a “merchant” extending loans was not necessarily a professional money-lender, but could be an active trader who at some point had silver available. The loan probably was a short-term one, when there was a temporary shortage of silver, perhaps due to the fact that a house had been bought in Assur (see *26:7-10). That our letter mentions the possibility that the loan had not yet been contracted shows that the financial problems were not urgent.

text: 21. ana barā’im kašādum occurs also in *82:15, OAA 1 45 (CCT 3,8b):9 and 62 (BIN 5, 52). Larsen doubts a connection with the verb barā’um, "to inspect", suggested by K. Hecker, KUG 80 ad 33:22. CAD B is of no help, since it registers these occurrences neither under barû B, nor under barû C, nor under kašādum, 1, a. Larsen suggests an idiom, which could mean something like "very soon"; it may be related to the expression ana nabrītim, which can mean “before the winter” (see Veenhof, Lex., s.v. barā’um). This would fit OAA 1, 45:4ff., where Aššur-nādā asks for silver and merchandise to be sent to Kanish without delay, to reach the writer ina barā’im, en route. Our letter too may ask for quick action, if (lines 16f.) the earlier request had not been met. The fixed combination with kašādum is understandable, because this verb may has the notion of "to meet, to catch up with", as in the circular letter BIN 6, 8, sent "to every single colony, wherever you (the messenger sent) meet/catch up with PN" (alē PN takaššadāni).

text: 7ff. Many entries concern men designated as rādi luqūtim, “the one who leads (donkeys loaded with) merchandise”, which I translate as “transporter”. Amounts of silver were sent to them during their trip, en route (ana pāni PN šēbulum, also in *42:30f.). The status of these men is not clear and they seem to be distinguished from kaṣṣārum, “harnessor”, the normal term for caravan personnel engaged by means of a contract that grants them a working capital (be’ūlātum). Hinnāya’s “transporters” are Ištar-pilah (lines 7f., 40f.), Iddin-Suen (l. 45; different from his namesake who served as kaṣṣārum of Karwaya, l. 17f.?), and Aššur-dān (l. 14f.). Perhaps the persons called rādi luqūtim traveled in Anatolia, while a kaṣṣārum, as is stated of the anonymous one in l. 24f., had packed and led a caravan from Assur (the one in line 17 appears in a judicial context, not in the framework of transport.

text: 19. The meaning of i-bu-ni-a-tí has been misunderstood in the past, but it is now clear that the verb is bu’ā’um, construed with a personal accusative object, frequently in combination with ina awātim, “by means of words, in a conflict”. It means “to intimidate, to trump, to defeat”. See Veenhof Lex., s.v.

text: 21. The man is also known as hamuštu-eponym, in function during REL 103 (Kt c/k 623+:29ff., courtesy of Dercksen), 106 and 109. I give the second part of his name in its usual spelling as tikal, the expected form of the imperative of takālum, of which takal (e.g. in *41:25) is a much rarer by-form (cf. Grammar § 16.23). The spellings alternate, even in the name of the hamuštu-eponym (cf. *353A:10 with TPAK 1, 89:7; –takal also in Kt f/k 13:8).

text: This letter was written by Aššur-mālik when he had arrived with a caravan in Kanesh, where he paid taxes in the palace, Elamma’s wife took one textile, and he deposited a textile for Elamma in the colonial office (lines 7-15). text: A long letter by Elamma’s business associete Hinnāya, which deals with a variety of issues. He tells what happened with a substantial shipment of textiles sent to him and of problems concerning a donkey. He next reports on the payment for textiles taken as tax and on problems with a donkey, asks for specific textiles to be sent to him, and mentions his intention to sell textiles of Elamma in Zimišhuna. Finally how Ištar-pilah, “our little brother”, acquired gold that belongs to the tamkārum.

text: The letter gives a good picture of what happened in Assur and how a trader acquired the silver needed to make purchases there. A large amount of silver derived from Elamma’s participation in a caravan (ellutum), described in OAI 168 as “groups formed on an ad hoc basis for the joint transport of merchandise in a caravan. The group consists of a ‘leader’ and of individuals known to him”. In our case the leader was Elamma’s brother, but Elamma also participated in caravans led by various other persons, as is clear from *5. That the silver available was what “remained” (l. 6) from a much bigger amount, could mean that for equipping an earlier caravan silver was borrowed (as was the case in *27:5f. and *41:5f.), which had to be repaid. A second source was Elamma’s investment in his brother’s joint-stock capital (also mentioned in *4), which here yielded 5 1/3 minas of silver, called “your dividends” (šipkātum), paid out by its manager, the tractator (see Larsen 1977:137); the can be said to “acrrue to” (kašādum) somebody.

text: The figure for the amount of tin in l. 17 is unusually detailed (and odd), other figures do not match exactly or are rounded off. In line 7 we have to read 23 in stead of 22 minas on the basis of the figures of lines 4 and 16. The export tax (waṣītum; 1/120 of the value of the caravan) apparently starts from a value of 25 minas of silver, which must be the 26 minas 9 shekels of l. 16 minus the loss of 55 shekels mentioned in l. 26f. Expenses plus the loss (lines 17ff.) add up to 26 minas 9½ shekels, which matches the capital available according to line 16 almost exactly. Other letters in such a case would write “all your silver has been spent” (kasapka gamrakkum). The low rate at which gold is converted into silver, the low price of the donkeys (at 15 2/5 shekels apiece) and of the tin (17¼ shekels for 1 shekel of silver) point to a temporary low in the market. The loss of ca. 4% due to refining the silver (line 26f.) is high (Veenhof 1972: 46f.). The amount of "loose tin", 30 minas, fits the value of the load, e.g. nearly 5 talents of tin (with 8 textiles for wrapping) and 61 textiles, which required 4 donkeys (the additional one, bought because one got ill, is included in the 5 mentioned in line 27) and two transporters, Uzua and Šumi-abiya, who are mentioned with their interest-free working capital in lines 31f.

text: The load, 260 minas of tin, 8 textiles for wrapping and 10 kutānū, is fairly big for two donkeys. The total amount of silver available after some deductions is 20 minas 25 1/3 shekels (l. 14), or 19 minas 56 2/3 shekel( if we also deduct the loss due to washing and checking mentioned in lines 25f., 30f.) The amounts paid according to lines 15-25, are a 21 minas 4 ½ shekels and to that we have to add the payments made in lines 26-33, amounting to 50 1/2 shekels. I assume that the statement of lines 34-36, that 58 5/6 shekels of silver were added to “complement the donkeys”, means that this silver was needed to pay for all the expenses. This additional silver was derived from the sale of barley, which is not surprising since merchants had large quantities of it in stock, which could be considered cash (cf. *2:27f.). The export tax of 1/120 on 21 minas and 4 shekels should be a little more than 10 ½ shekels and at the end of l. 29 one reads 10 shekels 20 [+x ŠE].

The names of only two of the presumably four writers, Pūšu-kēn and probably Aššur-r[ēṣī] (perhaps one of Elamma’s representatives in Assur) are preserved. Since they had informed the unknown addressees about a debt of and a payment by Elamma (lines 14-19), it seems unlikely he was on of the two addressees, but how and why this letter ended up in his archive is unclear.

text: 11-12. Išertum, usually in the plural, is probably derived from išarum, “correct, right”, cf. AHw 394b, “normale Menge”(?), accepted by Larsen 1967, 118. CAD E and I/J do not know the word, but CAD M/1, 429, s.v. maṭû, 1, 2’, translates 5 GÍN ina išerātim imṭi in TC 2, 14:23 by ‘5 shekels were missing from the “normal amounts”. This translation takes ina as partitive, but ina could also be instrumental, which would make išerātum refer to a specific procedure or treatment of the metal, for which I suggested long ago (AOATT note 88) the normalizing and finishing of the cast silver, which would entail some loss of weight. A third possibility is to take maṭā’um ina as “being less than, fall short of”, just like its opposite, watārum ina, can mean “be in excess of, more than”.[4] “Being less than the normal amounts” could mean that the weight of the purified silver fell short of what it should be or of the weight mentioned in the accompanying letter. The opposite is the case in AKT 6, 4:13f., where a shipment of tin transported to Anatolia “proved to be 2 1/3 minas in excess of the iširātum of the City Hall“. This suggests that the exact weight of the tin was assessed in the City Hall by means of its weights and Dercksen, OAI 17, even suggests that the tin was melted there and cast into ingots of standard size and weight, which might be the meaning of išerātum. Nevertheless, I have my doubts about a meaning “normal weight/quantity”, since loss of weight ina išerātim is similar to and mentioned alongside losses ina ṣa’’udim, “by melting” and ina masā’im, by washing”, where ina + infinitive is certainly instrumental. See now my analysis of the terminology and procedures in Veenhof 2014a.

text: 12-13. A second reason for loss of weight is kabāsum ana massuhūtim. Kabāsum means “to reduce, to deduct”, not as the physical result of a metallurgical treatment, but as an administrative measure: the loss of weight is accepted and written off in the accounts. The abstract noun massuhuttum, “dirtiness, bad quality”, is derived from the adjective massuhum, frequently used of metals, cf. Kt n/k 492:25-29 (courtesy of Günbattı): “We checked the silver under your seal and ....... we deducted 2 shekels each (mina?) for/as refining” (l. 29, 2 GÍN.TA ana ṣa-ra-pu-tim nikbus). In both cases ana + abstract does not refer to a particular treatment, but to its effects, which can be quantified, “loss of volume as (result of the) refining”. In CCT 3, 41a:3f. ṣarrupūtum is quantified at 1 mina 6 shekels of silver. See also Veenhof 2014a.

text: Of the original debt of 51 minas of silver, plus its accumulated interests (plural) - 4 minas 15 shekels (at the normal rate of interest this means a period of ca. 3 1/3 months) - after the payment of the 46 minas delivered by Abu-šalim and the collection of some outstanding debts (apparently owed to the addressees; lines 19-24) 4 1/4 minas remained (l. 27). With the interest due (apparently for 9 months) this has now become 5 minas 10 ½ shekels. The mention of interest, together with the wish to obtain the release of their debt-note (line 43), implies that this amount was again borrowed, presumably from the same money-lender, and that he drew up a dated, new debt-note for this amount, after which the debtors would have got back their original debt-note for 51 minas of silver. My interpretation of the damaged lines 34-40 is tentative. The writers seem to say that for the time being the original debt-note remains in their possession. But when they receive the amount due to them – the new loan plus its interest – it will be cancelled (by them; limūt). What they add in l. 40 is lost.

text: I present here a few letters, dealing with the arrival of a caravan in Kanesh, addressed to Elamma, apparently when he was staying elsewhere in Anatolia and had to be informed on what happened in Kanesh. He must have taken them home when returning to Kanesh, where they ended up in his archives. I add some memorandums that use the first personal singular and of which he could well be the writer, although this is not completely certain. But the fact that*46: 11-13 his wife Lamassutum is said to have taken some of the kutānu-textiles that had been cleared in the palace supports this interpretation.
