text: To fix Iliya's share in the costs of the joint caravan (ellutum), the value of his goods, merchandise and donkeys, called awītum, is computed in tin. Then it is stated how much was paid per talent tin for tolls-and-fees (da’atum), for the “head-tax” per person (A:7-10), for unforseen additional expenses (A:13-21) and to the transporter (see for the system of the awītum now Dercksen 204, ch. 8, and for the issue of the hand tin, AOATT ch. XI). Since the transporter had received only 15 2/3 minas of hand tin (A:3) and expenses and shortages amounted to 24 minas and 5/6 shekel (A:25), he will be balanced (napālum) 8 minas 2/3 shekels of tin (which he must have advanced out of his own pocket; A: 25-28). Then follows an enumeration of payments made to clear the merchandise imported, including payments made or received (the payment for 2 ½ textiles bought by the palace in A:34-36 is said to be received by Aššur-ṣulūlī, and in B:30f. he is said to have given it to Kūn-ilum). A:40ff. state how much merchandise is now cleared and that it was entrusted to Aššur-ṣulūlī. A balancing payment (napālum, nipiltum) to or by the palace (the anonymous "they") resulted from the fact that tax on textiles was paid in natura, but that usually no smaller units than half a textile were acceptable, so that the difference was balanced in silver. A balance payment by the palace (“they”) of 1 shekel of silver alongside an import-tax of 2½ textiles is odd in two ways. The import-tax on textiles, called nishatum, normally is 5%, while the so-called pre-emption (ša šīmim) or “tithe” (išrātum) amounts to 10%. But if the latter is meant no balance payment by the palace was necessary, since 2 ½ textiles = 10%. Non liquet. text: The first two records presented below deal with a trader’s awītum, that is the “declared value” of a caravan or the shares of the traders participating in a joint caravan (ellutum). It is a system whereby the value of its load is expressed in tin as single valuta, whereby one textile was valued at 2 minas and one donkey at between 1 1/3 and 2 minas. It served as a basis for sharing and apportioning expenses and losses incurred, especially the road-tax (da’atum), and it may also have been used en route to be shown to authorities levying taxes. See for a discussion ana anlysis of the system OAI Ch. 8. Some new “awītum lists” were published by C. Günbattı, ArAn 5 (2002), 81ff.
label: gold

text: The joint caravans, called ellutum, are named after one or two traders who lead and organized it. There are many records, such as the ones presented below, that deal with the revenues of its participants (in which the verb napālum is used) and mention what they obtain, usually in various stages, whereby the texts distinguish what comes from the “holding”, (mišittum), presumably a fund stocked in the colonial office, and what accrues to them as share in the profit, called “the one third parts” (šalšātum). text: “Caravan accounts” contain numerous passages where a transporter is indemnified, receives a “balance payment”, if expenses of various kind made during a caravan journey from Assur to Kanesh had required more money than he had been given along in the form of unsealed tin or silver (see AOATT 257ff.) and he had advanced it from his own means. In our case this is done in a record that gives an account of the expenses on the basis of the “declared value” of the shipment. This normally would not have been necessary for the transporter, but was probably done because Elamma had been charged a proportionate share of the total expenses of a caravan which his donkeys had joined on the basis of which his accounts with his transporter were settled. The expenses (excluding the working capital of ½ mina of silver), rated in tin, are those often mentioned in such accounts alongside the road-tax (see AOATT Ch. IX.5) and add up to 29 minas 32 ½ shekels, which lead, after deduction of the contested expense for the transport of extra textiles, to a belance payment of 2 ½ minas , which implies that the transporter had received 261/2 minas of unsealed tin at the outset of his journey.

Ina panîmma could mean “soon”,[5] but it is more likely that the expression refers to the fact that settling accounts and making payments could take place in stages, perhaps conditioned by the progress of the sale of the merchandise. This is shown by Kt c/k 260:6-7 (courtesy Dercksen), where a trader who has a share (adāmum) in the “holding” of a particular caravan states: “I will collect x silver, the two-thirds (šinepē), and 5/6 mina (in addition, or from it?) from the first (silver) that becomes available” (lit. “comes out”, ina panîmma / [ša] uṣṣianni). text: The preceding texts belong to the category of short notes that record the claims individual traders have (on the basis of their participation or investment, expressed by the verb adāmu, always in the stative) on a share in the fund of a collective caravan (ellutum), presumably stocked and administered in the colonial office, discussed in OAI 169-170 and 175-176 (on the settlement of accounts). He takes mišittum, “what is deposited”, “holding”, as a term for a storeroom, the goods kept there and the value they represent. Our records fit the pattern whereby ca. two-thirds of the claim is on the “holding” (note Kt 86/k 101:14-18, šinepē ina / mišit ellitim ....ilaqqe), and one-third on “the one-third fund”, but in *53 the latter is only half the amount of the share in the “holding”, which is also the case Kt 94/k 545 (courtesy Barjamovic), where the writer will take 5 ½ minas of silver from the mišittum of the caravan and 2⅔ minas as šalšātum.
label: gold

text: The mention in *51 of a balancing payment for textiles together with statements about collecting silver from the “holding” (mišittum) and the “one-third fund” (šalšātum) occurs in several other texts. There are differences in the formulation and the question is whether they are only terminological (use of synonyms, short and abbreviated versions) or refer to different procedures. Full versions can reveal what is going on and for our text Kt a/k 868, (presented in OAI 176) is illuminating. It deals with the accounting of a trader’s share in the caravan (ellutum) lead by Š. and it is helpfully explicit and gives exact figures. It starts by mentioning that the trader had “deposited” 25⅔textiles in the colonial office, apparently his share in a large lot (hence the fraction of a textile) shipped by the caravan and sold to the palace that paid for it via the colony (or perhaps, less likely, the lot figured in an enterprise organized by the colony itself). The trader will receive for his textiles 12 shekels of silver apiece and three entries specify how the payment will take place: 1) silver to be received from the “one-third fund” of the caravan; 2) silver he has as his share in the “holding of the caravan”; and 3) silver that will be balanced (napālum) by leader of the caravan, This agrees with *51, whose figures for the payments from the “holding” and the “one-third fund” imply a price of ca. 10 shekels per textile, which could rise to 12 shekels if there was also (though not mentioned here) a balancing payment by the leader of the caravan. Similar accounts show that payments by the palace for textiles bought were registered in and probably channeled through the colonial office, so that we read about “the holding of the caravan in the palace” (mišit ellitim ina ekallim), which presumably is an abbreviation for what is explicitly formulated in Kt a/k 814:30-33, “I have a share (admāku) of x silver in the caravan of PN in the palace; I have been registered (for it) on the tablet of the colony” (other texts also write “I have been registered (for it) in the palace”).

text: Depending the sitation the words “they will balance me” (*51: 2) apparently can refer to the caravan or have the colony as subject, e.g. in Kt c/k 331 (courtesy Dercksen): “18 textiles the colonial office will balance me”. Further research, which cannot be undertaken here, is needed to distinguish the various modalities and procedures (cf. OAI 176, note 475).

text: If we add the amounts of silver shipped to Assur, ignoring double mentions (above notes b-d), the loan mentioned in *27:5-6, and references to transports inside Anatolia (although some may have dealt with silver meant to be shipped on to Assur), but including the silver and gold of *20:1-8, to be brought to Assur, we arrive at a total of at least 6 to 7 talents of silver. We do not know which period the records cover, but perhaps not too many years, considering the fact that *8 alone mentions a total of more than 70 minas of silver and *10 even 75 minas (in both texts shipped by three different transporters). The at least three letters that refer to the loan of 30 minas of silver contracted for Elamma to make purchases in Assur (see the note on *16:9-13) cannot be separated very much in time and they mention, apart from this loan, the shipment of in all ca. 1 talent of silver.

text: Many smaller amounts to be delivered to particular persons are specified by their weight or called riksum (= ri), “bundle, small packet”, šēbultum (= šeb), “consignment, gift” (esp. for women), or ikribū, “votive gift” or silver derived from temple funds. This silver often is the yield of textiles they had made and sent off, entrusting them to trader as “free loan” (tadmiqtum) a term that also denotes their yield (cf. AOATT 111). The silver sent can be designated simply as ša fPN, but also as šēbultum ša or šēbultaša ša fPN (with a double genitive). In many cases this seems to mean “shipment for fPN”, but it can also designate its owner, who sends it to Assur, which must be the case if the women (persons) mentioned are known to have lived in Kanesh.

text: 3. Merchandise bought for or shipped to Elamma in Assur
label: gold

text: Notifying messages and caravan accounts list tin (in talents and minas; sealed and loose together), various textiles (te; kutānum = ku; šūrum = šu, a dark textile, also used for wrapping the tin; li = liwītum, textile for wrapping), including those “for wrapping” (the tin) and those “of the harnessers” (kaṣṣārū). Transporter or “harnesser” is the man who is subject of the verbal forms ublam, naš’akkum, or iraddeakkum (rare: irdeakkum). A few times we find instructions to buy tin or textiles; in *9:1-5 to buy tin, in *9:6-9 to buy kutānū, in *18:8-12 kutānū if tin is too expensive. Some reports only mention what merchandise is on its way or has just arrived, without stating how much silver was spent in Assur to buy it and for equipping the caravan. I have reconstructed the amounts of silver spent on the basis of standard or average prizes, 15 shekels of tin for 1 shekel of silver and 5 shekels of silver for the purchase of 1 kutānu-textile. These averages yield reliable results, but some textiles are somewhat cheaper or more expensive (e.g. “Akkadian ones”, in *42). The prices for the tin fluctuated considerably (see Veenhof 1988, 250ff.) and there is also some difference between the (generally slightly cheaper and much) smaller quantities of annak qātim, “tin for in the hand” (not sealed, to be used for expenses; šq in what follows) and the sealed tin shipped in packets (šuqlum). We find tin at: 12 ½:1 in *35:19, 13:1 in *38:20 (both šq), 13:1 in *34:22, 13 2/3:1 in *28:12 (called “expensive”), 14 ¼:1 in *40:8, 14 1/3:1 in *36:8, 15:1 in *18:8 (acceptable price) and *39:19 (šq), 15 5/12:1 in *39:16, and 17¼:1 in *37:19. A variation of up to 30% is substantial high prices could induce traders to buy textiles instead of tin (see below note a on *18 and *82:7-13). We are not informed about the reasons for these fluctuations and also cannot date them.

text: Insight in the status of transporters, apart from the names listed in the tables of § 1 and 3, is supplied by refereces to the “working capital” (be’ūlātum = be) supplied by contract to “harnessers” (kaṣṣārum = ka), who thereby enter the service of the creditor/employer, by payments to other transporters not qualified as such (in *19 also designated as “rādi luqūtim of PN”), and by references to small numbers of textiles belonging to them that are taken along by the caravan (general statements that a shipment of textiles includes an unspecified number of “textiles of the harnessers” are not listed). Ka behind a name means that he is identified as kaṣṣārum, (ka) that he must be one, since his “working capital (be) is mentioned. Amounts of 25 to 30 shekels of silver given to transporters (also when these amounts are simply listed as a man’s debt in memoranda) in many cases probably are to be interpreted as “working capital”, also when the term be’ūlātum itself is not used.

text: There is an overlap with the names in §§ 1 and 3, but several men, attested as transporters, are not identifiable as kaṣṣārū.[6] Some may have worked under an existing contract, so that the (earlier) payment of a working capital is not mentioned. Others, such as Aššur-nādā, the son of Aššur-idī, in *38:6-7, and Dān-Aššsur, the son of Šalim-ahum, in *38:4-5, both delivering amounts of silver, are young traders, who in other texts too ship goods and lead caravans, not on the basis of a service contract that bound them to a particular employer, but by accepting “transport commissions” from several traders. Others may have had a similar status, but that is difficult to prove. Aššur-nādā, Balṭu-šar and Hanānum, listed in memorandums (*72:1f, *69:36f. and *70:32) as owing 30 shekels of silver to Elamma, may well have received that silver as “working capital” (as we know from other sources of Aššur-rē’ī and Šumi-abiya, who are listed in the same way) and accordingly have been harnessers.

text: That all eight contracts are excerpted in the same memorandum means that they were debts owed to the same “firm”, which comprised Elamma and his son Aššur-ṭāb. That the two debts owed to the latter are later in date than the six debts owed to Elamma could imply that Aššur-ṭāb had taken over from his father, but not because of his death, because in REL 92 Elamma is still attested as week-eponym (VS 26, 94B = EL 172:7-12). Contracts 7 and 8 show that Elamma’s son carried out transactions in his own name, presumably for his own account. His two debtors, as far as I know, do not occur elsewhere with their patronyms. How long after the latest eponymy year mentioned (REL 95) this memorandum was drawn up, is unknown, but it registers (not in chronological order!) several debts that were between 10 and 20 years old.

text: This big memorandum (7.5 x 5.8), whose reverse is heavily damaged, lists many debt-claims, most in copper. It was excerpted from “tablets that are in the house of ........” (lines 41-42, name unreadable, but not Elamma). The first part lists claims in copper, in all more than 20 talents, later also some claims in silver follow, but the gap in and damage of the reverse deprives us of further data. The creditor remains anonymous, but this record is presented here because lines 17-21 list a debt of Uršiši for which Elamma and his brother Amur-Ištar had been registered as guarantors and this agrees with the date of two other occurrences of Uršiši (see below, note on lines 16-22). Being mentioned as guarantor means that Elamma, at least in this case, was not the creditor, unless the guarantors had paid for the debtor, which would have turned them into creditors of Uršiši, whereby his original debt-note would have been ceded to them. It is uncertain whether Elamma was the creditor of the other claims and in any case this memo must have been drawn up somewhat later. From memo *77 we learn that some of the tablets excerpted in *76 (lines 10-13) were “left to our Šu-Bēlum”, to all appearances Elamma’s son. That, according to that memo, no less than seven boxes with tablets were left to him was a drastic measure, possibly related to Elamma’s death. It is unfortunate that the name of the owner of the house(?), where the tablets excerpted in *76 were kept, is unreadable, but it is tempting to assume a connection with the transfer of the boxes of tablets mentioned in *77. ZI-lá-DÍ-a-am is a nisbe, from a town Zilad/t, also attested in TC 1, 31:28, which states that silver from the sale of textiles cannot be sent, because "people from Zilad/t and D/Tulan have retained it "(ZI-lá-DÍ-ú ù DU-lá-ni-ú uka’’ilūma). The first action is šaddudum, "to extend, to stretch", a unique D-stem, and its object then would be ṭurrū, "yarns, twines", not yet attested in OA. The result of this operation probably is (line 17a) that the writer "can make them fit for you (lussim + ak + ku(m) + šunu), from wasāmum D-stem (also unique in OA) for nibrāru-garments". Nibrārū (see Michel-Veenhof 2010, 237) occur in small quantities, both as imported from Assur and as current in Anatolia. Prag I 686:19-20 mentions "a nibrāru-garment, either of Šubarean make or of the City (of Assur)”, to be worn by the writer, but we do not know what type of garment it was.

text: Elamma has “taken” (in consignment?) a shipment of tin and textiles belonging to six business associates in Assur on the basis of an agreement, which probably meant that they had drawn up a sealed contract mentioning how much silver he would pay for it and when. It must also have contained the clause quoted in lines 11-15a, that specified how Elamma could indemnify himself should the colony levy šaddu’utu-tax on the shipment. This tax, recently discussed in OAI 110ff. and AKT 5, 85ff., here must be the high one of 3/60 (or 5%) of the value of a shipment, called “the šaddu’utum of the Kanesh colony”. The 36 minas of tin taken as tax (l. 29) then imply a shipment with a declared value of 12 talents of tin and it might have consisted of two donkey-loads of tin and three of textiles. This tax was a “once only payment” from which the important “licensed” traders, the so-called “dātum-payers”, were exempt and this must have been the reason why Elamma, asserting that the merchandise belonged to him, protested against its levy. The mere fact that the contract included a clause about a possible attempt of the colony to levy this tax, indicates that Elamma was not certain whether switching the ownership of the shipment would work. And indeed, the colony rejected Elamma’s request, because it considered the merchandise the property of Iliya, since it had been combined with, added to his assets, perhaps in storage or when it entered the palace. That such things happened is clear from CCT 3, 28b:14-16, where in view of the taxation by the palace, “the textiles were combined with those of A.” (ṣubātū ana ša A. šaknū). Iliya (see p. XXXVI) was a business associate of Elamma in Assur, as shown by *102:5, where a trader addressing Elamma, speaks of “Iliya of yours” (plur., kunu’um), i.e. of your firm. He was also the first-mentioned investor in Elamma’s joint-stock fund (*2:1), Elamma corresponds with him (*3:1) and sends him silver (*12:5). Iliya’s son Lā-qēp apparently lived in Anatolia and cooperated with Elamma.
label: gold

text: The refusal of the colony to consider Elamma as the owner of the shipment meant that the Assyrian authorities en route in Anatolia made him pay a šaddu’utu-tax of 36 minas of tin. Because 6 minas of it were somehow for Kūn-ilum’s account, Elamma in lines 33-39 asks the addressees to send him these 30 minas from Assur without delay, because (lines 36-37) “I do not (wish to) take it here from your silver”, a statement which shows his good will, because the agreement quoted in lines 11-15 authorized him to do (lines 11-15; was Iliya the manager of the joint operation?). A problem is that these 30 minas of tin in lines 33-35 are described as being the (total of) the dātum, muṭā’ū and the nishatum incurred by the shipment. Of these deductions (the verb used is normally ṣahhurum) nishatum is the tax paid to the local palace on imported tin, dātum the “road-tax” paid during the caravan trip from Assur to Anatolia, and muṭā’ū the underweight established when upon arrival a sealed packet of tin proved to contain less than normal (usually 65 minas) or than was stated in a relevant caravan report or bill of loading. But such expenses seem to be quite different from the šaddu’utu-tax paid to the colonial office, unless the latter was somehow an addition of such costs or expenses, not paid en route but charged by the colony. This raises a series of questions about the nature of these expenses and the role of the colonial office, which require a much broader analysis than is possible here
label: gold

text: I only mention here the possibility that the “road-tax” paid was the one for the final stage of the journey, from Hahhum to Kanesh, due to the Kanesh colony (cf. OAI 159 and see for many references to road-tax paid for this stage, Geography 89f.). This happened in Kt 94/k 351 (courtesy Barjamovic), where for a shipment of 140 minas of tin (one donkey-load) the transporter received 2 minas 17½ shekels (ca. 1,6% of the value of the load) as compensation for what he had paid as road-tax from Hahhum (until Kanesh)”. By also mentioning an underweight of 2 minas and the payment of 4 minas as nishatum,[1] this text is a nice parallel to our letter and it may support the idea that the term šaddu’utu-tax in our text was in fact the addition of several expenses paid to or charged by the colony. Another possibility is that the costs were those of transport further into Anatolia, beyond Kanesh. That the goods were indeed shipped on from Kanesh is shown by Elamma’s words “wherever they collected the šaddu’utu-tax for the colony” (l. 26f.), which must have happened inside Anatolia, at other colonies, as shown in OAI 112ff. and my observations in AKT 5:85-89. That Elamma had appealed “here” (in Kanesh) is understandable, because this tax was levied for the Kanesh colony and traders protesting against it in another colony had to go there to try to obtain a refund (AKT 5, 3:16-21). That the import-tax was levied upon arrival in an Anatolian town and the “underweight” was established when the packets were opened there, needs no proof. And we also have evidence for the levying of nishatum en route in Anatolia, in AKT 3, 34:7-9 and 15-18, twice at a bridge, at a rate of 20 and 15 shekels of copper per donkey, very small sums that looks like a “transit fee”. There are also a few occurrences of the payment of “road-tax” (dātum) in connection with transport inside Anatolia, e.g. in AKT 3, 34:1-6, where expenses for a trip from Wahšušana to Šaladuwar were “115 shekels of copper each” (donkey?) for the road-tax, donkey fodder and an inn, and in Kt c/k 263:39-41 (courtesy Dercksen), which mentions that for a shipment of copper “from Kanesh until Wahšušana the road-tax amounted for me to 3 minas per (donkey?)”. In Kt 87/k 465 (courtesy Hecker) amounts of copper paid as road-tax for trips from Šaladuwar to Burušhattum, vice versa, and from Wahšušana to Šaladuwar are mentioned, and in Kt 94/k 403 one for a trip from Hahhum to Burušhattum.

text: The letters are presented on the basis the alphabetical order of the names of their writers. Most writers are represented by one letter, but Ahu-waqar and Aššur-rē’ī by two, and most letters are addressed to Elamma alone, but *91 to Hinnāya and Elamma. In *92, to Elamma and Ali-ahum, and *94, to Elamma and Kurub-Ištar, the second addressee was the main one. In these letters Elamma is not mentioned in the body of text, nor asked to do something, but the writers apparently wished to keep him informed of what they wrote. This is understandable because the addressees and writers were his relatives (his brother Ali-ahum in *92, his son-in-law Kūn-ilum in *94) and business associates (Hinnāya and Kurub-Ištar in *91 and *94).

text: In both letters Elamma, who must be writing from somewhere outside Kanesh, asks Ahu-waqar to find (and send him?) two different letters by Ali-ahum (presumably Elamma’s brother), one (84*:5) addressed to Elamma alone, the other (83*:6-7) to Hinnāya and Elamma. The words written on them (lapit), which are quoted, are the address on their envelopes. But since 83*:4-5 identifies the first letter as “wrapped in a rag”, the reference to “its face” (panūšu) could also mean the text on a sealed bulla attached to the packet as a label for identifying it. Various archives have indeed yielded sealed bullae with such inscriptions (see Özgüç-Tunca 2001, 322ff., Kt c/k 832, 833, 835, 837, etc.). RA 59 (1965) 155, no. 24:9-12, mentions that “on the face of the packets (riksū) is written: Seal of A to/for P.” If so, this letter may have been a so-called “missive” (našpartum), a letter containing an authorization, a promise or a statement of facts, which was carefully preserved under seal in the archive for its evidentiary value (see Veenhof 2003a, 88f.). But panum may also refer to the “face” of the sealed envelope itself, as in ICK 2, 147:33’ (pani ṭuppim harmim KIŠIB PN). In *83:5-7 the statement on the inscription must refer to the envelope, for lines 9-10 mention that this letter had been sealed by two other men, apparently referring to the bulla attached to the packet (perhaps a textile wrap, as mentioned in *83:4), which contained the letter.

text: In 84* it is difficult (also due to the lacuna after line 11) to decide where the quote of what Elamma wrote (starting in l. 5) ended. Are lines 7ff. part of it or the beginning of Ahu-waqar’s answer? The information in 83*:8ff., that the tablet sought was supposed to be among Aššur-ṭāb’s tablets, is interesting. It may imply that the latter, who might be Elamma’s son or nephew,[2] had a special container with his tablets in Elamma’s house, to which Ahu-waqar had access, even during Aššur-ṭāb’s absence (l. 9). This raises the question who Ahu-waqar was, complicated by the absence of his patronym. The only patronym in our archive is in *283A:2, where, as son of Aššur-rē’ī, he figures as witness of a confrontation between Āl-ṭāb and Amur-Aššur. He might be the same man who, together with Aššuriš-tikal, writes *105 to Elamma and who, at Elamma’s instruction, according to *25:6, together with Aššur-mūtappil (presumably Elamma’s son) has to take tin belonging to Elamma.[3]

text: What the testimony by Eddinaya stated or confirmed is not clear. It might have concerned the debt of Ennānum of l. 10-11, if the testimony was instrumental in obtaining his debt-note, but it seems more likely that it is the record of another debt, probably credit extended to him by Aššur-ṭāb. That Aššur-ṭāb, before coming, will clear Elamma’s merchandise (lines 14-15), indicates that he is somewhere in Anatolia and this means that “the city” where it will be delivered must be Kanesh, where Elamma lived.

text: Bēlānum and Hinnāya tell Elamma that after he had left his son (apparently Pilah-Ištar, mentioned in l. 28) had sent two large amounts of silver to Ennam-Aššur (presumably another son of Elamma). The latter, as instructed by Elamma (his father) had converted one amount into gold, which he sent to the writers (who are in Kanesh), together with the second amount. They then arrange that Elamma’s representatives in Kanesh have it brought together with a third amount of silver, to Elamma. What happens become clearer if we assume that Elamma had left for Assur and that the money – in all 45 minas of silver - had to reach him there.

text: 9-14. Difficult, for ṭup-pí-i might be plural, but then one would expect tuppē’a, “my tablets”, and the spelling rather suggests “my tablet”, which might refer to a memorandum listing Iddin-Aššur’s debts. Since the words are addressed to Ali-ahum alone, am-ra-ma should be an imp. sing. with dative suffix, “look up / inspect for me”, with enclitic –ma to state the result of the action, namely to discover that the writer had already taken action four times. This action is esārum, “to press for payment”, very rare in OA (only BIN 6, 199:15, ana esār kaspim), generally construed with an accusative object and not with ana, but the alternative eṣārum, “to draw up” (a document) is also difficult (“I gave S. already four times a notice”?). The question is also how Ali-ahum could have learned that from inspecting the tablet. Considering these problems Kouwenberg asks whether amramma might not be a stative or rather a verbal adjective, “my checked tablet”, but it is not clear what that means and because also esārum ana is strange, uncertainty remains. Anyhow, in this passage the writer excuses himself for not yet having paid Ali-ahum, as “we” (he and a partner, perhaps Elamma, who is mentioned in the address) would have liked.

text: A. “Confirmation” (ka’’unum, kuta’’unum; 98-101)
label: gold

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: Establishing facts and recovering the truth was at times difficult due to the sophistication of the trade and because parties, witnesses and written evidence were often not in the same place. One of the strategies, when a liability was unclear or had been shifted to a third party, was to agree, at times by mediation or arbitration (as was the case in 101*), on “confirmation”. This was expressed by the verb ka’’unum, occasionally used in the G-stem, with an impersonal subject, to state that a fact had been “confirmed, proved” (see Veenhof 1995, 1729, and below 101*:10), but regularly in the D-stem, with a personal subject and a single or double object.[1] EL p. 176a ranged ka’’unum under the heading “Gestellungs-bürgschaft”, explaining it as “jemandem auf die Person/Sache ein Zugriffsrecht verschaffen”, but this is not correct, for the verb refers to proving a fact or a person’s liability.
label: gold

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: The D-stem occurs in various constructions (cf. CAD K 169, under kânu A, 4, b). Most common (also in Old Babylonian) is ka’’unum with a personal accusative (e.g. a presumed debtor) and with the dative of the person who had raised the claim and would benefit from the action (e.g. a creditor). In 100*:11-14, where I. claims silver from Elamma, who asserts that A. had already received it (in the name of I.?), we read: Elamma ana I. A. uka’’an, “Elamma will confirm A.(‘s liability) for I.”. This construction is also found in TCL 1, 241, where a man denies having received a payment, adding “I will confirm for you P. and Š.” (as witnesses?; P. u Š. lu-kà-i-na-kum).[2] In the construction with two accusatives, one refers to the item contested and the other to the person considered liable and this is made clear in some examples quoted below by providing the personal name (if possible) with an accusative ending (printed bold in what follows). We find it in ICK 2, 118A:1-5, “ x refined silver D. will confirm for me (as the liability of) I. and Š.” (x kaspam ṣa-ru-pá-am D I-dí-a-ba-am u Š. ukânnam), which we may render by “to bring confirmation/proof for something against somebody”. It is also used in 98*:1-4, 1 kutānam Š. A-lá-ha-am ahušu ana Elamma uka’’an). The same construction occurs in 68*:16-20, where the disputed item is introduced by ana: A. has to provide Elamma with proof that not he, but two other persons have to pay for or deliver him textiles” (ana 11 kutānī A. u B. ana Elamma C. [subject] uka’’an). The result of such an action is described in 101*:7-9 by means of the G-stem: šumma ṣubātū iṣṣēr A (debtor) iktunnū, and here the liability is expressed by the preposition iṣṣēr, common in statements of debt (creditor iṣṣēr debtor išû). It can also be done by means of the preposition ina libbi , e.g. in 100*:6, šumma illibbi A uka’’an, “if he (Elamma) proves that A owes (them)” (cf. TC 2, 75:10-11, silver ša ina libbika tuka’’inanni) and by itti (KI), e.g. in BIN 4, 189:12-15, “H. will bring proof for me (that) x silver, the price of 3 textiles, is owed by H. “ (KI H. I. ukânnam).
label: gold

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: We also have the reciprocal Dt-stem, when in a case of disputed liability two parties must try to confirm, prove each other’s liability, to find out who of them actually has to pay. Examples are given in CAD K, 171, kânu A, 5, where, however, the translations ”they acknowledged the indebtedness to each other” and “(silver) was debited to PN and to PN2 for mutual acknowledgment” are not correct. Both parties are ordered or invited to bring evidence in order to refute the other, so that it becomes clear who is really liable. This is clear from TC 3, 198:5-8, where the creditor declares: “As for the silver of U.’s son, K. and he will bring proof against each other and then I will collect my silver where it proves to be (owed) to me” (uktannūma / ašar ibūrranni / kaspī alaqqe). The verb buārum, “to appear, to prove to be”, shows that the purpose of kuta’’unum is to reveal the real debtor or creditor, The same verb[3] is used in CCT 2, 30:21-25, where the ownership of textiles deposited by the writer of this letter in the colonial office of Durhumit is at stake. The writer tells his addressee: “Let over there I1 and I2. bring proof against each other and where the textiles prove to be let them give my textiles to you” (I1 u I2 / lukta’’inūma / ašar ṣubātū iburrūninni / ṣubātēa liddinūnikkum). When in OIP 27, 62:10 silver is “laid upon” (nadi aṣṣēr) two men ana kuta’’unim they have to find (fight?) out who of them really owes them. This is nicely confirmed by our text *99:5-14, where two men must kuta’’unum to establish who has to pay for textiles and the one (A.) who proves to be liable for them (iṣṣēr A. iktūnu) will pay their price to Elamma.
label: gold

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: The presence of texts *98-101* and also of 68* in Elamma’s archive is understandable, since in four of them a claim of his is at stake. Proof of somebody’s liability has to be supplied “to Elamma” (68*:18 and *98:3) and in *100-*101 two persons have to establish (the Dt-stem) who of them has a liability to Elamma. Text *99 concerns a debt of Elamma, whose claim that a third person has collected it needs confirmation and it is natural that he kept (a copy of) this contract in his archive.

text: A:9-10, B:6-7. The texts mention two different eponymy years, REL 81 and 82, but the same month. A similar variation occurs in TC 3, 238, on the envelope REL 104, month VIII, on the tablet REL 105, month III. In both cases the envelope, the valid evidence to be consulted and by definition inscribed after the tablet had been placed inside it, has the earlier of the two consecutive eponymies. Since the name of next year’s eponym, selected by casting lots, was not known in advance, the tablets must have been drawn up during these later eponymies. In our tablet (B) the later eponym probably was a mistake, because the month was the same. It should have mentioned the previous eponymy year, when the debt (which apparently was overdue; note also in B:18 the mention of “accumulated interest”, ṣibātum, plural) had been contracted, not the current one, when this record was drawn up. In TC 3, 238 the mention of different months suggests a deliberate change, perhaps because the liability was indeed older or was antedated.

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: The solution of the problem here is similar to that in ICK 1, 114, where Imdī-ilum confronts Kabiya, who denies that he owes a debt to Šu-Labān. Elamma and Aššur-nādā wish to end their conflict and seize two arbitrators (see for this procedure OALP 320-330), who give as verdict (dīššunu nidīn) that (lines 11-16) “if the 1 mina of silver is proved be owed by Kabiya to Šu-Labān” (šumma kaspum 1 mana illibbi Kabiya Šu-Labān ibtūram) he will pay Šu-Labān 1⅔ mina, hence the debt augmented by a heavy fine. The role Šu-Labān is unclear and the absence of ana before his name could mean that he is not mentioned as the beneficiary of the action, but as agent (“proved by him”), whose name precedes the verb; it would mean that the verb buārum, basically intransitive, would be transitive here. I assume that this text, using ina libbi to express the liability (as in 100*:6), tries to combine two different aspects, the procedure and its result: that Šu-Labān proves that Kabiya owes him the silver (kaspam illibbi K uka’’in) and that Kabiya is revealed as owing the silver (kaspum illibbi K. ibtūram), scil. to him.

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: It is not easy to reconstruct what happened, also because the identity of Pilah-Aššur (without patronym) is unknown. In the texts we meet at least eight different Pilah-Aššurs, in Elamma’s archive only the son of Dannum-ilī (*197:15), witness during the year REL 90. Text 102* gives the best overview by offering the copies of two testimonies on two confrontations between Pilah-Aššur (P.) and Elamma (E.). From 103*:17-18 we know that P. “seized” three witnesses, Lāiqēp(um), Šu-Bēlum and Šarrum-Adad (the “us” of 104B*:3). 102* contains the testimony of Lā-qēp, son of Izzizam-ilī, and Šarrum-Adad stays out of the picture, but Šu-Bēlum is the subject of 105*. Here two friends of Elamma report on their seizure of Šu-Bēlum (no doubt at Elamma’s request), who then told them that he had already testified for Pilah-Aššur (when summoned in court) and proved so by producing the copies (mehrē, plural, l. 15) of his testimony, which confirmed that La-qēp had been with him (“L. was my fellow witness”, l. 18). Lines 20-27 then state that the writers by asking various people had confirmed Šu-Belum’s reliability. 102* must be of Šu-Bēlum, because it indeed contains two separate testimonies.[4] Moreover, Šu-Bēlum in 105*:12-14 asserts that the agreement between Pilah-Aššur and Elamma did not include the delivery of the silver in Assur, which is indeed not mentioned 102*, while it is in 104* and 105*. The latter then must be the testimony of Lā-qēp, the copy (mehram, singular) mentioned in 105*:6. Its original might have been 104*, sealed by Lā-qēp and still in its envelope.
label: gold

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: According to the first testimony in 102* Pilah-Aššur confronted Elamma, when he was about to depart on a journey to Assur (cf. lines 15-16, “when I return from the City”), with his need for tin, either because he had to offer tin to Lā-qēp (as his qīptum?) or because the latter had failed to give him tin. In both cases the credit term was very long (ca. 16 months), which must have been attractive for the recipient. Because Lā-qēp belonged to his firm or family Elamma feels that he has to offer Pilah-Aššur his own tin, but he asks a reasonable price,[5] payable within 20 weeks, which is a much shorter term. Pilah-Aššur then asks Elamma a favor in return and the latter promises to give him on his return from Assur (perhaps after he had sold the merchandise imported from there) 15 minas of silver, which Pilah-Aššur can send to Assur to make purchases. He will have full disposal of (be’ālum) the merchandise purchased with it, no doubt to sell it in such a way that he can pay back the 15 minas given him by Elamma and can earn money for himself.
label: gold

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: The reconstruction is complicated because 103* (Lā-qēp’s testimony) offers a different picture. Here Pilah-Aššur - not referring to what is reported in 102*:4-8, but only to Elamma’s offer of tin as something of the past (taddin, l. 6) - reminds Elamma of his promise of putting silver at his disposal for making purchases in Assur (cf. 102*:14-21), which Elamma then confirms. But he adapts Elamma’s promise to his own advantage: not when the latter returned from Assur (as stated in 102*:15-16), but when he himself wants to go there. Moreover, according 102*:18-21, Elamma had offered him the silver so that he could send it to Assur, while here Pilah-Aššur himself intends to bring it to Assur (to make purchases with it). An again different picture is offered by the second testimony in 104*:22-37, for it states that Pilah-Aššur had given Elamma, again when he was about to depart for Assur, 15 minas of silver (plus the necessary transport costs), asking Elamma to buy with it tin and textiles for him in Assur, to be sent to Kanesh with the first opportunity; this Elamma promised. I cannot believe that the two encounters and testimonies, copied on one single tablet, are not related and that two different journeys of Elamma to Assur are meant. The reformulation in 103*:11-13, where “I will give you to send to Assur” is changed into “you will give me when I go to Assur”, makes me assume that the second testimony of 102* reflects still another change: Elamma had given Pilah-Aššur the silver promised, but instead of sending it or going himself to Assur, Pilah-Aššur now asks Elamma to take it along himself and to carry out purchases for him (which he describes: tin and textiles), a request accepted by Elamma. The purpose of the granting of silver, making purchases in Assur, anyhow would be realized.
label: gold

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: The fact that all four texts record or mention confrontations and that the testimonies were given in the framework of a lawsuit before the colony, implies there had been problems, which must have been related to the change of plans by Pilah-Aššur. To solve them it was necessary to establish what had actually been promised and arranged and what had changed, which was done by asking testimonies from the persons who had been present as witnesses. It seems likely that the arrangements between Elamma and Pilah-Aššur had not been immediately recorded in writing and had to be reconstructed from memory. Ideally there should be a joint testimony by all three witnesses in agreement (šībū ētamdūtum), for which purpose the individual testimonies – written down as drafts or narrated – had to be coordinated (see Veenhof 2003a, 95 with note 39). This had not (or not yet) been done in this case. The testimony of Lā-qēp in 103*:17-19 mentions the other two witnesses, but they were apparently not available when he was put on the stand in the colony. Text 103* is very similar to 104* (still in its unopened envelope), but there is a difference: in 103* Lā-qēp states “I gave my testimony before the dagger of Assur”, but in 104* “I gave the tablet of the gate of the god”. The first is a record of the testimony given under oath during the lawsuit, the second may have been a tablet recorded earlier or elsewhere, which Lā-qēp simply handed in. The letter 105*:5-6 mentions that Elamma’s friends (in Kanesh) had available “the tablet, a copy, of Lā-qēp” and confronted the second witness, Šu-Bēlum, with it in order to hear his testimony, i.e. whether he could confirm what Lā-qēp had recorded. There proved to be a difference, for while La-qēp had stated that the first arrangement had included the promise that Pilah-Aššur should deliver the silver to Elamma in Assur, Šu-Bēlum asserted that “delivering (the silver) in Assur had not been said”. It must have meant that Pilah-Aššur could give the silver to Elamma in Kanesh and thus would not have to bear the costs of shipping it to Assur (the import duty and the transport fee). To prove his point he showed them the copies of his own testimony, which mentioned that Lā-qēp had been with him when they attended the encounter, which meant that he spoke the truth. The writers of 105*, confronted with this difference, then were able to establish, by questioning colleagues, that Šu-Bēlum was a reliable person and had a good record. This implied that, notwithstanding Lā-qēp’s claim, there was no obligation for Pilah-Aššur to ship the silver to Elamma in Assur. This must have been one of the reasons for the problems arisen and it may have made Elamma hesitate to meet his promise. It is remarkable that 102*:26-29 mentions that when, eventually, Pilah-Aššur asked Elamma to take the silver (that he had originally given him) to Assur, it is said to include the import duty and transport fee, so that Elamma would not incur additional costs.
label: gold

text: 10. The wording is not very clear, because mallu’um usually means “to compensate”, e.g. losses. Its use in bitqātim mallu’um (KUG 10:15) or šumma batiq PN umalla (EL 321:31) means that is also has the meaning of making a supplementary payment, to repair a deficit, also to make good for what somebody else had to pay (e.g. the cost of hiring of a transporter when a contracted harnesser disappeared). Here mallu’um must mean paying a little more for the tin than the current price. The normal rate of exchange for the sale of tin in Anatolia ranges from 6 to 8 shekels for 1 shekel of silver and this would then become 7 to 9. The raised price probably was agreed because Elamma would take care of the shipment of the tin from Kanesh to Burušhattum.

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: The verdict apparently deals with the consequences of the death of a trader, when investors and share-holders tried to obtain from his assets what they considered themselves to be entitled to. The City usually decided that nobody should take or “touch” (ṭahā’um, “approach”) anything, because all assets had to be gathered and evaluated in Assur in view of a regular liquidation; who prematurely seized assets would be considered to have stolen them. See for such verdicts Veenhof 1995, 1725-27, and also AKT 6-a, 294:19-22, where the prohibition to take anything “in the countryside” (ina eqlim), in Anatolia, matches ammakam, “over there”, in l. 1 of our text. Unfortunately we do not know whose death was the cause of this verdict.

text: 15-16. The expression ana bare + possessive suffix, or + A u B, means “to come for the account of / to become the liability/property of A and B jointly”. Cf. BIN 4, 52, whose writer states that the transporter of a sum of silver “that is our joint property” (l. 22, ša bareni), had paid the tax and fees from the silver of the writer, but that it “must come for our joint account” (33, a-ba-re-ni li-li-ik; not “will move as our joint property”, as CAD/B 246 s.v. biri 1, a, translates). See ibidem for combinations of bare with the verbs izizzum, “to belong to .... jointly”, and nadā’um, “to deposit as/to turn into joint property”. The unpubl. text Bruxelles O 3679:4-5, qualifies “making textiles available to PN as your joint property” (ana 4 PN a-ba-re-tí-ku-nu 5 nadā’um) as “forming a partnership” (10 .... tappā’utttam .....12 epāšum).

source_file: 8. V. Legal records of various nature, 98-120.txt
text: This record was kept in Elamma’s archive as proof that he had handed over the silver he had received, but much remains unclear, also because most of the persons involved are further unknown. The “seizure” by Hinnāya suggests that he had a claim on the two men of lines 6-7, which he collected from an outstanding claim of a third man (their boss?). But why he entrusted the silver to Elamma, who in turn entrusted it to two other men (who sealed this record as proof of this fact) is unclear and also why this silver is now the joint responsibility or property of these two men plus Hinnāya. Note that the verb paqādum can mean “to entrust (for transport)”, in this case perhaps to Assur, but also “to give in safekeeping”, e.g. when the ownership of goods is disputed or unclear, which could be the case here, because Hinnāya had “seized” the silver.

Dercksen, and Kt. o/k 196, ArAn 4, 2000, 21; see the photo in Anatolia’s Prologue 338 no. 443), preserved with their envelopes, the testator is not mentioned as such. text: These records reflect the accounting of the colony, which concerned the substantial annual contribution, called dātum, which important traders, called “dātum-payers”, owed to the colony in exchange for certain privileges (see the description in OAI 125ff.). The “shares (qātum) of the traders were “deposited” (nadā’um) on several occasions, called “pouring” (šitapkum), by paying amounts of silver or depositing textiles, which were then sold by the organization, presumably to the local palaces. The book value of a trader’s deposits in the colony was registered and at the time of the annual accounting (nikkassū), after the size of that year’s dātum had been fixed, it was calculated how much a trader still had to pay in addition to the deposits already made (OAI ch. 11). Our texts record an itemized settlement of Hinnāya (already discussed in OAI 226), which summarizes what he had already contributed and what still had to be paid (napālum) to meet his obligation.
label: gold

text: The total of the assets, 25 minas 15 shekels, consists of 23 minas 20 shekels of silver already deposited, to which are added amounts for various lots of textiles, including a few of the addressee’s “temple fund”, which, as B is helpful in adding, are owed to him by the colony Adding the balancing payment still to be made (lines 12-13) would yield a dātum amounting to 26 ½ minas of silver or 27 minas according to Kt m/k 91. The final lines of B concern different (“separately”) small claims and debts.
label: gold

text: In the texts two persons appear: 1) the speaker “I”, explicit in A:14 and B:13, 18, who must be the person addressing “you” in A; 2) Hinnāya, whose account is the subject (A-B:2, A:14-15) and who must be identical to the “you”, because of A:10-14, for he is the one who had made the deposits and has to make balance payments to the colony and (B:21) to Elamma. “I” must have been a trader representing the absent Hinnāya at the accounting and reports its outcome to him (“you”). Dercksen, OAI 226, suggests that it may have been Pūšu-kēn, but that is difficult to prove and the presence of 122* in Elamma’s archive suggests that he is speaking. That he is mentioned in B:16 and 19 is not a problem, since this is not a letter and the few items dealing with Elamma are added at the end, perhaps to update the memo. Elamma as writer fits his close contacts with Hinnāya, who seems to have been his partner.
label: gold

text: Text 121*, also about the accounting of the kārum, is related to 122* and deals with the dātum contributions of Elamma and of Šu-Kūbum. Here the balance payment by Šu-Kūbum, 2 minas 10 shekels (lines 13-14), added to his deposit of in all 24 5/6 minas, yields a total of 27 minas, the same figure as deduced from 122*. This suggests that Elamma’s dātum had the same size, which implies that to the total of lines 1-6, 25 minas 42 ½ shekels, a balance payment of 1 mina 17 ½ shekels has to be made, but according to lines 19-21 he has to pay only 42 shekels, because (small) balance payments already made for him by Hinnāya and Šu-Kūbum (lines 15-18) are deducted. How to restore 121*:10-12 is unclear. The amount of l. 9 might be the balance payment due by Hinnāya according to 122*:12-13 and be meant in lines 15-16. Anyhow, we have to distinguish balance payments to be made to the colony in order to arrive at the required amount of dātum, and balance payments among the traders who helped or represented each other. All in all it seems very likely that 121* and 122* refer to the same accounting, based on a dātum of 27 minas of silver per trader, whereby the first text focuses on the accounts of Elamma and his partner Šu-Kūbum and the second on that of Hinnāya, who had been represented by Elamma.

I assume that the 1 mina of silver is the value (or purchase price) of the 7 textiles registered as share of the writer and together with the first lot they would make one full donkey-load. The mention of the šaddu’utu-tax for a large amount of silver and some gold must be what was paid for their transport to Assur, normally to the transporter, who could be Aššur-imittī, if ša before his name means “due to”, but it might also mean “due by” (and paid for), if l. 20 would state its consequence. The name in the last line is obscure and the absence of a preposition does not reveal whether the amount of silver mentioned was also a debt (to the writer?).

text: The amount of tin and the average price of textiles and donkeys suggests a load of two donkeys. What Elamma did is called sanāqum, basically “to check”, but with a dative suffix the verb is also used for to hand over while checking and weighing or counting. Elamma acquired the ownership of this lot, probably part of a larger caravan, from the writers via a transaction that must have been arranged or prepared in Assur, because the price of the tin is the one current there, which is confirmed by the mention of “loose tin”, always made available in Assur to transporters of a caravan. The payment for the donkeys and their load must have taken place in Kanesh, when it was delivered to him. The identity of writers remains unknown, but the presence of this record in the archive suggests they were associated with his firm.

text: The issue of this memo are losses, presumably suffered by a joint caravan in which the three persons of l. 2 had shares, They presumably want to obtain satisfaction or compensation and to do so they have decided to address Pilah-Ištar, whom we know from *51:12-14 as the leader of such a caravan. Where this is to happen is not mentioned, it could be with the ruler of the town in whose territory the losses had occurred and who by treaty was responsible for compensation, or perhaps to the City Assembly in Assur, which could pass a verdict about the sharing of the losses of such a caravan, as is clear from the verdict Kt n/k 1570, discussed in Veenhof 1995, 1731 and taken up again in OAI 172.

text: We have two more lists of the distribution of jars with beer (kirrum), APU 324 = CCT 5, 42a and 364 = RA 81 (1987) 16 no. 5, in which a number of persons each receive one jar, apart from two cases of two in CCT 5, 42a. Expenses for such jars with beer (usually “I paid ... for a kirrum”) are mentioned repeatedly in OA texts (cf. CAD K 409f., 2, a). Bread lists are more numerous and those known previously were edited as APU 309, 314, 334, 338-340. Additional lists are Kt c/k 180 (courtesy Dercksen), with eight entries, and Kt f/k 188 (courtesy L. Umur; beginning rev. destroyed), with at least 24 entries; they list in all at least ca. 2500 breads. In most of these lists people receive 50 or 100 breads, with a few cases of 40 or 60 (APU 334: 31, 35, 38; 338:6; 339:3) and twice 200 (Kt f/k 188:6-7). The lists suggests that their writers (in our case presumably Ali-ahum) supplied them to the persons mentioned. In Kt f/k 188 (presumably from the archive of Peruwa) several of the recipients have Anatolian names (e.g. Balhaziya, Šašahšušar, Šuhurpiya). The slightly damaged list ICK 1, 181 (APU 334), which also mentions several Anatolians among the recipients, also lists other items, presumably bakery products (tahšimam and kukam tahšimam, also in Kt c/k 95: 2, after bread), beer, wine, footwear and jars with beer, and APU 340 also a few shekels of silver alongside the bread. Our lists can be compared with those that register that a large number of people each receive a kind of sheep (lakannum, šalinnum, in APU no. 370), alongside amounts of 5 or 6 minas of wool.[1]
label: gold

text: One could consider such lists records of expenses for a meal or a drinking party, but when whole sheep are distributed it must be either a special occasion or a measure to provide people with meat rations. This last interpretation is also suggested by the large numbers of breads, 1350 in our text, even 3080 in APU 334, which the recipients could at best consume over a long period of time, redistribute or take along on a caravan journey. The numbers of breads and vessels with beer are too big to assume that they were prepared by and in the house of one prominent trader, e.g. for the members of his household, his personnel, agents, and colleagues. It is much more likely that such a trader had ordered and acquired them from a local bakery and brewery.
label: gold

text: While most lists, acquired on the antiques market, cannot be connected with a particular archive, ICK 1, 181 (APU 334) was excavated by Hrozný in “locus 4”, which means that it belonged to the archives of Imdī-ilum. The study of the persons appearing in this text, who certainly did not all belong to his household or firm, has to wait for a reconstruction of his archive. But I note that among the recipients are well-known traders, such as Elamma and Pūšu-kēn (lines 6 and 34, for respectively 50 and 100 breads), which shows that also friends and colleagues were supplied. It also includes two deliveries to “the household of PN” (lines 8-9). In *142 several of the twenty recipients of bread are well-known from other texts of the archive - e.g. Amur-Ištar, Aššur-rē’ī, Aššur-ṣulūlī, Aninum, La-qēp, Kurub-Ištar, and Šu-Kūbum - and it probably includes personnel, business partners or relatives (the last one is “my brother’s son”). Aššur-imittī, son of Halābum, appears in *70:4 as recipient of a be’ūlātu-loan, which identifies him as a member of Elamma’s personnel. In other cases identification is difficult due to the lack of patronyms, but we also meet persons who certainly did not belong to Elamma’s family or firm, such as Imdī-ilim (l. 11), an important, independent trader, and Tupizi, who receives 50 breads in APU 334:26 and 100 breads in Kt c/k 180, a list that also mentions Pūšu-kēn and Šu-Kūbum, both as recipients of 100 breads. In Kt f/k 188 several of the recipients as designated “the wife of PN” (of Iliš-tikal, Zurzur, Hanu, Arawa and I-na-[x (x)]).
label: gold

text: The lists show that a trader – apparently a prominent one, such as Elamma or his brother, Ali-ahum, and Imdīlum - acquired large quantities of bread and beer to supply them to others, possibly including his personnel, but also his business associates and colleagues. The anon-ymous writer of the short memo Kt c/k 95 (courtesy Dercksen) states that he had 100 and 50 breads brought (šēbulum) to other men. The breads are not gifts, since the list APU 314:13-15 ends with the words: “All these men are (hereby) indebted to me” (mimma awīlē anniuttim habbulūnim) and the fact that the size of the debt is not mentioned may be explained by assuming that breads had a standard price. This makes such lists memorandums of claims by the writer on the recipients, but they do not mention why a trader provided this service. Did they take turns in doing so or was it a commercial enterprise, which allowed the trader in question to earn money as a kind of whole-sale supplier? The existence of such a service fits the specific nature of an Assyrian colony, which comprised many men who lived and worked without women to care for their daily needs and many people involved in the trade who visited it (caravaneers, transporters, messengers) did not have houses of their own. They had to be helped by others, possibly their employers or associates or simply merchants engaged “catering services”, who provided the food and drinks they needed.
label: gold

text: um-ma a-šùr-ma-lik ù ša-lim-a-šur a-na ša-lim-a-šur qí-bi-ma la-ma a-šur-ša-du-e i-li-kà-ma lá-ma ṭup-pí-kà ub-lá-ni ITU.2.KAM-ma šu-be-lúm i pá-ni a-šur-ša-du-e i-li-kam-ma šu-be-lúm šu-ku-ba-am DUMU a-šur-be-el-a-wa-tim ù a-ḫi-šu iṣ-ba-at-ma a-na a-lim{ki} ir-de₈-šu-nu-ma ù né-nu a-wa-tám nu-ta-er-ma um-ma né-nu-ma a-wa-tù-šu-nu gám-ra a-na ša ni-iš a-lim{ki} i-tù-a-ar a-lúm{ki} dí-nam i-dí-in-ma šu-be-lúm ù DUMU.MÍ i-sú-rik₁₃ a-na šu-ku-bi-im ù a-ḫi-šu lá i-tù-ru šu-ku-bu-um a-na kà-ni-iš i-lá-ak-ma i-tur₄-DINGIR ù ku-a-tí a-na šu-be-lim ú-kà-an ki-ma lu-qú-tám ip-qí-da-ku-nu-tí-ni ša a-na gám-ra-tim a-na ša ni-iš a-lim{ki} i-tù-ra-ku-ni ta-lá-kam-ma a-dí MU.1.ŠÈ a-wa-tám a-na É a-bi-kà ta-da-an SAG ITU.1.KAM be-el-tí-É.GAL-lim li-mu-um e-lá-lí DUMU i-ku-nim a-pu-tum ṭup-pí-kà ší-bi-kà da-a-a-ni-kà ga-me-er a-wa-tí-kà ša a-na a-lim{ki} i-lá-kà-ni li-li-kam ša lá i-lá-kà-ni ša-sí-ḫa-am ṭup-p | From Aššur-malik and Šalim-Aššur to Šalim-Aššur: Before Aššur-šadue came and before he brought your letter, Šu-Bēlum came - two months before Aššur-šadue - and Šu-Bēlum seized Šu-Kūbum son of Aššur-bēl-awātim and his brother, and led them to the City assembly, and then it was us who rebuffed the matter and said: Their case is closed. He is reopening a matter which has been sworn by the City." The City assembly passed a verdict that Šu-Bēlum and Issu-arik's daughter must not raise claim against Šu-Kūbum and his brother. Šu-Kūbum will go to Kanesh to confirm Itūr-ilī and you to Šu-Bēlum, (namely) that he entrusted the merchandise to you (plur.). Since he raised claim against you for everything that had been sworn by the City, you are to come and within 1 year you are to open the case for your paternal house. Beginning of the month Bēlat-ekallim, eponymy Elāli son of Ikūnum. Urgent, as to your tablets, your witnesses, your judges and those who settled your case - let he who will go to the City come here, extradite the one who will not go - confirm your tablets and your witnesses, come and open the case for your paternal house! If you have not come, they will take 4 talents of tin and 100 on your account. The tablets blelonging to him with his witnesses have been placed before the City assembly and they have entered the City Hall and are in the City Hall. He holds a certified tablet sealed by the king, stating that you are to come within 1 year and that you must answer his case. Since the matter was concluded 2 months ago, we heard the tablets that Aššur-šadue son of Tu'imum brought, and we made enquiries but we will not go back to the City assembly. Kuziziya brought 10 minas of silver; hinnaya brought 10 minas of silver and 20 minas of silver has been deducted from your debt. Then later Šu-Bēlum came and Šu-Bēlum said to hinnaya: "I entrusted 20 minas of sealed silver to you." hinnaya without those who know did not confer with us, but said: "Yes, you did entrust it to me. I shall ask, and if they did not bring it I shall buy it in a merchant-house and pay you." Šu-Bēlum said: "The 10 minas of silver that Kuziziya brought, are available." hinnaya gave in in the matter and borrowed 10 minas of silver from a merchant-house and paid, and hinnaya got a certified tablet stating that it will be deducted from your debt. In all, 30 minas of silver will be deducted from your debt. Send the silver to hinnaya so the interest will not hurt you. In the matter concerning Aššur-bāni ... he turned to the City assembly and said: "A bribe!" Had you been present would they (not) have treated his word like chaff? For the statement you made, namely: "Let the City judge my case!" - you are to pay 1 mina 10 shekels of silver. As he claimed that it was a bribe, but did not prove it against you, if you had come, would he (not) be dead? We borrowed 1 mina 10 shekels of silver against interest and paid. Send silver. Urgent, do not act superior in this matter! Come and clear your paternal house. What can your investors do for you? You have no answer for them except saying: "I have been extradited." You do not consider your losses. You do not seek your god's face. Urgent, when you have heard the letter, secure your tablets and your witnesses, set out and come! In the sacred precinct you have been accused five times already! Are you not ashamed? How long are you going to wait?"

Urgent, set out and come since you have heard a letter with falsehoods.

Thereof Šu-Nūnu earlier brought you 6 talents; Šalim-wardī and Šu-Nūnu bring you 8 talents of washed copper under our seals. 18 minas good copper we paid as the transport tariff on your copper and your donkeys; 1 mina per talent was lost during the breaking up; 2.5 minas of good copper we deposited out of your copper and gave to Ab-šalim for the carriage of Ab-šalim's and Dan-Aššur's copper. We did not give them anything for expenses and food. Your copper ... The rest of your copper ... I shall credit to you. Šalim-wardī 30 minas of good copper ... to us ... we checked They said: 3001 talents 10 minas of your copper ... Šalim-Ištar ..."

Šu-Laban, Ilī- ... 2.3333 minas of silver ..."
